\opage{1}

\unnumhead{INTRODUCTION.}

The task that I have undertaken to solve in this book presents
special difficulties. In all fields of science and of practical life there are ideas that, with greater or lesser
consciousness, guide the work and characterize its nature and direction.
Hence the characterization of the century that
ended twenty years ago is also divided among a series of authors, each of whom
is a specialist in his own field. What, then, can remain
for the one who is to write about leading ideas for the century
as a whole? Can ideas be pointed out in which all
those special fields of thought meet, or can it be shown that
the life of thought, as it has moved in the various fields, presents
to a retrospective view a common stamp, so that the characterization of the whole
century is given with this common stamp?

My task must be to seek an answer to these questions through
a comparison between the ideas that in the course of the century
asserted themselves in science, in social life and in religion, the three
most important fields in which human thought can test its
strength. My earlier studies mean that I do not stand wholly unprepared
before this task, and I have not waited for the other authors'
accounts, each in his own field. The way I go is that I set up
a hypothesis about what is characteristic of the century, and
then try to show the justification of this hypothesis partly through
an examination of the principal ideas that gather attention
about themselves, partly through a comparison between the intellectual work of this century
and that of the preceding centuries. It is not given in advance
that the lines of thought that can be traced in the various fields,
--- in the various sciences and in the various practical
endeavors, --- must point in one and the same direction, so that they
% --- p. 2 ---
\opage{2}can be gathered under common formulas. The life of thought of a century
cannot without more ado be conceived as running along a single line,
whether a curve or a straight line. The subjects that are thought about may
be so different that the ideas that are to master them must
take shape in highly different ways. In one and the same personality different
directions of thought can assert themselves without harmony
becoming possible. And directions of thought that seemed to have been displaced once
and for all can crop up again under more or less new forms and
come into conflict with the new directions into which the striving life of thought
has turned. This will happen not least where an age in its
joy over its new ideas believes it can conclude for good and all,
forgetting Goethe's word of wisdom that there can only be talk of rounding off,
never of conclusion, and overlooking that the rounding off itself
will as a rule have an individual character, so that it is not universally valid.


If a common type can be pointed out, more or fewer traits of character
that can rightly be said to be peculiar to the
nineteenth century, then this presupposes a mutual connection
between the directions of thought in the various fields, in any
case a certain analogy between them. As already indicated, science,
social life and religion will be the most important fields
for our investigation.

I shall at once present, in the form of a hypothesis, the general conception
of the intellectual peculiarity of the nineteenth century
to which my studies have led me.

The boundary between centuries cannot, where the leading
ideas are concerned, simply be drawn by the almanac. A characterization
of the leading ideas of the 17th century must begin with the last
decades of the 16th century, for the germs of these ideas lay
in Kepler's and Galileo's first works and in Giordano Bruno's philosophy.
A characterization of the leading ideas of the 18th century must begin
with Newton's physics and with the ideas that Locke and Leibniz developed
in the last decades of the preceding century. And a
characterization of the 19th century must begin by pointing
to the significant striving that in a series of great spirits
--- Rousseau, Lessing, Herder, Kant and Goethe --- stirs to get
beyond the limitation in which the 18th century, with all its greatness,
was caught. Since the end of the Middle Ages men had worked on
confidently in enthusiasm over the great outlook that the Renaissance had
opened. A new intellectual world was built up in opposition to the scholasticism of the
% --- p. 3 ---
\opage{3}Middle Ages, founded on authority. And the most important, or supposedly most important, results of the new intellectual work were
then in the 18th century made accessible to larger circles and constituted
the spiritual content of the so-called educated classes. One was
proud of what one had attained and looked with contempt or pity
upon the ignorance and superstition of earlier times and of the great mass.
The circle of men mentioned saw, each in his own way, that there were
questions that had not been answered. They asked quite particularly how
the new abundance of knowledge and the new critique were to be reconciled with
the collected energy, the concentration, which life cannot do without,
and which had been so easy to attain as long as instinct and
authority ruled and kept all divisedness away. By posing this
problem and protesting against the Enlightenment's claim to possess
the only true culture they point forward to the new century,
and from a very essential side the intellectual work of the latter consists in a continuation
and carrying through of their great ideas. A fundamental
originality cannot be ascribed to the 19th century, unless
one is willing to count that circle of men as belonging to it.

In the field of natural science too we must go back in
time in order to understand the new century. In the midst of the strong movements of the Enlightenment
and the Revolution, French inquirers in particular,
men such as Lavoisier, Laplace, Bichat, labored to carry through
the natural-scientific conception that had been founded in the 16th and 17th
centuries. And here too the 19th century stands as a continuation
and furtherance, not as founding, however essential
a trait natural-scientific work is in its intellectual
physiognomy. It is through progressive specialization and, in connection
therewith, through confirmation by experience of the fundamental ideas for exact inquiry
pronounced at the beginning of modern times, that the natural-scientific inquiry
of the 19th century gets its great significance. Ever new
regions are drawn under the treatment of thought in order to find new, often
more special and often unforeseen applications of the fundamental viewpoints.
And the great unfolding of technology, which in the eyes of many
is the most characteristic thing about the age, is to be regarded only as a
single side of the great work of carrying through and confirmation.
Ideas are tested through practical application as well as through
experiment and calculation.

The Enlightenment and the Revolution in their way also set tasks
for the following century. The principle of freedom was asserted as that
which was to be leading in all spiritual, social and political
% --- p. 4 ---
\opage{4}fields. But this principle stood as an ideal demand that was first to be
applied and carried through in the particular case. And as in the field of science
so too in the field of social life it is the greatness of the 19th
century that what hitherto had been asserted only as
general principles and in limited application was now recognized and
in part carried through in reality.

The same trait will be found in what might be called the thoughts of life,
that is, the ideas that form men's refuge
amid the conflicts of life and in the face of life's riddles, and which are not
accessible to strict grounding, since they move on the borders of scientific
experience. Here it has in the course of the century been impressed upon us,
often with genial energy, that in whatever direction the faith one
holds to may go, the mark of its value is nevertheless first
and foremost that it has its root in the personality's own soil and own
striving. A new religion or confession has not been founded in the
19th century. But in this field too the confirmation by experience that is possible
has been demanded, namely personal trustworthiness.

In this connection historical critique must also be emphasized
as characteristic of the century. Closely connected with personal
trustworthiness is the honest investigation of the traditions
one holds to. It is a counterpart to natural science's striving
for confirmation by experience of its ideas and hypotheses. Historical
investigations play on the whole so great a role that one can
rightly call the 19th century the historical century. ---

The hypothesis that I set up is thus that the peculiarity
of the 19th century consists in being an age of carrying through and
confirmation by experience. It has not forgotten the great ideas that were pronounced
three hundred years ago; they lie consciously or unconsciously in the background;
but the real work aims at carrying through in
the particular case. Through an examination of the special fields of
the life of thought, --- science, social life and religion, --- this
characterization is to be confirmed. ---

The conception of the 19th century that is pronounced in the hints now given,
and which is in this book to be more closely grounded,
I have already set forth in a speech that I delivered at the University in my
last lecture hour in the 19th century (Dec. 19, 1900),
and which was published the following year under the title ``Ved Aarhundredskiftet''.

In several respects I side with the viewpoints that Eugen
% --- p. 5 ---
\opage{5}Dühring, my older contemporary, had asserted. Above all I must
concede him right in his claim of the fundamental
significance of the 17th century as far as modern science is concerned. But Dühring
was inconsistent in that, though a positivist, he did not ascribe sufficient significance
to the confirmation by experience that the great ideas can win;
for him, with his feeling for the great beginnings, for the
genial creation of the new, carrying through and the demonstration by experience
(verification) receded as subordinate. And he becomes
unjust to the century whose son he is when he quite
predominantly conceives it as a great reactionary period directed against the 18th century. It stands before him in its entirety as a relapse;
only in the technical field can he see progress.
He overlooks, I believe, that the strict demand itself for confirmation by experience
for all ideas leads to critique of all tradition and of all
faith in authority and thereby makes possible progress which the mere proclamation
of great ideas and outlooks would not have been able to bring.
The following presentation will, it is to be hoped, establish this, both
in the scientific, the social and the religious field.

A later author, Theodor Merz (History of European Thought
in the 19th Century), gives a characterization of the departed century
that goes in the same direction as Dühring's and mine. Yet
he places its significance especially in the accumulation (accumulating) of
knowledge that it has brought about; on the other hand it is said to stand far behind other centuries
in capacity for concentration
(condensing) and to be able to measure itself neither with the Periclean age, with the
Italian Renaissance, nor with the 17th century. It seems
to me that Merz is unjust to the 19th century in characterizing
it as accumulating, and in laying the main stress thereon. To heap
up is not the same as to seek confirmation by experience. In the most eminent
spirits it is precisely interest in the great ideas coming
into their own that makes them strive to show that they
in every case approximately find confirmation in experience. The work
is done --- in the very century of realism --- in the name of ideas.

% --- p. 6 ---
\parthead{I. SCIENCE.}
\chapterhead{1.}{ROMANTICISM.}

\opage{6}German Romanticism thought it could open the century with a
new concept of science. It was prepared by German humanism
at the end of the 18th century, --- by Lessing and Herder,
Kant and Goethe, --- and is at bottom a translation of the latter's
ideas into speculative form. The confidence that something new was about to break
through led to the belief that the concept of science too had to be
renewed, and this belief found expression in the demand that all science
should be grounded on a single principle, a fundamental idea, which was to
prove itself in all particular ideas, in all phenomena of nature and in all
historical processes of development. The 18th century, it was thought,
had hollowed itself out by critique and analysis; now it was a matter of letting the
human spirit's need for unity and coherence be fully
satisfied. Not as if it were merely intellectual satisfaction
that was sought. One was convinced that in the principle that lay at the foundation
of all science a key was given to the innermost
essence of existence itself. Does not nature's kernel lie in man's heart?
--- one asked with Goethe. Like Goethe's Faust one was not content
merely to work in the particular fields of knowledge, but sought
an idea that could disclose what holds the world together in its
innermost. And here --- it was thought --- the difference between
thinking, religion and poetry would in the end have to fall away. Only this difference remained,
that in religion and poetry the pictorial plays a greater role
than in science; but this does not prevent them from being, in their way, just like
science, organs of the deep unity that stirs in everything.
Not by taking reason captive, as orthodoxy does, nor by
confronting, as rationalism does, the religious conceptions with a prosaic understanding
could the highest be reached, but only by seeking back, in enthusiastic
devotion, to the source from which thought, faith and
art in the end spring.

The word ``romantic'' was used at the end of the 17th century in
England of what made a foreign, strong and lively impression
and stood to what moves in clear, familiar and limited
forms as romances stand to daily life. It
% --- p. 7 ---
\opage{7}is used of free, wild nature, of the Alps, of the English gardens
as opposed to the strict French art of gardening. From England the
word came to France and was established above all through the enthusiasm for wild nature
awakened by Rousseau. In Germany it was
transferred from external nature to art, to the free movement of the imagination,
which nevertheless contains an intimation of a deeper connection than
sober everyday understanding and critical science knew. And this
word we now rightly use of the new concept of science that
was attempted to be asserted in Germany at the beginning of the new century.
Just as a romantic region or a romantic poem seems to
burst the accustomed frames of apprehension and understanding, yet
lets a unity be sensed in the background, so it was the endeavor of the Romantic
philosophers to take up the whole rich fullness of existence into their
thought and yet to show the origin of this fullness from a single principle.
The external division between existence's various regions was to
fall away, and one idea to shine through everything. Both manifoldness
and unity were to come into their own quite differently from
how it had happened in the past.

The history of the Romantic systems is not to be presented anew here,
nor criticized again. What interests us here is that these
directions of thought sprang from a need for immersion in nature and in
history, for getting beyond the external opposition between
thought and its subjects. Through full devotion a fuller
understanding was to be reached. It is to that extent a craving for reality that here expresses
itself; things were to come into their full rights by becoming
content of thought, not merely objects of thought. When, despite the often
obscure and abstract form that the Romantic systematizers give their
presentations, one works one's way into their train of thought, one sees that
it was really their earnest purpose to let the subjects be fully satisfied, but that they
were at the same time convinced that this could only be done by converting
them into determinations of thought. For only of that which one has completely
converted into one's own thoughts can one be really convinced. This
intimate mutual interpenetration was the ideal of Romanticism. Applied
to religion, the consequence is that one can only be convinced of
the existence of God when he does not stand as a thing, an object,
a subject-matter, but as that which works in all our thinking and acting.
--- This view Fichte developed in one of the last years
of the 18th century. (Zweite Einleitung in die Wissenschaftslehre.
1797). In a very energetic way Fichte later (Grundzüge des
% --- p. 8 ---
\opage{8}gegenwärtigen Zeitalters. 1805) expressed himself about the opposition in which
he and his fellows felt themselves to stand to the train of thought of the 18th century.
The ``present age'' is, namely, the 18th century, in so far as
its train of thought, in spite of the almanac, still ruled. Fichte reproaches
it with having detached itself not merely from faith in authority, but also
from the whole involuntary, instinctive foundation of life, that in
which the germs of a high and noble life are found. It is the age of empty freedom.
One trusts in the concepts one has once formed
for oneself, sees in them the sum of all wisdom, while one looks with contempt
upon earlier times as sheer darkness. Yet it is not merely in the field of thinking
that the fault lies; it goes back to the whole character.
The fundamental fault is an egoistic individualism, which has arisen from
one's having lost all interest in and all sense for what has eternal and universal
value, the age has, Fichte thinks, made it the highest
that has value only as an intermediate stage, namely liberation from
external authority.
In this train of thought in Fichte there appears an idea that we shall often
meet in what follows. Enlightenment and freedom he regards as conditions
for a higher development of the spiritual life, in particular for thorough science
and for ideal development of character. Science is for Fichte
not the highest. On the basis of scientific knowledge there ought
to develop an instinct of reason, an immediate need and capacity to
live in the Eternal and Universal. He looks forward to a time when men
through the labor of will and thought are able to let such a
life rule in them. He hopes for a new religious breakthrough.
As the Reformers brought the renewal that their time needed,
``so too in our time, when it has got beyond the
many kinds of errors by which it has been tossed about, enthusiastic
men will arise who will satisfy this need.''

Schelling felt that Fichte's train of thought needed a supplement.
For in Fichte there was talk merely of human thinking and acting,
not of nature, which really stood only as something subordinate.
But we must find again in nature the same forces, the same
need for unity, that shows itself in our thinking and acting. And the different
forces of nature and forms of nature can then only be different
manifestations of a unity, the same unity that makes itself known in
the spirit of man. Schelling interprets nature from spirit. ``Since the
ground of all activity is a single one, which is omnipresent
and not conditioned by any other ground, the different natural
% --- p. 9 ---
\opage{9}activities can only be different with respect to form, and none
of these forms can be understood from any of the other forms,
since each in its kind is the same as the other. Not in this,
that one phenomenon is dependent on another, but in this, that all phenomena
spring from a common ground, does the unity of nature consist.'' (Methode
der akademischen Studium. 1803). --- Here the ``new''
concept of science stands clearly forth. For the concept of science that was
founded in the 17th century aimed precisely at finding the causal relation
among the particular phenomena themselves, at ordering them in
series, within which the place of every phenomenon is determined according to
a law. Now, on the other hand, --- in Romanticism --- it is asserted to be true
science to derive all phenomena from a single principle. Schelling
in his presumption even rejects the science of the preceding age
as a great misunderstanding. Boyle and Newton have --- he says
--- corrupted physics. He rejects entirely the mechanical conception of nature,
which seeks to trace all material changes back to motions
in space. But the conception of nature that he wished to put in its place
became really an interpretation from above downward; nature was to be understood
from man. The ``deduction'' that Schelling wished to carry out became in
reality a symbolizing; he also declares straight out that
nature, as we know it from experience, is a symbol, and that
the particular things are copies of ideas that appear in another form in
the human spirit. This leads rather to poetry than to philosophy.
The Romantic urge for knowledge could now once and for all find an outlet only
in that way. Characteristic is Schelling's reference to Goethe's
Faust (which at that time existed only in its first form, as a fragment):
``To the inner strife that springs from unsatisfied craving
for knowledge of things the poet has pointed in the poem
peculiar to the Germans and has thereby opened an eternally fresh source of enthusiasm,
which would in and by itself be sufficient to rejuvenate the
science of our time and spread the spirit of a new life over it. Whoever wishes to
penetrate into the sanctuary of nature, let him draw nourishment from these
tones from higher regions and imbibe in his youth the power
that, as in dense rays of lightning, goes forth from this poem and sets the
innermost of the world in motion.'' --- But for the long journey Faust
had to undertake in order to reach fulfillment, Romanticism was too impatient.
It demanded the Highest as something immediately present, wanted to
behold it in the Omnipresent and could not wait in endurance
for what faithful labor could bring to light.

% --- p. 10 ---
\opage{10}Hegel began as Schelling's collaborator, but later came
into sharp opposition to him, because he found his procedure
too schematic. It is not enough to proclaim a unity for all oppositions
and then schematically to arrange the particular phenomena as
members of the various relations of opposition. It must be shown how
the various members lead over to one another with inner necessity,
and thereby come to stand as ``moments in a higher unity,''
a more comprehensive whole. Ordinary consciousness, which
also lies at the foundation of the special sciences, gives its concepts
an external, mechanical independence that is untenable for a deeper
view. A concept is determined through its relation to other concepts,
and through this reciprocal relation the unity of the world of thought
reveals itself. What Hegel called the dialectical method consists in this,
that the analysis of the single concept leads over to another concept
that cannot be separated from it, and thereby to a higher concept in
which both the first concepts are moments. According to Hegel it is existence
itself that forces us to think in this way and to give up
the external difference between thoughts. ``Scientific knowledge,''
he says (Phänomenologie des Geistes. 1807), ``demands that
one give oneself up to the life of the object, or, what is the same thing,
have the inner necessity before one and pronounce it.'' The facts
on which Hegel relies are partly the lawlike connection
in the world generally, which shows that things are not independent of one another,
partly in particular the way in which in nature and history
contrasts lead over to one another. His ``Dialectic'' is from an essential
side a theory of contrast effects, a doctrine of catastrophes. Through
perishing, which is transition to an opposite state, the
particular thing or event proves that it is a moment in a larger whole.
Truth is not something single, something sundered from other things, but
a great totality, in which everything particular enters in order to get its place in
a definite connection. And in the law of totality, which conditions
the essence, subsistence and working of the particular things, thought finds again its
own law.

If it were said to this that modern natural science, which
in its first, founding period had set up as its principle
to trace all qualities back to quantities and to that extent to make all
science mathematics, had thereby already made it possible for
thought to find itself again in reality, since the laws of mathematics
are the laws of thinking itself, then Hegel would not be satisfied
thereby. For, he says, mathematics operates with pure identities;
% --- p. 11 ---
\opage{11}in its equations the differences of things do not come into their
own, since the qualitative oppositions cannot be derived from them. Only
by the dialectical method can both identities and differences
come into their own, since the differences take their definite
place within the higher unity, the comprehensive totality, whose
identity asserts itself in the connection between them. --- Hegel
here undoubtedly touches a real problem. For it is one thing that the laws of nature
can be formulated as equations, another that the special
phenomena in their qualitative peculiarity should be derivable
from these equations. Between the mathematical equations and the
qualitative changes whose laws they express there is only analogy,
not identity. But Hegel did not see that the very totality of thought,
the ``higher unity,'' to which his method was to lead, rests on analogy,
--- namely on the analogy between the connection of concepts in our
thought and the factual relations of things in experience. As Schiller has
put it: ``Leicht bei einander wohnen die Gedanken, doch hart
im Raume stossen sich die Sachen.'' And in order to carry through his method
in the particular case Hegel was compelled, through a play with analogies, to
construct the series of ever higher unities that makes up his
system. In his philosophy of nature the arbitrariness of this play appears still
more strongly than in Schelling.

To designate the way in which all things and events,
just as well as all thoughts, lead over to one another and thereby prove
their connection within a great totality, Hegel often uses
the expression ``development.'' But this word is not to be taken in the sense
of a factual transition, running in time, from one form to
another. The assumption of such a transition, which later came
forward in the modern doctrine of evolution, but which in Hegel's time was
espoused only by a few, Hegel expressly rejected. ``Nature,'' says
he (Encyclopädie der philosophischen Wissenschaften. 1817), ``is to be
regarded as a system of stages, the one stage necessarily springing
from the other and expressing its real truth, --- yet
not to be understood as if the one stage were produced in a natural way
by the other, but in the inner thought, which is the ground of nature.
Only thought can have a metamorphosis, for all development is a change
in thought ..... It has been an unsuitable notion in
older and newer philosophy of nature to regard the transformation and transition
from one form or sphere in nature to another as an external,
% print: Protektion (misprint: Hegel has Produktion)
actual production.'' --- Like Schelling and Steffens, and like
Goethe (in Metamorphosen der Pflanzen und der Thiere), Hegel
% --- p. 12 ---
\opage{12}admittedly assumed a logical, systematic transition from a concept of one natural phenomenon
to the concept of another natural phenomenon, but not in such a way that
the different phenomena themselves were members of a series, running in time,
of predecessors and successors. The transitions take place, on the Romantic
conception, so to speak in nature's creative imagination, not in the
actual nature, given in experience, itself. It would therefore be
wrong without more ado to conceive the Romantic conception of nature as
a forerunner of modern evolutionism.

In a similar way as it goes in Hegel's philosophy with the concept of
development, so it goes also with the concept of religion. The definite, historically
formed religious conceptions stood for Hegel as symbolic
expressions of ideas to which philosophy by its own road had come.
The difference between religion and philosophy is supposed to be merely this,
that what in philosophy appears in the form of the concept, that makes itself
felt for religious consciousness in the form of the image; the content
is supposed to be the same. In a later section I shall return to this
point; here I touch on it merely as a characterization of Hegel's philosophy.

What guided the thinkers of Romanticism was an inward and full-of-character
conviction that the innermost essence of existence is akin
to what stirs in the human spirit, and therefore must be
capable of being grasped by it, since the laws are the same. It was an impatient
idealism, which in reaction to the Realism of the 17th century
and the critique of the 18th century put forward the demand that the human spirit
should immediately --- without mechanical laws as intermediary and
without considerate analysis as preparation --- find again its own
essence in the forms of nature and in the events of nature. The differences
and oppositions that nature and history presented were to stand as
stages, by which the spirit --- that is, the human spirit in its unity
with the world-spirit --- attains full clarity about itself.
What for special inquiry and for sound human understanding
stands as an obscure background was now to be brought forward in its whole
fullness. It was a great ideal, for whose carrying through the age was now thought
to have come. To use an image that Hegel himself employs:
philosophical idealism thought itself related to special science,
to sound human understanding and to religious faith as the open hand
is related to the clenched one; what for ordinary consciousness
lies folded together as in a wrapping, that is unfolded in philosophy to
full consciousness! ---
In the Romantic philosophy's conception of the state, as it is
presented in one of Hegel's most considerable and most significant writings,
% --- p. 13 ---
\opage{13}``Grundlinien der Philosophie des Rechts'' (1821), there appears at
once the craving to immerse oneself in reality, in what factually exists,
and the tendency to convert reality into the forms of thought
and ideals. To find reason in reality was for Hegel the
same as to make reality one with reason. In the preface to the
work mentioned Hegel pronounces the much discussed principle that what
is rational is also real, and that what is real is also
rational. He saw in the state a fruit of a great historical course of development,
which with right could be called God's march through the world.
It is not the opinions and resolutions of individuals that support
the state and determine its laws. It is conversely the value of individuals,
as well as their rights and their duties, that rests on their
participation in the life of the state and their significance for it. The state endures,
but individuals perish, and their self-conceit, their supposed
``Besserwissen'' means nothing in relation to the eternal reason
that is expressed in the state and its institutions. The state is the
true spiritual totality, within which all spiritual life finds its
place, as well as all economic life.

By this conception Romanticism came to work as a foundation
for a reaction, which cared more that the Real should be recognized
as rational than that the Rational should be recognized as that
which was to be realized. The Romantic school met here the
so-called historical school of law, according to which right has sprung
from the life of the people and from its history, is not the work of single individuals,
nor sprung from speculation, and which therefore warns against
all conscious interference, indeed is apprehensive of any systematization
or codification of the involuntarily developed right. To be sure
the historical school of law admitted that the historically given right had to
be developed further, and Hegel himself admitted that the forms and
laws of the state have come to be ``not without'' (nicht ohne) the
knowledge and will of the single individuals. But it was nevertheless in both directions an entirely
subordinate, vanishing position that was assigned to the experiences
and deliberations of individuals. And in both places one was inclined to
wrong the individuals in advance when their conviction came
into conflict with the existing order of things. The conservative way of thinking
begins in both places by demanding recognition and piety
toward the historically developed, but in its practical carrying through
comes to end as cult of mere power, of that which has once
and for all won the victory. Power sets right as the norm for the exercise of power
in the particular case; but this right of power can inhibit the
% --- p. 14 ---
\opage{14}power of right, that is, prevent new ideas of right from becoming known and recognized.


Romanticism and conservatism thus easily passed over into one another. To be sure
the Romantic as a rule began as a free thinker, often with titanic
presumption. But his interest in a venerable past, the flexibility of his
thought and the capacity of his imagination to see reality in an ideal light
had to lead him to live himself into what exists, whose justification
his speculation was thought to have proved. All critique, especially in the
religious and the social field, now came to stand as an overcome
standpoint. ---

The Romantic direction in thinking was bound, by the nature of the case,
to find assailants from three sides. Philosophical critique had to
rise against the demand for conclusion that the systems thought to
have satisfied. The greatest and best in the thought of the 18th century
was not overcome, even if for a time it was flooded over by
the Romantic stream. The sense for problems and the interest in investigating
the presuppositions of knowledge held on as an undercurrent
throughout the Romantic period and came by the middle of the century
again up into the full light of day. Furthermore the real sciences
found themselves by no means sufficiently represented within the higher
unity that Romanticism proclaimed, and they too came forward by the middle of
the century with ideas and with results that demanded recognition
from the side of philosophical reflection. Finally, religious
consciousness was unable to rest content with the speculative philosophy of religion,
which wanted to hold fast the dogmas of the existing Church,
but made this ``reality'' rational through symbolic interpretation.
In so far as religious consciousness seriously held fast the dogmas,
it would not have them reinterpreted, and in so far as it went its
own road of free development, it would not build its conceptions on
dogmas, but on life itself and its experiences.

Before we go more closely into the three directions here indicated,
we must bring forward another circle of philosophical ideas, which worked
their way forward at the beginning of the new century.

\chapterhead{2.}{POSITIVISM.}

The so-called positivist direction in philosophy is no less
characteristic of the 19th century than the Romantic direction.
Common to both directions is a craving to immerse oneself in the whole fullness
of existence, a craving that in both places was felt in marked opposition
% --- p. 15 ---
\opage{15}to the 18th century's critical attitude toward everything that lay before it
as given and as historically handed down. One did not think that everything
was attained by formulating certain abstract principles, but demanded
that the content of existence should come into its own through the work of thought.


In time too the two directions appear approximately simultaneously, only
in different countries, Romanticism in Germany, positivism in France.
It is a frequent misunderstanding that positivism is supposed to be due to
a reaction against Romantic philosophy. But both directions appear
at the beginning of the century, Saint-Simon simultaneously with
Fichte and Schelling, Comte with Hegel, and there is a certain analogy between
the appearance of these men in different camps. The misunderstanding arises
from the fact that positivism came to assert itself in larger
circles especially after the middle of the century, when the Romantic direction had
played out its role, while Stuart Mill and Herbert Spencer asserted
new viewpoints within the positivist direction.

St. Simon and Comte admired the Middle Ages, like the Romantics.
It stood for them as a time when great common ideas in
inward faith dominated life and the conception of life in all circles. It
was what the St. Simonists called an organic period. In opposition
to it the Enlightenment stood as a critical period that essentially
had a negative and dissolving significance. What now mattered was,
according to the positivist thinkers, to pave the way for a new condition in
which life is again lived wholly and fully, without dissolving critique, and in which
there is a positive and common foundation for life and conception of life.
These are ideas related to those Fichte asserted
in ``Grundzüge des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters''.

The opposition between the two directions comes forward in the question
of how a new content is to be won. Romanticism sought
world-embracing ideas, which were to be won either through a contemplation full of presentiment,
as with Schelling, or, as with Hegel, through a
dialectic that at once followed the laws of thought and of existence itself.
By both roads one was assured of reaching immersion in that which
Goethe's Faust sought, --- ``that which holds the world together in its
innermost.'' Such roads St. Simon and Comte could not follow. St.
Simon (Introduction aux travaux scientifiques du 19. siecle. 1807)
pointed to the great work that natural science had done,
not least in the last generation, --- Laplace's, Lavoisier's and
Bichat's works. The viewpoints that lay at the foundation of these works
he demanded also applied to the nature and position of man
% --- p. 16 ---
\opage{16}in the universe; then the foundation would be given for a positive philosophy,
through which a new world-view, grounded on experience and common to all,
would be possible. What St. Simon hinted at, Comte
carried further in the remarkable work he published while he was still
St. Simon's disciple (Plan des travaux nécessaires pour réorganiser
la société. 1822). A new social system, it is said here, cannot
be constructed at once, but must develop successively. The
old society rested on a theological foundation, which cannot suffice
under the new conditions. Mere enlightenment and critique (which
Comte is accustomed to call ``metaphysics'') has only negative significance. A
new foundation can be found only in the positive sciences, that is, those building
on facts. There is, Comte maintains, always a
close connection between the ordering of society at a given time
on the one side, and the development of science and industry on the other
side. What Comte here pronounced, he spent his life carrying out.

The word ``positive'' is used by the positivists especially to designate two things.
It designates an opposition to the supposedly dissolving, negative
character of the thinking of the 18th century, and it designates at the same time
what is factually given, in opposition to what speculation
might think up. Positive philosophy, however, does not build immediately
on facts, it builds on the work done by the single, special sciences
to show and interpret the facts.
The task of philosophers becomes here first to order the sciences in
a definite way, thus to give a classification of them. At the foundation
of this classification are laid two viewpoints, which prove to lead
to the same result. The one viewpoint is taken from the historical
development of the sciences. This development presents three stages, --- a
theological, where the interpretation is found in the intervention of supernatural beings,
--- a metaphysical, where certain general ideas or
forces are presupposed, --- and a positive, where each single fact is interpreted according to
its relation to other facts. It now proves that the various
sciences pass through these stages with different speed,
and in the classification those are then placed first that first have reached the
positive stage. The other viewpoint is taken from the sciences'
mutual relations of dependence. There are some sciences that form
necessary presuppositions for other sciences, and in the classification
those are then placed first without which the others could not
be understood. Both viewpoints lead to forming the following series: Mathematics,
Astronomy, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Sociology. When sociology
(the theory of society and cultural history) is placed last, it is partly because
% --- p. 17 ---
\opage{17}it is the newest positive science (Comte regards himself as its
real founder), partly because it presupposes all the other
sciences, since the theory of man and of human society
treats the most composite of all phenomena.

Although the following sciences in the series presuppose the preceding,
they cannot nevertheless be derived from these. Each single member in the series
brings something new, which is not contained in the preceding members. Positivism
stresses e.g. very strongly that biology cannot be derived
from physics and chemistry. The various sciences, and with them the various
fields of experience, stand according to Comte very independently
over against one another, and the principles of the one cannot without more ado be transferred
and applied to the other. In the 17th century, the first period of modern
natural science, a decided tendency asserted
itself in the direction of making all science mathematics. That was connected
with the application of the deductive method. But a comparison
between the various sciences shows that the richer
and more special a field of experience is, the less can its problems
be solved by the deductive way, but demand inductive methods applied.
Biology and sociology assert their independence and displace mathematics
from the leading place in science. By this view
the way of thinking of the 18th century, which believed it could
remold life according to certain general principles, is corrected.

Also within every single science positivism stresses differences
that cannot be reduced. Thus in physics the various
forces of nature (heat, light, electricity etc.) stand as independent
over against one another. The various branches of physics cannot be reduced
to a unity. Within biology the various organic
species stand as independent types, which cannot be explained as having arisen
from common basic forms. Positivism thus lays great weight
on discontinuity and thereby becomes a doctrine of manifoldness, while
Romanticism by its tendency to seek a unity in everything became
a doctrine of unity. The opposition between the two directions comes
forward here from a new side. Comte says of this at the end of his chief work
(Cours de Philosophie Positive. 1830---1842): ``Instead of blindly
attempting to reduce all phenomena to a single series of laws
and thereby asserting an unfruitful scientific unity, --- a chimera
that inhibits thinking, --- the human spirit will
end by regarding the various classes of phenomena as
subject each to its special laws, which nevertheless unavoidably point in the
same direction and present certain analogies.''

% --- p. 18 ---
\opage{18}What could be attained by understanding the scientific work
and the mutual relations of the various sciences was, according to
Comte, the great thing, that the methods and results of science would no
longer stand as indifferent specialties, but become determining
for men's faith and conduct of life. Also in earlier times
the knowledge and understanding that had been won exerted its
influence on faith and conduct of life. But this influence was exerted
predominantly involuntarily and unconsciously. Now, on the other hand, the time has come
when the influence can be exerted with full consciousness. Positive science
cannot answer all questions that can arise in men's
minds, but the conviction that science is the only road to
grounded knowledge will gradually lead to such questions
falling away, since one will no longer feel a need to pose
them. Quite involuntarily one will cease to demand answers and to pose
questions that no longer fit into the whole way of thinking that
has become the prevailing one. When one nowadays does not believe in Apollo
and Diana, it is not because the real existence of these deities has
been scientifically refuted, but because one no longer feels
the need that led to holding fast their existence. The decisive thing
in such cases is the influence of scientific work on
the whole involuntary spiritual life. By this road there will gradually
come a unity and harmony in the spiritual life such as not even
the Middle Ages has parallels to,

This conviction, that the final decision of men's faith
rests on the disposition that forms itself involuntarily under the influence
of the knowledge that can be won, led Comte, in the
struggle that the Catholics in France (especially under Louis Philippe's reign)
waged for freedom of teaching in opposition to the state universities' monopoly
of giving higher instruction, to place himself decidedly on their side.
He wished a direct debate between Catholicism and positivism,
without the interference of unclear intermediate forms such as Gallicanism, Protestantism
and Deism, and he had no doubt on whose side
victory would finally be won.

Comte's own religion was a cult of humanity, ``the great
being,'' in which we all have a share, and which comprises all the beings who
have worked for progress and happiness. Toward the preservation
and perfecting of humanity all thoughts and actions are to be directed.


% --- p. 19 ---
\chapterheadii{3.}{ROMANTICISM AND POSITIVISM IN COMMUNITY AND}{CONFLICT}

\opage{19}In Romanticism and positivism great tasks were set for thought in the first
half of the century. In both directions a consciousness asserted itself of the difference between the new century
and its predecessors. The common task, which was thought to be solved
by highly different roads, was the overcoming of the oppositions with
which the former centuries had struggled. A new, ``organic''
period was to come, in opposition to the ``critical'' period that
had lasted ever since the end of the Middle Ages. The theory of the opposition
between organic and critical periods was in general
characteristic of the first half of the 19th century. It has its
origin in ideas in Rousseau and Lessing, which were carried further by
Kant and Fichte. It was now presented most clearly by the St. Simonists,
especially by Bazard (Doctrine de St. Simon. 1829). It asserts itself
in Hegel, when, after naive security has been replaced by reflection
and critique, he demands a higher unity, in which both the preceding
stages come into their own, in that a new security, won through
purgatory, is gained. Likewise it appears in Comte, when
the positive stage is to let both theology and critique (metaphysics)
come into their own. Both Romanticism and positivism look forward to a
spiritual condition in which inquiry and critique had completed their
work in such a way that immediate faith and devotion can again
come to rule, though under other forms than before. Yet
they did not really think that that time was distant. The essential foundation
had been provided. It was only a matter of becoming conscious of what
the spiritual development had led to. Here too Goethe could give
a motto: The world of spirits is not closed; it is mind and heart that
are lacking! It is only a matter of grasping what already lies near,
--- of reflecting on what treasure one has come into possession of
in the course of the ages.

What was not seen, but what the further course of the century was to
prove, was that the opposition between organic and critical periods
again and again repeats itself, even if it happens under new presuppositions
and in new forms. Every ``higher unity'' that is really
won is itself a foundation on which new oppositions can assert
themselves and demand new harmonization. And Comte's ``positive
stage'' gives rise to new problems, since the foundation of experience on which
it rests can always be changed and extended. An ``organic''
% --- p. 20 ---
\opage{20}condition can only be a provisional resting position, an equilibrium that can
and must be removed if life is not to stand still. The education of humanity
is not completed once and for all. That was the lesson that experience
was to impress in the course of the century, and that not merely
in the scientific field. In face of philosophical systematization
it was the task of natural science and the human sciences to bring
this instruction. But before we pass on to bring forward their contribution
to the characterization of the century, we must first bring forward the memory
of a man who at the middle of the century stood as the most
esteemed philosophical thinker, and in whose inner life Romanticism and positivism
were refracted in a peculiar and instructive way.

John Stuart Mill is an example that it was not easy to overcome
an opposition such as that between Romanticism and positivism. In
his development, moreover, the after-effects of the thought of the 18th century were refracted
against the new directions of the 19th. In
his Autobiography, which is one of the most remarkable books of the 19th century,
he has described these refractions. He could neither systematize
in Hegel's nor in Comte's way, but the motives that
lay behind these attempts at system he knew from his own experience, and they
both stood in peculiar opposition to the direction in which his
energetic father, James Mill, a pronounced representative of the Age of
Enlightenment, had wished to lead him. Through a supposedly
strictly rational education the young Mill was accustomed to look upon
everything in the light of the understanding and to harbor distrust of everything involuntary, of all
feeling and imagination. The result was a violent crisis in his youth.
Life lost its value for him, and he groped in darkness. He speaks
later in a letter of
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``the petrification which was wrought by a narrow way of thinking,
in which one felt quite sure of everything that
concerned truth, only that one did not see how many-sided truth
is.'' A Romantic life of mood broke forth and demanded satisfaction
--- and yet he could not and would not give up what he had
learned. And he wished to unite the Romantic conception with the strict
method of positivism, the claims of personal life with honest inquiry,
the manifoldness and many-sidedness of life with a walk along the
narrow way into which science leads us.
In scientific respect his greatest achievement is his Logic (System
of Logic ratiocinative and inductive, being a connected view
of the principles of evidence and the methods of scientific investigation.
1843). This work, which had for a book of this kind a unique
circulation, shows him as the clear and critical thinker.
% --- p. 21 ---
\opage{21}Yet he was anything but a thinking machine, as Carlyle called
him. One of his close friends, the historian George Grote, said of
him:
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``Yes, he is a logician, but he trembles with emotion right
out to the tips of his fingers.'' For Mill himself this psychological opposition found
its solution in the definite conviction that the greatest
danger for an inward and free spiritual life lay in the assumption that moral,
religious and social truths could be established merely
from immediate feeling or intuition. If this assumption were right,
it would be impossible to root out prejudices and illusions. No, all
knowledge must be built on definite experiences, and all spiritual
states, even the most inward and exalted, must be capable of being investigated,
as regards their origin, by way of psychological analysis.
In his Autobiography he states:
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``The difference between the two philosophical
schools, the philosophy of experience and the intuitive philosophy, has not merely abstract
significance; it is rich in practical consequences ... The practical
reformer must constantly demand that a change take place in conditions
that are supported by mighty and widespread feelings .... and it is
often an unavoidable part of his argumentation to show the origin of these mighty
feelings.'' Apart from the interest it had in and by itself
for him to investigate the nature, tasks and procedure of human thinking, it was this conviction that led
him to write his famous logical work. Far more sharply than Comte
he investigated the limits of the possibility of scientific grounding.
His work received precisely thereby its limitation; it shows how
truths are grounded and confirmed, but not how they are discovered.
But within this limitation he presented the scientific
methods with such mastery that an astronomer such as
Herschel, a chemist such as Liebig, and a physicist such as Helmholtz declared
that they had derived great benefit from his work.

The limit of grounding Mill finds in the end in involuntary
association, by which an idea that occurs together with
another can call up the latter afterwards. There is here, as
the last foundation of all thinking, a purely factual connection that
only observation can show, --- which is a condition of inference, but
cannot itself be grounded by logical means. The attempt Mill thus makes
to show that at the foundation of all rational thinking there lies something that
is not rational, namely a blind but factual transition between two
ideas each independent in itself, forms the complete
counterpart to Hegel's attempt to show that every thought with inner
necessity leads over to other thoughts. In this sharp
% --- p. 22 ---
\opage{22}opposition the treatment of the problem of knowledge in the first half of the century
ends. While on the Continent, especially in Germany, one was
sure that Kant (and Hegel) had solved Hume's problem, Mill's
Logic led to this problem's being posed anew. English and German
philosophy again stepped up against each other.

\chapterhead{4.}{NATURAL SCIENCE}

A Danish philosopher has said that what philosophy was for the aristocratic
antiquity, and what theology was for the hierarchical Middle Ages,
that physics is for the bourgeois present. This much is also
true, that in no age has natural science yet played so great
a role for men's life of thought as well as for their practical
life as in the 19th century. To what high degree men in general
have appropriated a natural-scientific way of thinking is another
question. The situation is probably rather that it is particular more
or less sensational discoveries or inventions that lay
claim to interest. It is the new that awakens wonder
and admiration. One forgets that already the old and familiar was
wonderful enough. Many fell into an ecstasy of wonder over wireless telegraphy
as a great marvel and forgot that already the
electric telegraph had been a riddle for their intelligence. It
is the results that impress. The roads, the methods, the presuppositions
are accessible to few. It was not otherwise, either,
in times when philosophy or theology held the great word. The grounding
was then too accessible only to a few; most took only the
catchwords or dogmas that they could --- or were to --- use. The
Romantic philosophy and positivism were likewise in their innermost
kernel accessible only to philosophers by profession. But the general
idealistic fundamental idea, that the innermost ground of existence is akin
to what stirs in men's spiritual life, made in a more
or less indefinite form an impression on many. And the fundamental idea of positivism,
that all conception of the world and of life should be built
on experience, became of significance for many who could not
enter into Comte's philosophy. Romanticism and positivism denote two
spiritual directions, which can be traced also in those who do not know what
philosophy is. Within so-called sound human understanding as well
as within the special sciences each for itself this opposition can be
traced, especially in so far as it appears as an opposition
between a doctrine of unity and a doctrine of manifoldness.

% --- p. 23 ---
\opage{23}It is, as indicated, especially through technology, which is its offspring,
that natural science intervenes in human life. Most
people have more interest in inventions than in discoveries,
and the most grateful thoughts that are sent to science
are called forth by the utility that is experienced. And thousands of people
enjoy the inventions without thinking of the spiritual work
without which they would not come to be. Yet inventions can become an occasion
for natural-scientific thinking to be awakened in larger circles,
since already the use of tools and machines makes it necessary that
definite rules be followed and definite procedures applied. One
thereby gets an impression of a lawlike connection that cannot
be broken, and interest can thereby be awakened in pursuing this
connection further. Already from the very beginning of modern natural science
this influence of practice on theory asserted itself.
Thus Galileo emphasizes at the beginning of his ``Discorsi''
how the collections of instruments and machines that
Venice commanded ``present to thinkers a great field for
research, especially in the fields of mechanics.'' What can thus
become of significance for the greatest spirits also exerts to a certain degree its
influence on the many. And on this point the justification of
physics's being conceived as characteristic of ``the bourgeois
present'' proves itself especially. It was the burgher class that, already from the Middle Ages
on, entered upon the path of industry and was thereby led to take inventions
into its service. From strict science, which is only
the concern of the few, we come through polytechnic institutions, which
give both theory and practice, to technical schools and technological institutes,
where intelligent workers are trained in independent understanding and
application of the inventions to which science has led. Through
practice thought thus clears its way out into life.

Less weight must be laid on popular presentations of the results of natural science,
though these too can awaken reflection
and make the general viewpoints that rule in science accessible
to larger circles. There are many whose whole philosophy consists
in what they have been able to appropriate through such presentations.
Popular-scientific writings of this kind became especially numerous at
the middle of the century, when the hopes that many had cherished
of speculative philosophy and theology burst, and when --- as we shall see in what follows
--- natural science at the same time presented a great upswing,
especially through the connection that could be shown between
the various forces of nature and forms of nature.

% --- p. 24 ---
\opage{24}It would be wrong to think that natural science as such
stands in absolute opposition to philosophy, because it stands in opposition
to the speculative or Romantic spiritual direction, which in
many circles ruled in the first part of the century. There was also
in the Romantic period a critical and empirical direction in philosophy;
for Germany, men such as Fries
and Beneke may be mentioned here. This direction was quite able to give natural science
what was due to it, and itself made use of natural-scientific
viewpoints. And furthermore natural science itself works with
presuppositions and viewpoints which it is one of the tasks of philosophy
to investigate with regard to their grounding and their origin.
In the last part of the century there also arises, as we shall
see, a new philosophical movement, which takes up the old problems
in a more critical way.

While Romanticism overvalued the unity in world-view
that can be scientifically grounded, positivism was inclined to
undervalue it. The former wanted by the way of thought to go beyond all possible experience;
the latter halted at the difference between the various fields
of experience and between the subjects within each single field.
Natural science, as it developed in the course of the
19th century, can be said to have led to a limitation of the Romantic
viewpoints and to an extension of the positivist. It impresses
upon speculation that we have no sure knowledge beyond the limits
of experience, and upon positivism that we cannot once and for
all establish unshakable limits within experience. It asserts
the fullness and manifoldness of existence against the Romantic
wallowing in higher unities, and it shows against positivism that
by the very way of experience a greater and greater connection can be shown
between the various fields and subjects, however independent
these may for the time being seem to stand over against one another.

The natural science of the 19th century stood in more continuous
connection with the preceding century than the two philosophical
directions mentioned above. Here again must especially be emphasized the
magnificent period that French natural science had at the end of the
18th century. In general, by the nature of the case, there will not occur
such great oscillations in the field of natural science as
in that of philosophy. After its foundation had once been laid, it developed
step by step. The foundation was, as already
mentioned, laid about the year 1600. All later natural science, also that of the 19th
century, is carrying through and special application of Kepler's,
% --- p. 25 ---
\opage{25}Galileo's and Descartes's great ideas. Oscillations may come,
especially in the field of hypotheses, and hasty ``discoveries'' may come;
but on the whole there is here a solid foundation for progress
in thought, which again and again --- especially when the results become
striking for ordinary consciousness --- intervenes in a mood-setting
and perhaps determining way in men's thoughts about life and existence.
Often this influence occurs without being noticed, so that it
becomes clear only after a longer time what change has
occurred in the general way of thinking. And very often the change
that has occurred stands in a purely external relation to the direction in
which human mental life otherwise unfolds. Only through
energetic work of thought, whether this is exercised involuntarily or with
consciousness of aim and means, can harmony be attained between
the viewpoints of science and the other longings and strivings of mental life.
There will always be problems that natural science by its nature
cannot take up, in any case not for the time being. Already in
the task that modern natural science has set itself from the first start,
a limit is given for its influence on men's
faith. This task is that of converting all content of experience into quantitative
forms, or, as it has been expressed, ``to describe things
in all respects with numbers.'' But if there are experiences, lived experiences,
whose value rests on their quality, whatever may be the case
with their number or their quantity, then there lie here problems
that will constantly set thought in motion, and in whose treatment
natural science has only indirect significance. And of that
kind are the most important experiences that can be had in the field of spiritual life.
To this kind of problems and their appearance in the 19th century
we shall return later. Here we shall keep to natural science
in itself as one of the greatest testimonies to the power
and genius of the human spirit and try to bring forward the leading
ideas within it in the 19th century. No single author,
especially when he is not himself a natural scientist, will be able to give a presentation
of this on his own. On certain points he may perhaps
have source studies, but otherwise he must orient himself by means of
monographs or by works on the history of natural science.

When the question is of leading ideas in the field of natural science
in the 19th century, there is hardly any doubt that
there are two ideas that gather interest about themselves, in that they at once
denote results and new points of departure, and in that they moreover
are not only of the greatest significance for science itself, but
% --- p. 26 ---
\opage{26}also will naturally intervene in a determining way in men's whole conception of life.
These are the doctrine of the conservation of energy and the hypothesis of the
successive origin of species in interaction with the conditions of life.
It is with these two ideas that the following presentation will be concerned.

\sectionhead{a.}{The Conservation of Energy.}

The great ideas that in the preceding centuries had come forward
in the field of natural science were applied in the 19th century
to a whole series of particular fields, so that they thereby
got their progressive confirmation, while at the same time a
wholly new and great connection of nature revealed itself.

Chemistry had been made by Lavoisier into an exact (quantitative)
science, in that by his weighing experiments he had found confirmation
of the old principle, stemming from antiquity, of the conservation of matter
in the world under all dissolutions and compositions. A
scientific foundation had thus been laid for the idea of the cycle of matter
in the world, this thought which in the time of the Renaissance was pronounced by Montaigne
and Bruno, and on which Shakespeare's Hamlet makes moving
reflections. French and English natural scientists, men
such as Saussure and Priestley, carried the idea further through the application of chemistry
to the physiology of nutrition. In the new century
Dalton's application of the atomic theory to chemistry (1805) brought greater exactness
in. The conservation of matter now meant the conservation of parts by weight.
The atomic theory, which hitherto had had a qualitative character, now got a
quantitative character, in that it was shown that the chemical combinations
take place according to the relative weight of the elements.

Chemistry moreover acquired, about the middle of the century, cosmic
significance, in that spectral analysis, which investigates the refractions of light of the various substances,
made it possible, through investigations of the light of the stars,
to discover what substances they consist of, a discovery that
--- after Newton and Laplace had shown the validity of the law of gravity
for the heavenly bodies --- gave a new proof that the same laws of nature
that hold here on the earth hold in the whole world accessible to us.
Even Auguste Comte and Alexander v. Humboldt thought that the heavenly bodies
could only be the object of determination of position and
gravitational mechanics. Now it was revealed that they also had other
properties, which were known from earthly phenomena. The foundation was
laid for a developmental history of the stars similar to that of the earth's
developmental history on which geology was working.

% --- p. 27 ---
\opage{27}In physics a connection was shown between forces of nature
that had hitherto been regarded as independent of one another.
On this point Romanticism was proved right against positivism. It was
undoubtedly under the influence of Schellingian ideas that H. C. Ørsted
was led to the discovery of the influence of the electric current on the magnetic needle.
Thereby the theory of electromagnetism was founded, which in
a brilliant way was carried further by Ampère and Faraday.

Toward the middle of the century a still closer connection between the various forces of nature
was shown in the principle of the conservation of energy. The physician Robert Mayer was led by physiological
investigations to the thought that there existed an exact
relation between motion and heat. (Bemerkungen über die
Kräfte der unbelebten Natur. 1842.) When a motion ceases, the
energy that has found its expression in it does not become nothing, but
is converted into heat in a definite ratio, which Mayer, with the imperfect
means that stood at his disposal, sought to determine. And
the heat thus produced can in turn (in part) be converted into motion.
Mayer was led to his great thought by the conjecture that
there must hold in physics a law corresponding to the conservation of matter
in chemistry, so that every change was only conversion into
another form. Just as little as the single substance in chemical change
disappears without replacement, just as little could, he thought, a
force of nature cease to act without replacement in the form of another force of nature.
Cause and effect must correspond completely to each other.
What Mayer, whom Ernst Mach has called ``a modern Galilean nature
free from all influence of schools,'' put forward in a brilliant but still indefinite
way, was asserted independently of him and by different roads
by the Englishman Joule, the Dane Colding and the German Helmholtz,
--- a testimony that here was a leading idea that lay in the air.
And yet all four authors had difficulty in getting their
works printed and met on the whole doubt and lack of understanding.
This must have seemed to themselves all the more strange,
as they were all convinced that the principle they asserted
was a principle of reason and as such self-evident. They all proceeded, like
Mayer, from the view that there must be an inner relation between cause
and effect, as between ground and consequent; as that which is
contained in the premises comes again in the conclusion in another
form, so they thought that what was contained in the cause had to
come again in the effect in another form. The correctness of this line of thought,
which without more ado makes the relation between cause and effect
% --- p. 28 ---
\opage{28}into one with the relation between ground and consequent, will not be discussed here.
But for a historical consideration it is of great interest to see that
the discovery of the conservation of energy was a continuation and confirmation by experience
of a principle that had already been put forward in the seventeenth century.
Descartes put forward a law of the conservation of motion,
according to which no motion came to nothing and no motion arose
from nothing; there was always the same sum of motion
in the universe, only it was distributed in different ways. Leibniz criticized
this doctrine, maintaining that according to it every transition
from motion to rest and from rest to motion within the universe
would be incomprehensible. There is, he further maintains, no absolute
opposition between rest and motion; rest is arrested motion,
due to an equilibrium between forces (tendencies), and motion
is released anew as soon as the equilibrium is removed. It is thus not motion
but its possibility, ``force'', that is conserved, and while there
is not always the same sum of motion in the universe, there is the
same quantity of ``force'' (energy, in the modern expression). Leibniz
laid such great weight on this principle that he even called it
the foundation of all the laws of nature (fundamentum naturæ legum). In
the natural science of the following period, this principle receded for various reasons,
although it has again and again been at work as
a tacit presupposition. When it now came forward again, it was not as
a proposition of pure mechanics, but as a principle asserting
a definite ratio of conversion between the various special forces of
nature (motion, heat, light, electricity, etc.), and it was
now carried through by experimental investigations. It now stands as
a law for all material manifestations of force. --- Nowhere is it
so clear as here that the science of the nineteenth century, in all its
greatness, consists after all in carrying through ideas that stem from
the remarkable time when modern science was founded.

It has been said of the principle of the conservation of energy that it
is only a generalization from a limited experience. It is also
true that a confirmation by experience of a principle such as this can in a certain
sense never be concluded. One will never be able to isolate and
close off a part of the world in such a way that every supply or removal
of energy would be absolutely excluded. And there always remains the
possibility that the principle holds only for the part or parts
of the world that we have so far been able to investigate. And since ``the world'' can never
come to lie before us as a whole concluded once and for all,
it is an infinite task that is set for research here. But the
% --- p. 29 ---
\opage{29}principle of the conservation of energy here only shares the fate of all the
propositions to which research into actual nature can lead. The
concept ``world'' in the sense of absolute totality has the scientific
significance that it shows us the possibility of ever new tasks
as the horizon widens. And it marks a significant
progress that the principle put forward in the seventeenth century has now
proved accessible to progressive confirmation by experience. Like
every great hypothesis, the principle supplies an important maxim for
research, namely, always to look for new forms of energy as
equivalents for those that disappeared, and to look for the preceding
forms of energy from which the new ones have arisen. Maxwell has
particularly emphasized the epistemological significance of the principle
of the conservation of energy, that it leads us, at every new
natural phenomenon, to put definite questions. This is indeed the significance
of all living principles in science, and this significance
cannot be overstated.

The principle says that in every material change there is only a conversion
of energy, without any energy being lost; but it
says nothing about the direction in which the conversions take place, and
in particular nothing about whether a conversion in the opposite direction can always as
easily take place. A French inquirer had, as early as eighteen years before
Mayer's treatise, put forward a principle that throws light on this matter.
Sadi Carnot (Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu. 1824)
showed that, for heat to be a motive force, there
must be a difference of temperature. Motion is produced only
when such a difference arises between the states of the bodies
between which the action is to take place. But since temperature
always tends toward equilibrium, heat passing over from warmer
to colder bodies and thereby being distributed, the possibility
of a new conversion of heat into motion thereby falls away within
the same circle of bodies, considered as a closed whole.

Carnot's principle, too, holds only for a limited world. And
if by ``the world'' one understands a limited whole, there prevails in
it a process that leads in the direction of a complete equilibrium, a
state in which no new release of energy is possible.

Carnot's principle, which, like Mayer's, had to wait long for
full recognition, does not conflict with the principle of the conservation of
energy. For in the state of equilibrium that there is a constant tendency to bring
about, no energy has been lost; only, all energy has passed over from
being actual to being potential.

% --- p. 30 ---
\opage{30}An optimistic philosophy of nature will hold to Mayer's principle, a
pessimistic one to Carnot's. But both principles hold only for a
limited horizon, and since natural science always seeks to widen
its horizon, the discussion of which standpoint is the decisive
one will always have to be taken up anew.

--- A still more intimate connection between the various forces of
nature than that which follows from the principle of the conservation of energy
was shown when it was established that forces of nature which had so far stood as
different in kind follow the same laws and must therefore be assumed to be
of the same nature. Thus Melloni and other inquirers showed that
light and heat were one. H. C. Ørsted had already divined a connection
between light and electricity, conceiving the lightning flash as
a series of electric sparks. And after Maxwell had by a mathematical route
put forward the electromagnetic theory of light, according to which light
can be traced back to electricity, the laws of these two activities
being the same, Hertz showed experimentally that light and electricity,
as regards wave motion, velocity, refraction, etc.,
present the same relations. Optics could now be regarded as an appendix
to the theory of electricity.

On the whole, the confirmation by experience that the principle
of the conservation of matter and force gained in the nineteenth century
is far from having brought the scientific conception of the world to
a conclusion. It was in itself a magnificent picture of the world that was unrolled.
The world came to stand as a whole within which constant
conversions of matter and force took place, without any matter or force at all
arising or perishing. As we have already seen, this picture of
the world cannot be concluded, since the widening of the horizon can always
bring new possibilities. But on another side too, in the very foundation,
research goes beyond the picture of the world just indicated. The
development of the theory of electricity has led to this: that far down beneath the
matters and forces of earlier science a new and rich world comes
into view, in which perhaps the real foundation of the world of matter
and force in which we move is to be sought. The theory of electricity
has led to the discovery of minute particles, so-called electrons, which are
smaller than Dalton's atoms and of which these must be thought to be
composed. The change in the scientific conception that was thereby
heralded at the end of the century is described in the following
way by a Danish physicist. ``In the last half of the century
the theory of electricity has pressed forward so strongly at the expense of the other
forces of nature that it seems about to swallow them
% --- p. 31 ---
\opage{31}all. One is now inclined in advance to refer not only
optics but also the other forces of nature to it; electricity
alone is so manifold in its forms of manifestation that it can be thought
capable of comprising them all. Even the very concept of mass can be
dispensed with, if the atoms are thought of as charged with electricity, since
in that case every acceleration must produce induction in the surroundings,
and thereby in turn a resistance to the motion. The dissolving power of
the theory of electricity has extended to chemistry as well, to which
physical chemistry bears witness. Even the old concept of the atom
is in danger of collapsing. Thus J. J. Thomson and
Zeemann have believed they could demonstrate masses a thousand times lighter
than the chemists' atoms'' (C. Christiansen: ``Før og nu'', first
volume of Tidsskrift for Fysik. 1908).

There thus opens up, at the end of the century, the prospect of
an entirely new physics, which goes further back than the one founded by Galilei and Newton
and will derive the maxims of the old physics from still
deeper-lying principles. From the world of the great masses one has
% translated from Høffding's Danish
begun to descend to the world of the small elements. ``The time,'' says
an American physicist, ``seems not to be distant when there will be
room for a new `Principia' and for a work that will accomplish for the
