molecular systems what the `Mécanique Céliste' accomplished for the solar
system.'' (Woodward: The Unity of Physical Science. Congress of
Arts and Sciences St. Louis 1904).

If it is asked what it is, then, that moves according to the laws of electricity
and under special conditions appears as light, heat,
etc., the natural scientist answers with the beautiful name ether. But
the ether is known only through its special forms of manifestation, among
which electricity is regarded as the fundamental one. The famous
French physicist Langevin declares that it is impossible to give a picture,
a representation, of the ether, since its properties are entirely different
from those of matter and probably far simpler than these.
And he thinks that the difficulty we face here perhaps
hangs together with the present constitution of human consciousness:
for centuries we have been used to thinking by means
of the concept of matter, and are therefore unable to form a
concrete representation that does not have a material content. The ether
can be thought only by means of the concepts of the electromagnetic
properties we ascribe to it (Langevin: Congress of Arts and
Sciences. 1904).

Plato already saw that a thoroughgoing atomic theory cannot be built
% --- p. 32 ---
\opage{32}up by means of the ordinary concept of matter, cannot be grounded in
sensuous representations, but must make use of analogy. The result
he reached by a critical thinking-through of Democritus's atomic
theory, modern physics has now reached by its own route. ---

For no science have greater possibilities and tasks shown themselves at the beginning
of the twentieth century than for physics. But
what has already been won --- the progressive carrying through and
confirmation of the great ideas that three hundred years ago led
to the rise of a ``new science'' --- is a great achievement, which will be of
incalculable significance for the human conception of existence,
once its scope really dawns on consciousness.
Both in the great and in the small, in the world of the heavenly bodies and in that of the
imperceptible elements, a greater connection has shown itself
than one could have divined.
\sectionhead{b.}{The Doctrine of Evolution.}

The science of organic life could not remain untouched
by the great movement stirring in the physical and chemical
domain. Ever since the first rise of modern natural science, one had
sought to bring the doctrine of life under the general laws of
nature as physics demonstrates them. The principle that all change
is motion, one sought to maintain not only in the domain of inorganic
but also in that of organic nature. Descartes
insisted emphatically that organisms were only mechanisms,
set going according to the general laws of motion, and he
held that Harvey's discovery of the circulation of the blood confirmed this
view, which became the prevailing one in the seventeenth century. As a
reaction against this mechanical view there appeared the so-called
vitalism, which maintained that organic phenomena could find
their explanation only if one assumed a peculiar life force, independent of all physical and
chemical forces. Vitalism reached its most pronounced form
in the medical school of Montpellier in the eighteenth century.
The ``life force'' directs the physical and chemical processes in the organism in
definite directions, brings about a connection among everything that
goes on in the living being, so that it can subsist as a whole,
provides for the formation of the substances that life needs, and for sufficient
strength to overcome the resistance that life meets from without.

The nineteenth century appears here, as on other points,
as a carrying through and specialization of the fundamental ideas of the seventeenth century.
Mechanism and vitalism at bottom designate only two
% --- p. 33 ---
\opage{33}natural tendencies within science. The former seeks to explain
the whole from the laws that hold for its parts; the latter
regards the parts from the standpoint of the whole and as means for its conservation.
When the two tendencies in the history of science rhythmically succeed one another,
it is a consequence of the fact that experience must at one time point in the direction
of the dependence of the whole upon the parts, at another in the opposite direction. And
when the same tendency returns again, it will come in a new
form, conditioned by the experiences gained in the interval, and
the criticism that has been raised from the opposite side. The rhythm thus does
not exclude progress and is by no means to be conceived as an alternation
between two bankruptcies.

Already the eminent French natural scientists of the end of the eighteenth century
had demonstrated the circulation of matter in the world and
with it a constant interaction between inorganic and organic
nature, and in the first decade of the new century chemistry began
to show that substances which one had hitherto believed could be formed only
in organisms could also be produced outside them. But it
was only toward the middle of the century that the strictly scientific
conception of organic life was maintained emphatically
and with full consciousness. In Germany it was Johannes Müller and
his disciples (Ludwig, Helmholtz, Dubois Reymond) who demanded that
all individual phenomena of life be explained through the application of
physical and chemical laws. Johannes Müller is --- like H. C. Ørsted
in the physical domain --- an example of how Romantic
speculation can spur scientific inquiry. For he was a vitalist
and inspired by the ideas of Schelling and Hegel; but he proceeded from the assumption
that the ``life force'' must act according to definite laws of nature, such as
only physics and chemistry know them, and he applied his brilliant
and energetic inquiry to finding these laws. His ``Handbuch
der Physiologie'' (1840) marks a turning point in this respect.

A few years after this work came Robert Mayer's discovery
of the energy principle, which he at once applied to the organic phenomena
(Die organische Bewegung. 1845). Throughout the whole course of the life process
there takes place, he maintains, only a transformation of matter
and force, never a creation of them.
In France they proceeded more directly, the great experimenters
Magendie and Claude Bernard seeking, by means of vivisections, to
demonstrate the conditions under which the organic functions take place.
For the brilliant inquirer Claude Bernard (Introduction à la Médicine
% --- p. 34 ---
\opage{34}expérimentale. 1865. --- Leçons sur les phénomènes de la vie communs
aux animaux et aux végétaux. 1878) it stood as decided that
physiology, whatever subjects it may face, has to do only with physical
and chemical elements.

The great inquirers who in the nineteenth century took up again the mechanical
(physico-chemical) method in physiology by no means proceeded dogmatically
from the assumption that all organic phenomena could ever be explained
purely mechanically. They maintained only that the said method was the
only one that was scientifically possible, and that all real progress
was due to it. They regarded life as a given subject whose connection
and conditions are to be investigated. They acknowledged that no
exhaustive definition has yet been found of what life
is; they do not employ an appeal to the ``life force'' as an explanation,
precisely because one does not know what life really is. Life stands
for them as an irrational quantity, toward which we can only take
the road of finding more and more decimals without being able to reach any
conclusion. When Claude Bernard rejects vitalism, it is because
it does not lead to individual investigations, but stops with an appeal
to the ``life force''; it does not set to work but makes lazy,
it is ``une doctrine paresseuse'', vitalism cannot be the basis of
a working hypothesis, except when it is conceived in the way Johannes
Müller conceived it; but that is in reality to give it up.

When toward the end of the century vitalistic ideas seem again
to assert themselves, this nevertheless does not mean a direct resumption
of genuine vitalism. Neo-vitalism does not hold that
an appeal to a ``life force'' contains any real explanation.
It holds that not all organic phenomena have been explained
by the physical and chemical route, --- that (as Pasteur's investigations
of the simplest organisms in particular have established) the origin of life
from inorganic matter cannot be demonstrated. What authors such as Bergson
(Evolution créatrice. 1907) and Driesch (History and Theory of
Vitalism. 1914) under various designations (élan vital, psychoid)
put forward as supposedly indispensable fundamental concepts in the organic
domain, is rather an expression of wonder at the peculiar nature of organic
life, never fully commensurable with physical and chemical processes, than it is concepts that really play
a positive role in scientific work. They are thoughts that
can be used to ask questions, but that give no answer. ---

This whole consideration concerning the science of life might
very well have found its place in the preceding section. For it is
% --- p. 35 ---
\opage{35}above all the law of the conservation of physical energy under all changes
that makes the physico-chemical method in physiology possible and necessary,
in that for every quantum of energy that seems to disappear in
the organism an equivalent must be sought --- in or outside the organism,
and in that likewise, whenever new energy announces itself in the
organism, the question must be asked what equivalent has corresponded to
it --- in or outside the organism. --- If I have chosen to present
the biological problem as an introduction to the doctrine of evolution, it
is because in both domains it is characteristic of the nineteenth century
that it --- with all acknowledgment of the peculiarity of life
and of the validity of the idea of evolution --- nevertheless holds strictly that
in both respects definite laws hold, which it is the task
of science to find.

When the principle of the conservation of energy was first enunciated and
at once applied to organic life, Charles Darwin was already
absorbed in the long investigations that led him to put forward
his hypothesis of the successive evolution of the species. And in the same year
in which Robert Mayer's treatise on ``the forces of inorganic nature''
appeared, Darwin wrote in all quietness the first draft of his
theory. (The Foundation of the Origin of Species. A sketch written
in 1842. Edited 1909). Already during his voyage round the world
(1831---35) observations and comparisons had laid the foundation of the doctrine of evolution
in his mind.

It was no entirely new hypothesis. Inquirers had often pointed out
that the species could not subsist independently of one another, and that it
was unjustified to ascribe absolute validity to the concept of species. In the seventeenth-century
philosophy there is a decided skepticism toward this concept.
Bruno and Bacon interpreted the Platonic ideas, which were originally
concepts of species, as laws and could acknowledge them only in this
sense. In Spinoza and Leibniz this view emerges still
more strongly. Spinoza explains the origin of concepts of species by the fact that
we lack the ability to comprehend a larger number of phenomena in a
clear and distinct manner, that is, in such a way that the different qualities
show themselves to be connected as ground and consequent. Leibniz
emphasizes above all that no concept of species can exhaust the manifoldness of nature,
and that observation shows us so many transitional forms that
no concept of species can have more than provisional validity. Thus
both from the demand for knowledge of laws and from the experience of
the manifoldness of differences and transitional forms, doubt had been
raised about the validity of the concept of species and about the right to stop
% --- p. 36 ---
\opage{36}at the differences between the species as original. Within
the circle of natural scientists itself the way had to be paved for a conjecture
of the successive evolution of the species, the more one made exact
comparisons between the different organic forms. Two
French natural scientists, Cuvier and Geoffroy St. Hilaire, conducted (about
the year 1830) a noble contest here, the first zealously
seeking to demonstrate differences of form where one had so far found
identity or analogy, the second maintaining that in the whole organic
world one and the same mode of composition prevails (unité
de composition). The dispute concerned (according to Cuvier's account in ``Histoire
des Sciences naturelles'') in part whether within the vertebrates such a
unity of structure can be demonstrated, in part whether it can lead to filling up
the gap that was generally assumed between vertebrates
and mollusks. The dispute led to the finding of new similarities and new differences
and was a dispute about continuity within morphology. Goethe, who
followed this dispute with so great an interest that over it he quite
forgot the July Revolution, sympathized with Geoffroy St. Hilaire, whose
view agreed with Goethe's doctrine of metamorphosis. This whole
dispute stood in the domain of anatomy and morphology; but when
Cuvier here so strongly stressed discontinuity, he was naturally bound
to be in advance an opponent of the idea of a real,
historical evolution of the organic forms out of earlier existing
forms. Inquirers who occupied themselves essentially with anatomy
and morphology and did not enter upon the question of the relation of the forms
to the conditions of life, had no sense for the question of the origin
of the forms (or they answered it by means of theological
or teleological representations). Their view did not become much
different from that of the Romantic philosophers, who, as we have seen, by the very
word ``development'' understood only a transition from thought to thought
(so to speak in the fantasy of nature), not a real transition in time from
one form of existence to another.

Lamarck took in 1809, in his ``Philosophie zoologique'', the significant
step of maintaining a real process of evolution in the organic
world, basing himself precisely on the dependence of the organic forms
upon the organic functions and, through them, upon the conditions
under which organic beings lead their lives. That such a
view did not at first win great adherence was due in part
to the fact that sufficient knowledge of the extinct forms of
life was still lacking. In geology there prevailed Cuvier's theory of a series of upheavals,
``catastrophes'', in the history of the earth, a theory that
% --- p. 37 ---
\opage{37}carried with it the assumption that after each catastrophe a new world of organic species had to be produced,
not descended from the perished species. According to this theory one could still hold fast to
Linné's principle that we assume just as many different species as
God has created, only that one no longer thought of one creation
at the beginning of the world, but of a series of creations, each
introducing a new period of the earth, --- and so that one conceived the
last of these creations as one with the creation that the first book of Moses
speaks of, the one that underlies our present zoology and
botany. Long before, two such different spirits as
Jacob Böhme and Ludvig Holberg had by a similar route sought to unite
their natural history with their theology.

It then became of decisive importance that Lyell in his ``Principles
of Geology'' maintained that the same forces that now bring about changes
on the surface of the earth have also been at work in the past, and that
a continuous transition between the different periods of the earth
can and must therefore be assumed. ``Uniformitarianism'' was now maintained in
opposition to the theory of catastrophes. Darwin's teacher Henslow had
given him Lyell's book to take along on the great voyage, but with the admonition
not to believe what stood in it. This admonition was not
followed; the book worked together with Darwin's own investigations
to lay the foundation of the modern doctrine of evolution. When between
the organic species in different periods of the earth there are found both similarities
and variations in manifold degrees, and when no sudden
upheavals take place that set sharp divisions between the periods of the earth,
there is reason to suppose that to the continuity of the forms and conditions
there corresponds a historical or real continuity between the different
species. It was this thought that Darwin seized and to whose carrying through he set his life's
work.

The first time Darwin disclosed his great thought to one of his scientific
friends, he added that it was like confessing a murder.
(Letter to Hooker. January 1844). This aptly expresses how
strange and unreasonable the thought must have stood to the natural historians of the time,
who were occupied with describing and determining species. Eminent
natural scientists such as Weismann and Huxley, who later became zealous
evolutionists, have described how little foothold the idea of evolution
had in the science in which they were initiated in their
student years. A doctrine of the origin of organic species by
natural evolution was considered fantastic speculation. This state of affairs
forms an interesting parallel to the manner in which the idea
% --- p. 38 ---
\opage{38}of the conservation of energy had been received. In both cases it was a matter of carrying through, by means of observations and experiments, views
that already prevailed in the domain of general ideas.
Just as the conservation of ``force'' was to become the thought of a definite,
experimentally demonstrable relation of equivalence between different physical
processes, so the ``kinship'' of the organic forms was to
become the thought of the successive evolution of the species under the influence of definitely
demonstrable causes. The history of both theories in the nineteenth
century serves to throw light on the intellectual
character of this century in relation to the preceding centuries. Its
significance consists in the patient carrying through of points of view
that had already been put forward earlier. Its great discoveries were made
in the work of winning confirmation by experience for principles
that had long waited for one, and that in this period of waiting perhaps
had fallen into oblivion. Under Newton's mighty influence the
idea of the conservation of force had ``for more than a century disappeared
from physics'' (Rosenberger: Isaac Newton und die physikalischen
Principien. 1895). And Weismann remarks of his student days: ``It
was as if our teachers had drunk of the waters of Lethe and had completely
forgotten that a theory of evolution had ever been discussed.''

What was new in Darwin was, first, the comprehensive collection of
geological, morphological and zoogeographical and phytogeographical facts
on which he relied, and, second, the zeal with which
he sought a definite cause, demonstrable in experience (a
vera causa), that could explain the origin of new species. Lamarck's
assumption of an inner need of development, a need that was to lead the
living beings along new paths through the influence of function upon
structure, did not satisfy him. Such a need was for him
no fact and therefore no scientific cause. He was,
as he had already stated in the above-mentioned letter to Hooker, in agreement
with Lamarck as to the result, but not as to ways and means. His chief merit
is precisely that he posed the problem more strictly than it
had been posed before; indeed, he posed it so strictly that he could not even
satisfy it himself, much as he believed in the
hypothesis he put forward. The cause to which he pointed lay in a
fact that already in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries had been
impressed by English inquirers (Hobbes and Malthus), namely the
conflict and struggle between living beings that arises from the need
for self-preservation and reproduction, in that need and capacity are not
the same in all, nor the command of external means. In the
% --- p. 39 ---
\opage{39}struggle to subsist and to spread in existence, Darwin holds, those
individuals and species have the best prospect of subsisting whose need and
capacity fit best the conditions of life as these actually are. Such
individuals and species will then form the foundation of the future evolution of life,
while those that do not fit the conditions of life will perish.
Moreover Darwin assumed, like Lamarck, that characteristics
acquired by exercise or external influence will be preserved
in the succeeding generations.

Darwin's book on the evolution of species (1859) aroused, besides much
indignation, great enthusiasm in many circles. Insufficient heed was paid
to the reservations Darwin had made, and the
new doctrine was proclaimed as a solution of all riddles. It was
even often regarded as an inconsistency that he did not maintain the original
origin of life from inorganic matter. It was forgotten that, shortly after
the appearance of Darwin's book, Pasteur (1860) had shown that even
the lowest organisms known arise from germs and not, as
many had believed, from inorganic substances. It was like a dizziness
that seized inquirers and laymen alike. The only one who did not become
dizzy was Darwin himself. As has rightly been said:
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``The empty enthusiasm shown by Darwin's followers became so wild that
Darwin himself, the most modest of all men, felt quite
ashamed of it.'' --- Max Müller, in whose autobiography this statement
occurs, compares the Darwinian intoxication with that which
some decades before was aroused by Hegelian philosophy, and he
mentions yet a third immature enthusiasm in a third domain, namely
the enthusiasm over Sanskrit studies, which, in the opinion of many, and for
a time of Müller's own as well, solved all problems of the origin of language,
thought and religion. --- Such times of intoxication are
perhaps unavoidable when significant thoughts break through.
Critical reflection comes afterward.

--- Darwin's lasting merit with respect to the conception of nature is first and foremost
that, by the way in which he presented his
hypothesis, he stimulated new investigations. He conceived his doctrine as
a thread of thought that could connect facts from different
domains (geology, paleontology, comparative anatomy and
physiology). His doctrine was for him not a dogma, but a means
of casting light on nature. And he was clear that it could not be directly
proved. He says accordingly in a letter about one of his critics:
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``He is one of the very few who see that the change of species cannot be directly
proved, and that my doctrine will go under or maintain itself, according as
% --- p. 40 ---
\opage{40}it is able to group and explain the phenomena.'' The fruitfulness
of his points of view is also acknowledged even by opponents. The hypothesis of evolution stands, after his energetic appearance,
constantly as a background for all scientific biologists, and although
Darwin's own explanation of evolution did not suffice, he has yet
the merit of having drawn attention to the finding of
a cause that itself appears in experience and is not merely speculated out.
In the treatment of this problem, after Darwin's time, the experiment
more and more takes the place of the merely comparative method, which Darwin
was at the outset compelled to employ.

The criticism of the new doctrine came from three sides. --- Weismann showed
that there was no real evidence from experience for the assumption
that acquired characteristics could be inherited. The weight that
Darwin, here following Lamarck, laid on this direct form
of adaptation to the conditions of life had therefore to fall away. It
has not been possible to demonstrate that the functions that the conditions of life require
bring about changes in the structure of the organs, which are then inherited by
the descendants. Against Herbert Spencer, who grounded a hope of
the progress of the race on the heredity of acquired characteristics,
Weismann maintained his standpoint in an interesting polemic. --- Weismann
was led by this rejection of direct adaptation to
lay so much the greater weight on the indirect adaptation that
takes place in the struggle for existence, in that only those individuals and
species subsist whose organs and functions fit the conditions of life
(The All-Sufficiency of Natural Selection, a reply to Herbert Spencer.
1893): But Hugo de Vries (Die Mutationstheorie. 1901) showed
that, for variations to be able to become of significance in the
struggle for existence, they must be so far-reaching that a new
species has already come into being by their origin. Small variations
(in de Vries's expression ``fluctuations'') play no role. It is otherwise
with large and suddenly appearing variations
(``mutations''). And in face of these species-forming variations (whose
causes, according to de Vries, have not yet been found) the struggle for
existence plays only the role of eliminating the nonviable types; it
acts as a sieve. But it does not at all explain how viable
and nonviable types arise in the first place. Darwin himself
had, moreover, constantly acknowledged that the causes of the small but constant
variations on which he relied were unknown. --- Finally, long
overlooked investigations by Mendel (Versuche über
Pflanzenhybriden. 1866. 1870) established that the individual, elementary
% --- p. 41 ---
\opage{41}characteristics appear each by itself quite independently in inheritance, that
they can occur together in all possible combinations, --- and that,
once they exist, they persist tenaciously and without change
in the succession of generations. --- Nature has thus proved to be both
more conservative and more given to leaps than Darwin supposed. The riddles
have proved to lie further back, both as regards the heredity of the characteristics
and as regards their first origin.

From a more general point of view, where it is not a matter of contending
for or against a special hypothesis, it nevertheless stands as significant
that Darwin opened our eyes to the manifoldness of
variations. It made nature richer in possibilities for him,
although in his systematic works it stood as an obstacle to
the ordering into delimited species. It points out toward life beyond the limits
of the system. There is constantly a tendency in men to stop
at hastily formed general concepts, instead of recognizing
--- and seeking out --- the great individual differences within the
groups or species we form for the sake of overview. Both in the
spiritual and the material domain an eye for the manifoldness of life
is of great importance, and Darwin, who by many was regarded as a materialist,
has here contributed much to the understanding and appreciation of
spiritual life.

And of no less importance is his insistence that even the forms of life
most glorious in our eyes must satisfy definite conditions
in order to subsist and act. In face of much false idealism
his emphasis on the struggle for existence has been a word in
season, although this struggle could not play, in the service of his theory,
the role that he had intended for it. ---

The idea of evolution was not applied merely to the organic domain.
Already in the eighteenth century it had been applied in
Kant's and Laplace's hypothesis of the origin of solar and stellar systems.
Resting on what spectral analysis and telescopic investigations have
established, astrophysics too has now set up a doctrine of evolution.
The great sidereal evolution presents a series of stages:
nebulae, self-luminous stars (``suns'', arisen through a condensation
brought about by gravitation), dark stars (which perhaps
present conditions for organic life). In face of sidereal evolution
one stands in most cases as in face of organic
evolution: the real cause of the variations is enigmatic.
% --- p. 42 ---
\sectionhead{c.}{Popularization.}

\opage{42}It is a magnificent continuation that the natural science of the nineteenth century
has given of the work on a comprehensive and internally coherent
picture of the world that the preceding centuries
had begun. One traces more and more a great connection between
all forces and between all forms, a deep unity in the great
manifoldness. Since the great turning point that marks the time from
Copernicus to Newton, such a widening of the horizon,
both outward and inward, had not taken place. And this new widening
took place by virtue of the same principles that lay at the foundation of the
science of the two preceding centuries. Of particular significance it became
that thought now, through the greater practice and by means of the
new instruments, could follow the ways of nature with greater suppleness, both
where they lead down into the infinitely small and where they lead up into the
infinitely great. And further, a scientific technology has developed
that earlier times did not know. Finally there is in
scientific circles an increasing clarity as to how great and high
the ideal of knowledge is, and that we are always only on the way in the direction
of it. There still prevails, to be sure, among a number of natural scientists a certain
dogmatism, which expresses itself either in their believing existence to be exhaustively
explained by the fundamental concepts with which the science of the material
side of existence works, and which are assumed to be the
only possible ones, --- or else shows itself in the haste with which one
calls upon supernatural causes merely because no natural causes
could so far be found. But there can --- in connection with the
role that epistemological points of view, as we shall later see, have
played in philosophy toward the end of the century --- generally be traced a deeper understanding of the presuppositions
and range of knowledge.

Such an understanding one can naturally expect to find only in
scientific circles. As already indicated earlier, there are two ways
in which science influences wider circles that stand outside
the strict scientific work. The one way goes through the practical
application of science in the various technical domains,
the other way goes through popular presentations of the results of science.

It is probably technology that gives natural science its greatest
prestige outwardly. Even those who do not know what method is, and who also
cannot assess the significance of the individual discoveries, are seized
% --- p. 43 ---
\opage{43}with great admiration, or at least with wonder, at the great inventions.
It might be of interest to have the history of wonder written for
the nineteenth century. Often fear of the indeterminate and mysterious
has been the first effect of a new invention. When the first
steamboat appeared on the Seine, French peasants had the church bells rung,
because they feared disasters. Wellington and Cavour did
not like to travel by railway, and many ordinary people shared this fear.
Gradually one has become accustomed to the new things, has taken them as
matters of course and has even become somewhat blasé toward new novelties.
These also followed quickly upon one another and gradually changed
the course of daily life. The nineteenth century has been called the century of
steam, of electricity, or of chemical technology.
In a welter of forms there are daily applied all over the world
inventions that are due to long and quiet labor in the service of strict
science. Matches and dynamite, the telegraph and the telephone,
electric light, photographs and gramophones --- all such things strike
the eye and for many supply the standard of the culture that has been
attained. Living at the end of the nineteenth century, many have thought chiefly
of the fact that they lived in a time when one traveled by railways
or automobiles, read by electric light (not by tallow dips),
telephoned (instead of writing letters), etc. But there have
also been those for whom all these splendors receded before
the thought of the power of mind that has made them possible and in future
can take them into its service. And there have also been those who felt
that, despite all this external change of life, there was yet, through
the inner spiritual life and its eternal tasks, a connection with a
past that led its life under other external conditions and had to get
by with more imperfect means.

Popular presentations of scientific principles and results
easily take on a dogmatic character, in one of two directions mentioned above.
Either one rests content with the view that natural science knows only
what is extended in space and moves in space, and
that within this circle of subjects it demonstrates that no matter and
no force arises or perishes except by conversion from or into
other kinds of matter and force, and one then believes the riddle of the world
solved by this. Or else one follows natural science as far as one
is able to obtain tolerably intuitive results and then calls upon
either traditional religious representations or spiritistic representations.
Doubtless presentations of the first kind, that is, in a decidedly
materialistic direction, have found the widest circulation. A literature
% --- p. 44 ---
\opage{44}of this kind arose especially in the middle of the century, when one had
turned away from Romantic philosophy, and when at the same time significant
thoughts and results came forward from the side of natural science.
One of the most widely distributed writings of this direction was Büchner's
``Kraft und Stoff'' (1855), of which before the end of the century
nineteen editions appeared. He teaches that, just as the steam engine produces
motion, so organic compounds of
certain substances in the brain produce a sum of effects, which is called spirit or
thought when it is gathered into a unity. More drastically Carl
Vogt expresses himself (Köhlerglaube und Wissenschaft. 1855) in the utterance that,
just as the liver secretes bile and the kidneys urine, so the brain
produces thoughts. Yet these authors do not hold to their
ideas with full consistency. And the most considerable man among this
circle of authors, the physiologist Moleschott (Der Kreislauf des Lebens.
1857), declares chemistry indeed the highest science, but
he is, as especially his interesting autobiography shows, rather a monist
in Spinoza's sense than a materialist. Later
Häckel popularized the doctrine of evolution in a very bold and drastic manner in
his ``Welträtzel'' (1899).

The philosophical significance of this literature is not great. But
through it, scientific representations have been propagated
to places where they would otherwise not have reached, and it has
been a means of arousing reflection, precisely by its dogmatic
character. For materialism is dogmatic in spite of any theology. But
perhaps it is the case that with dogmas one must drive out dogmas.

\chapterhead{5.}{THE HUMAN SCIENCES}
\sectionhead{a.}{Psychology.}

Both Romanticism and positivism took a stand in opposition to
the individualistic intellectual tendency of the eighteenth century, according to which
the single personality stood as independent in its life of thought and feeling,
in so far as this was not inhibited and crippled by domineering
authorities that had an interest in the persistence of prejudice and superstition.
The historical powers were overlooked through which the single
individual, without knowing it, may be determined in his innermost being.
For the tendencies that came most strongly to expression in the first part
of the nineteenth century, the independent individual was only a fancy
or an abstraction. Just as one now had a greater
% --- p. 45 ---
\opage{45}understanding of the spiritual life of earlier times, so one now saw the single
individual as a member of his people, borne by its customs and usages and led by
its traditions. This conception could often lead to mysticism,
in that the unconscious paths by which the spiritual life of the race determines the
personal life of the individual were one-sidedly emphasized at the expense of
what more or less conscious self-activity could accomplish on the
basis of the individual's own peculiar nature and of the new experiences
that he was able to make within his circle. One was inclined
to see the best in existence in the mysterious world
that lies beyond the domain of clear consciousness, and in order not to
be disturbed in one's cult of it one was ill disposed toward all
criticism.

Nevertheless the tendencies mentioned, both positivism and Romanticism,
meant an enrichment of spiritual life. It was impressed that spiritual life
commands a greater fullness than can at any given time
be unfolded with full and clear consciousness. It is indeed in every generation
the duty of thought to draw up the intellectual account; but there will
always be items in this account that cannot be definitely formulated,
indeed, there will undoubtedly also be both receipts and expenditures
that do not enter into the account at all.

In peculiar contrast to the mystical tendency, which in
various forms had the floor in the first third of the century,
stood the line of thought followed by the most scientific psychology of the time.
Here an energetic continuation made itself felt of the direction
that English psychology had taken in the eighteenth century.
The theories of Hume and Hartley were developed further in the so-called
psychology of association, which conceived mental life as consisting of
a multitude of individual elements independent in themselves (sensations,
representations, feelings of pleasure and displeasure), which can enter into looser
or firmer connections (associations), when they come
to appear together (simultaneously or in immediate succession), or
when they greatly resemble one another. A principal work of this psychological
direction is James Mill's ``Analysis of the Human Mind''
(1829). In Germany a kindred direction asserts itself in Herbart's
``Psychologie als Wissenschaft'' (1824). This psychology exercised
a salutary opposition to the tendency of the time toward mysticism. It demanded
a definite account of the origin of every connection of representations,
and it moreover saw the validity of such connections as determined
by the way in which they had been formed; the validity
could not extend beyond the original occasion of the
% --- p. 46 ---
\opage{46}representations' connection. Thereby this conception acquired significance not only
for psychology as a distinct discipline, but also for epistemology,
in that it had to lead to a restatement of Hume's
problem, which Kant thought he had solved, and which Romanticism had entirely
pushed aside.

Purely psychologically, the principal question now had to become whether
mental life could be explained as a mere sum of independent elements.
By different paths this question has been discussed in the course of the century.
A principal point of view here became that a sharp distinction had to be made
between involuntary mental life, the actual
mental states on the one hand, and on the other hand the individual
``elements'' that reflection and analysis can separate out. It is
not justified to regard such elements as original; they
come about in fact only when attention, the clearer consciousness,
is directed upon what is involuntarily experienced. Reflection is always
something derived, however great and far-reaching its significance may become.
With great energy this point of view was maintained by Schopenhauer,
who in his doctrine of ``the Will to Life'' pointed back to the
original instinctive foundation of mental life. Furthermore closer investigation
of our representations showed that they never occur except in
certain connections. They can go out of one context, but only
to enter into another. Only at the boundary points of mental life, in
transition to ecstatic states and in certain mental diseases, can
they take on an approximately isolated character. In the domain of sensation,
the contrast effect, demonstrated by Chevreul
(1832), and the law set up by Fechner for the dependence of sensation
upon the relation between the degrees of strength of the stimuli
(1860), established that there were no absolutely independent sense-sensations.

By these different paths one was led to take up again the concept
of human mental life to which Kant's epistemological investigation
had led him, and according to which its fundamental form
is a gathering together, a synthesis, an involuntary formation of wholes,
which in science can become a function that is carried through
with full consciousness. There is thereby introduced no special
``force'' into psychology, in analogy with the ``life force'' that people have wished to
introduce into physiology. Synthesis is a law that makes itself known in all
mental states; it is the form of all mental work. What
reflection and psychological analysis can find will always prove to
be special examples or forms of this fundamental form.

The historical character of mental life, so strongly emphasized by Romanticism and positivism,
% --- p. 47 ---
\opage{47}can thereby come into its full right, in that experiences,
memories and representations from the past, by virtue of the
law of synthesis, will be continually interwoven with the new experiences and the
new representations. The psychology of association too comes into its
own, in that the association of representations is precisely only a form of synthesis.
In particular the life of will, on which the voluntarism founded by Schopenhauer
laid special weight, comes into its own, in that on all stages
of mental life, from the blind, involuntary up to that guided by a conscious aim,
there manifests itself, in many degrees and forms, a need for concentration.
Instinct and genius, deliberation and decision here all come
under the same fundamental concept.

The psychological conception thus characterized was prepared at
important points by Fries (Neue Kritik der Vernunft. 1806.
--- Psychiche Anthropologie. 1820) and Beneke (Psychologische Skizzen.
1825). Later it was taken as a basis in one of the century's
principal psychological works, Wilhelm Wundt's ``Grundzüge der physiologischen
Psychologie'' (1874, since then a series of ever more extensive
editions). The present author in his critique of the psychology of association
(``Den engelske Filosofi i vor Tid''. 1874) took the same
point of view as a basis and developed it in detail in his ``Psykologi
paa Grundlag af Erfaring'' (1882). In French literature Alfred
Fouillée (``La psychologie des idées-forces''. 1893) has in particular developed a
similar conception.

As regards methods of psychological inquiry, four different paths
have presented themselves in the course of the century. The different methods
can often lead to oppositions in principle, since the individual inquirer
is unable to apply them all, and since mental life easily comes
to appear in a different light according to the different path by which
one seeks to penetrate into it.

First, it had to be a matter of penetrating observation and
description of mental states, with attention to nuances
and complications that the more abstract conception of earlier times
had not allowed to come into their own. The most important condition for
psychological study is and remains, after all, psychological sense, and
one can be an acute analyst or a capable experimenter
without possessing this sense. In two men, one from the first half
of the century, the other from its end, this
condition has been present in rich measure, and they have achieved excellent things
in descriptive psychology. The one is the Danish psychologist Frederik
Christian Sibbern (d. 1872), the other the American psychologist
% --- p. 48 ---
\opage{48}William James (d. 1910). Both had, besides the gift of direct observation,
an open eye for the necessary connection between
psychology and physiology. A characteristic contrast between them
appears in this, that Sibbern, besides the many fresh observations
he gives, has a tendency to divide his material into sharply delimited
rubrics, whereas in James the classifying interest recedes
before the picture of the total interplay of all the forces of mental life.

Second, the interest in psychological inquiry has led to this, that
one everywhere, where it can be done, goes over from observation
to experiment. This transition was prepared by physiological experiments by
E. H. Weber (Tastsinn und Gemeingefühl. Wagner's Handbuch der
Physiologie. 1846), who established the possibility of a measurement of
sensations. Gustav Theodor Fechner carried this thought further
through experiments of his own and by collecting material from the literature, and
set up the law mentioned above, according to which the
increase of a sensation does not correspond directly to the increase of the stimulus,
but to the ratio between this increase and the stimulus given simultaneously or
immediately before. Through its relation to external
stimulus, sensation is thus accessible to measurement.
Fechner's work (Elemente der Psychophysik. 1860) founded
experimental psychology, and a new science was thereby formed,
an intermediate link between the human sciences and natural science.
Fechner himself is --- like Kepler in his day --- an interesting example
of how acute and energetic inquiry can carry through a
thought in such a way that from a mystical-speculative initial form it
can find grounds through exact investigation. On the basis of
his work, without however quite reaching up to its level, experimental psychology
has worked further to illuminate mental life, especially its
more elementary functions, by way of experiment. In Germany it is
especially Wundt and his disciples, in France Binet, in Denmark Alfred
Lehmann, who have worked in this domain. Much indicates, moreover,
that physiology is so essential a condition for experimental
psychology that the new subject must rather be said to belong under physiology
as one of the paths by which the latter can illuminate mental life.

Third, mental life is studied not only by the path of direct observation
and experiment, but mediately, through the works in which it
has revealed itself, that is, by the historical method, which at the same time becomes
the comparative method. The study of literature supplies psychology with new
material through the endeavor to go back from the literary works
% --- p. 49 ---
\opage{49}to the forces from which they have sprung. Here the works of Ste Beuve,
Taine and Georg Brandes are especially to be mentioned. The study of the visual arts
can cast light not only on the mode of operation of the artistic imagination,
but also on the different way in which the human
life of feeling at different times relates itself to the same
subject. In this direction Julius Lange's work ``Menneskeskikkelsen
i Kunstens Historie'' (1898) is of great interest. Besides
the psychology of literature and art, the psychology of religion must especially be mentioned,
in that the history of religions leads to knowledge of the mental
need that underlies them, and of the peculiar formations of representations
to which this need leads. Of works in this direction
Tylor's ``Primitive Culture'', Erwin Rhode's ``Psyche'', and
Durkheim's ``Les formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse'' are especially to be mentioned.

Finally the study of mental diseases has been able from many sides
to illuminate the general nature of mental life. There present themselves here, so to
speak, experiments that nature itself makes, in that we learn the effect of the weakening
and dropping away of mental functions and thereby gain insight
into the really supporting forces in mental life. Of quite special significance
here has been Charcot's work. From his school
came psychologists such as Th. Ribot and Pierre Janet.

By these different paths an understanding is striven for that
does not confound its own means and forms with the mental life
itself that is to be investigated, but step by step seeks to penetrate into its
subject, the most significant subject of all, and yet to acknowledge it
in its peculiar being. In this respect the Romanticism
that introduced the century has had a salutary after-effect. Even the
most critical inquiry into the phenomena of mental life stands yet with
greater sense, perhaps even with greater reverence before it than the
Enlightenment of the eighteenth century often did. A comparison between
Voltaire and Ludwig Feuerbach would clearly demonstrate this.

The opposition between clear consciousness and mysterious
unconsciousness, which --- now for the benefit of depth, now for the benefit of
obscurity and fear of light --- played so great a role in the reaction
against the eighteenth century, came forward again in the course of the nineteenth century
as a reaction against the progressive intellectual
work of the time. Most strongly and most dogmatically it was expressed in Eduard von
Hartmann's ``Philosophie des Unbewussten'' (1869), whose fundamental thought
is that conscious reason is only criticizing and controlling,
never creating and inventing, for which reason man would lose his
source of life if receptivity to the influence of the unconscious
% --- p. 50 ---
\opage{50}vanished. Psychologically speaking there is certainly much that is apt in this
view, especially when one speaks not merely of the unconscious but
of the involuntary. Just as, according to Carnot's principle, there is a constant
tendency toward a distribution of heat, so that the condition for a new release
of motion can thereby be removed, so there obtains in
the domain of spiritual life such a relation between the involuntary
life in instinct, feeling and impulse and the clearly conscious life
in reflection and deliberation that, while the conversion can take place
easily and involuntarily from the former to the latter, the division of energy that the
intellectual life entails makes the conversion in the opposite direction not
take place so easily. Long ago, especially in Rousseau's criticism of the modern
culture conditioned by division of labor, warnings
in this direction had appeared. --- But in Hartmann's philosophy ``the
unconscious'' appears all too often as an obscure power which, in spite of its obscurity,
is to solve all riddles. He calls upon this power where his thinking
can no longer solve the problems that it believes it must
set itself.

In a more defensible manner William James has later pointed to
what goes on beneath the ``threshold'' of consciousness or outside
its ``margin'', and which is known only through its effects in consciousness.
% translated from Høffding's Danish
He emphasizes especially the way in which fear, remorse
or anger can suddenly arise or resolutions be taken that
are not fully understood from the preceding deliberations. He
finds it very difficult to draw the boundary between what is
above and what is below the threshold. Very often that which
emerges from the ``subliminal'' or ``extramarginal'' comes forth as
if it were an external, objective power making itself known to us. And
here the seed may lie both for all manner of superstition and for inward faith.
More important than all the forms and ways in which men seek
to interpret these intrusions from the world of the unconscious, which may recall
Hugo de Vries's mutations, is for James the very fact
that they are possible at all. After he had already, in his ``Principles
of Phychology'' (1890), put forward this conception, he has
developed it through a series of special examples in his work on the psychology of religion
``Varieties of religious experience. A study in
human nature'' (1902).

There are, as is seen from this exposition, two principal problems that
have occupied the psychological inquiry of the nineteenth century. The one
concerns the relation between the manifoldness that every mental life presents
in all degrees, right up to threatening chaos, and on the other side
% --- p. 51 ---
\opage{51}the collectedness and unity that is in part a presupposition for a mental life being able
to subsist at all, in part --- in its pronounced forms --- characteristic
of what we call the higher stages of mental life. The other
problem concerns the relation between the involuntary, perhaps unconscious,
and the clear consciousness, of which reflection is in part an expression,
in part itself the cause. That this problem does not coincide with the
first can be seen from the fact that the involuntary, perhaps unconscious mental life
may precisely present a closedness, a concentration, that reflection
may have difficulty in reaching. Both the unity and the manifoldness
in mental life may have the character of the involuntary. But the two problems
can in many ways overlap, and thereby
the most intricate mental relations come about.

Not only in theoretical psychology did these problems stir. They
appear also in the practice of life and are characteristic of the mental life
of the century, wherever this reached into the depths. Many a battle
has been fought in silence to find a way, when on the one side the
impulses of involuntary life and dawning representations press
forward, and on the other side stirs the great need for clarity
and understanding that was the good inheritance from the eighteenth century.
In the autobiography that one of the century's eminent
men, John Stuart Mill, has left behind, and which I have already
had occasion to mention, one can study the conflict between
these two tendencies in the first half of the century. For Mill
it nevertheless remained firm that both understanding
of life and a firm bearing in life could be won only when honest work was done
to win clarity and to discover inner connection between our
experiences. In other natures it was the fullness and need of mental life
that gained the upper hand, but critical thought continually struggled with
them, so that the thoughts one made about life could be uttered only
in the form of paradox, as more or less convulsive attempts
to combine what could not appear in inner, natural
connection. Natures of this kind, who through brilliant paradoxes
won expression for a strongly strained inner life, were men like Carlyle
and Kierkegaard in the middle of the century, Nietzsche and Tolstoy
toward its end. These men take up, each in his own way, the
problem of culture that Rousseau had so energetically brought forward
in the middle of the eighteenth century. There was also (as I have sought
to show in an essay on ``Rousseau og det nittende Aarhundrede'')
a certain analogy in the spiritual situation in the middle of the nineteenth century
and that which prevailed a hundred years earlier. In both
% --- p. 52 ---
\opage{52}cases a sharp opposition asserted itself between immediate
experience of life and the personal striving conditioned by it on the one
side, and the support that thinking and empirical science could give
on the other side. However different from one another the men mentioned
were, there is yet something common in their relation to the intellectual
culture that their time had won. Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, e.g.,
stand indeed in the sharpest opposition to each other, but precisely this
makes a comparison between them instructive in a psychological respect,
and from an attempt I once made in this direction I shall here
adduce some features that may be suited to the characterization of an essential
side of the spiritual life of the nineteenth century.

The opposition might admittedly seem so sharp that it
must stand as a strange thought to bring them together. The one
maintained Christianity in its strictest form, sharpened orthodoxy
to paradox and placed its doctrine in absolute and hostile opposition
to natural human thought. In particular he placed
Christian ethics in the sharpest conflict with human need and
striving. The other was a radical free-thinker with so strong an antipathy
to Christianity and to every conception of life akin
to it that he could not find words strong enough
to express his aversion. On the other hand he maintained with ecstatic enthusiasm
the health and strength of human nature and believed in an ideal
elevation of it. What the God-man was for Kierkegaard, the Superman was
for Nietzsche.

But they meet in this, that both see far beyond the usual,
delimited, rationally arranged paths of life. They maintain the innermost,
the original in man as something that cannot be analyzed
and formulated in an exact way, but which can nevertheless show itself as
the strongest force and have the highest value. They apply, seen from a
purely psychological standpoint, the same standard of personal
value. The mental life stands highest for them in which the strongest oppositions
and the pain they cause are overcome by a power of spirit
that is able to go through purgatory. By toning down the oppositions
one lowers the level of life. The highest is the great courage
that is required to subsist in the spiritual struggle. Kierkegaard saw the danger
especially in aesthetic play with life; Nietzsche saw it in weakness and
complaint. But both maintained that life must be conceived as a struggle
to preserve both the fullness of life and its unity. Both denied
that modern culture, with all its science, art and industry,
satisfied the need of personality, and they were led at the same time --- from two
% --- p. 53 ---
\opage{53}opposed points of view --- to sharp opposition to the existing
religious and church establishment. They are symptoms of something that stirs
in the age, and it has taken on a volcanic expression in them.

--- From a purely psychological point of view, men such as these are regarded as
subjects that set reflection great tasks. It would have to be a matter of
finding how and to what extent what we know about the nature and
laws of mental life can cast light upon the development of such figures, and how
and to what extent this their development is connected with the
spiritual conditions that prevailed in their time.

\sectionhead{b.}{Historical Science.}

When already within psychology, the central branch of
the human sciences, a historical and comparative method asserts itself alongside observation and experiment,
this must be still more the case with more special, more spiritual subjects. The development
of the science of language in the nineteenth century is a great example of this.


The founder of the comparative science of language, the Danish
inquirer Rasmus Rask (d. 1832), went beyond the earlier age's
inclination, in investigating the mutual content of languages, to
confine itself to the individual words and to find resemblances between them. He
set explanation of language in opposition to explanation of words. The
whole structure of a language and the changes it can undergo is more important
than the transferences and changes of the individual words. The grammatical
is more important than the lexical. For Rask, however, historical
linguistic inquiry was subordinate to the systematically
comparative. Without comparison with other languages the individual language
cannot be understood either, and no distinction can be made between
word and thought. Language was for Rask rather an object of nature, and
knowledge of it recalled in his eyes natural history. He
sought to find a clear and natural system, in part in the classification of
languages generally, in part in the investigation of the individual languages.
Bopp (d. 1867) carried the development of the new science further, and
Jacob Grimm (d. 1863) founded historical linguistics, in a certain
opposition to Rask and yet in essential respects building
on Rask's thoughts.

Vilhelm Thomsen, the brilliant successor of these inquirers, from whom
I have taken these notes, makes the following comparison
% --- p. 54 ---
\opage{54}between his three great predecessors. ``Rask, Bopp and Grimm have each in
his own way contributed to introducing a new development of the science of language
and laying the foundation of the comparative science of language:
Rask first and foremost by his investigations of the Nordic
languages, especially Icelandic, and by his systematic demonstration of the position
and relation of this language to the other related languages in Europe,
but next also of the various relations of kinship and points of contact of these and many other languages; Bopp by the way in which
he takes Sanskrit into the comparison of the languages belonging to our stock
and by his acute investigations of the whole structure of these languages;
Grimm finally by his treatment of the Gothic-Germanic
languages and by the fundamental way in which he applies
the historical point of view.'' (Sprogvidenskabens Historie
1902).

What was here founded was carried further in the course of the century,
in that ever new language families were taken up for investigation.
What is of interest for an investigation of the century's leading
ideas is especially the way in which scientific linguistic inquiry
takes up the old question of the origin of language.
Formerly this origin was regarded either as the fruit of human
invention or as a divine gift to men.
Eilschou found even a proof of the existence of God in the fact that
men could not themselves have produced language. Both conceptions
are equally external. Modern linguistic inquiry has even been
inclined to push the question entirely aside. But just as one
in geology proceeded from the view that the changes that now take place
on the surface of the earth can cast light on the earth's revolutions in the past,
so the linguists too became more and more aware
that in the more recent languages one could study the changes
that have conditioned the development of language. It was seen that language is something that
is constantly coming into being, and it was concluded that the origin of language could not be thought
in any other way and according to any other laws than those to which the changes now
taking place in language point. The first to emphasize this with full clarity
is J. N. Madvig, who in a long overlooked treatise
from 1842 (Om Sprogets Væsen, Udvikling og Liv) maintained
that we can find the very ``act of language formation'' in the way in which
even now men's need for expression and communication continually manifests
itself. Language must have been produced by men, for only ``the language
that men create can men understand''. But it came into being
as involuntary outbursts, which were conditioned by influences that
% --- p. 55 ---
\opage{55}were accessible to several men; thereby the outbursts could become
common signs. Under the need to communicate ever more numerous experiences
the development of language has taken place.

This so-called ``principle of actuality'' appears in the nineteenth century
in various domains. In its generality it rests
on the fact that we can understand the past from the present. In a certain sense
this maxim was also applied in earlier times, but then it happened
in such a way that the conditions
and forms of the past were taken without further ado as if they were the same as those of the present. The closer
determination that the principle of actuality receives in the nineteenth century consists
in this, that it is not conditions and forms but laws and forces
whose identity with those of the past is taken as a basis. One conceives
how the laws we know would act under other conditions than
those now obtaining. Both in the human sciences and in natural science
this principle finds application. We shall meet it also in historical
research in the narrower sense. It is connected with the principle of continuity,
so strongly emphasized in the seventeenth century,
which Leibniz in particular took as a basis in his philosophy, and which he grounded
by reference to the many transitional forms in nature and
by his mathematical theory of infinitely small quantities. (See especially
his Lettre à M. Bayle and his Réplique aux réflexions de Bayle).
And it manifests itself in the constant striving of science
to convert qualitative differences into quantitative ones. ---

Hitherto only two human sciences have been mentioned, psychology and
the science of language. Comte wished to include them both as well as all
other special human sciences that might be set up under sociology,
which was to present the general laws, forms
and processes of development of social life. Mental life and language were for him just as much
social phenomena as morals and law. Sociology regards the single
individual as a mere abstraction and maintains social influence
in every spiritual manifestation of life. Thereby a great task is rather set,
namely the demonstration of the individual's constant dependence on
society, than a scientific discipline is delimited with full clarity.
Experience shows us a constant interaction between individual
and society, an interaction without which no new experiences
and no new thoughts could acquire social significance. Without this
interaction the transitions between the different
stages that human social life, according to Comte, presents would not become
intelligible either, for such transitions are traced first in a single, or at any rate relatively few individuals.
According to Comte's sociology the different stages of
% --- p. 56 ---
\opage{56}social life are conditioned first and foremost by the development of knowledge,
and this passes through, as we have already seen, three
stages, the theological, the metaphysical and the positive. Comte now seeks
to show that to these three stages there correspond different social forms of life.
The theological stage is at the same time the proper period of militarism; to
the metaphysical stage corresponds the rule of the jurists in the state;
in the positive stage it is the industrials (employers and workers)
who are in command. This ingenious generalization cannot
be carried through in detail without constraint, and it lays
--- which may surprise in the very founder of sociology --- not
the chief weight on the real chief social problem, which springs
from the relation between society and individual.

From this principal problem another sociological generalization,
which appeared after Comte's time, takes its point of departure. Henry Maine
(Ancient Law. 1861), and after him inquirers such as Herbert Spencer,
Ferdinand Tönnies and Emile Durkheim, lay the weight on the opposition
between the more primitive forms of society, where the single
individual involuntarily shares the life of the horde or the tribe, and where perhaps
not even the family exists as a tolerably independent whole,
and the forms of society that are founded in detail on conscious agreements.
The difference is designated as a difference between condition
(status) and compact (contractus). It corresponds to the difference between the
first and the second term within Hegel's dialectic, and to the difference
between the theological and the metaphysical stage in Comte. It is
certainly characteristic that this later sociological generalization
dwells upon the very intermediate stage from which the century's older
thinkers, Comte as well as Hegel, hastened with a certain haste over to the
stage of consummation that Hegel called the higher unity, Comte the
positive stage. It is at the intermediate stage that the real problems
arise. Contract presupposes that the individual appears with independence,
--- that the one individual stands over against the other and over against
society, with which in the first stage he involuntarily felt himself one.
The question became whether the results to which his liberated and independent
experiences, experience and thoughts led could agree with the
life of representations that had hitherto prevailed in the society from which
he himself had come, and from which he could never quite isolate
himself. In a very interesting manner Tönnies (Gemeinschaft und
Gesellschaft. 1887) has shown how the opposition maintained by Henry Maine
between condition and compact is connected with the opposition
between the involuntary forms of mental life, need, instinct, habit,
% --- p. 57 ---
\opage{57}faith in authority, on the one side, and the decisions and convictions
founded on conscious deliberation on the other side. To individualism
in society there corresponds as analogue reflection in the single
individual. In religious respect it is here that the opposition between
faith and knowledge comes forward. In general condition and
compact designate two different ways in which the fate of the single individual
may be bound up with the group or society to which it nevertheless
still belongs. Of the prospect of a higher unity, a harmony between
condition and compact, this theory expresses itself very reservedly.
As will be seen, it recalls the St. Simonian distinction between
organic and critical periods, and it will later appear that it
asserts itself in a significant way in what is called the
social problem in the narrower sense.

Sociology, as it is conceived by Comte and his successors,
recalls what in the time of Romanticism was called the philosophy
of history. And like this it arose at the outset as an attempt
to demonstrate a progress in the evolution of mankind. There
made itself felt here an after-effect of the enthusiastic
optimism of the eighteenth century, which has borne its most characteristic fruit in
the Girondin Condorcet's ``Esquisse d'un tableau historique des progrés
de l'esprit humain'' (1795), which he drew up while he
kept himself hidden to escape the guillotine of the Jacobins. Sociology
has, like biology, learned that evolution and progress are not the
same. The bad evolves just like the good. And whence do
we in the end derive the standard of bad and good? It is a problem by itself,
and Comte was led in his last period to acknowledge this by distinguishing
between ethics and sociology and extending his classification of the sciences
by adding ethics as the seventh member of the series.

Sociology does not, however, stand in opposition merely to ethics, but
also to historical research in the narrower sense. It does not count ``history''
as science. Sociology is to demonstrate definite social
conditions according to their general nature, not to occupy itself with individual
personalities and events, as history in the narrower
sense does. From a purely historical standpoint Jacob Burckhardt
(Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen, written from 1868 on, published 1905, after the author's death)
has in contrast to this emphasized that in human history we do not have a single continuous
process that could make the setting up of general laws possible, but
several processes running simultaneously. Since simultaneity makes itself felt
as well as succession, history cannot be laid out in a
% --- p. 58 ---
\opage{58}single line. Moreover Burckhardt's studies led him to lay
greater weight on the differences between peoples and between cultures
than on similarities that could justify the setting up of general
laws and of a common standard. He represents the opposition
of history to sociology, denies the latter's scientific character, just as
the latter conversely denies the scientific character of history.

However it may now stand with the solution of this dispute,
the interest in history in the narrower sense has so little declined
in the nineteenth century that one might on the contrary with just as much right
call it the century of history as it has been called
the century of physics. There has undoubtedly in this century been
greater historical sense than in earlier times. One no longer saw
past ages either as in their essence like one's own age,
so that the latter's representations could without more ado be laid back
into them, or as quite opposite in essence, so that they came to stand
as absurd. There is more capacity to enter into foreign psychological
and social conditions and to see personalities, events
and institutions in relation to the age from which they sprang, and which
lived in them. In addition, the sources of historical knowledge were opened
on a far greater scale than before, and among those who drew at
first hand from these sources there developed a critical sense and capacity
that measured and rejected the transmitted testimonies before they were allowed
to determine the historical presentation. If a single man is to
be named, it is the German historian Niebuhr who has given the program
for the century's historical research. In a survey of historical
studies in France, Langlois admits that the renaissance of these studies
after the Revolution and the Restoration is due to the influence
of German science, and he names Ernest Renan as one of the first
who saw that Germany had continued the historical work that the scholars of
old France had practiced, but which new France
had let lie. Niebuhr declared that we never stand before the very
events of the past, but only before the sources of our knowledge
of them. This critical sense and capacity, which conditions the scientific character
of historical research, is closely connected with the historical
sense. When a testimony is rejected, it is precisely because it is regarded
as unhistorical, as not being what it gives itself out to be. History
is criticized from history itself. Every testimony must, after all, bear
the stamp of its age, not merely the stamp of the events of which it wishes to
report. --- As an organ of this critical sense and capacity historical research
is undoubtedly science, however it may stand
% --- p. 59 ---
\opage{59}with the possibility of finding laws for the relation between the events
that historical criticism leads to acknowledging.

The historical sense developed under the aegis of Romanticism and positivism
and had in its first forms the stamp of a reaction
against the critical and revolutionary tendencies of the eighteenth century.
The so-called historical school found a deeper connection there
where Enlightenment and Revolution had seen only superstition or arbitrariness,
and it had a great distrust of all works and institutions
that were the fruit of conscious reflection. In the domain of the legal system
one was thus, as has already been mentioned, an opponent of codification,
of conscious regulation and systematization of the laws, such as
among others the English philosopher of law Bentham (who coined
the word codification) demanded. A logical formulation of
the laws was held to be impossible. Law was conceived, like folk poetry, as
a child of the soul of the people, an involuntary expression of it. Mockingly
Anselm von Feuerbach declared, against this view maintained by Savigny,
that this child of the spirit of the people should thus at once be put out to
nurse with the jurists; he pointed, against this German tendency,
to England, where the science of law stands in close connection with practice,
as this develops in the spirit of practical jurists through
the administration of law itself. (Einige Worte über historische Rechtsgelehrsamkeit
und einheimische deutsche Gesetzgebung. 1824).
The historical school acted on the whole as a damper and a check on all striving
for reforms, all initiatives in the political, social and
religious domain, even if it did not directly subscribe to Hegel's
proposition that the real is the rational. Leopold Ranke, whom one
has called the greatest historian of modern times (Gooch: History and
Historians in the 19th century), regarded the war of 1870, like
that of 1813, as a victory of conservative Europe over revolutionary Europe.
The historical school, in and after the time of Romanticism, was bound
on the whole to arrive naturally at the view that the victorious
has right on its side, --- that power in and of itself is right. It was especially
the Prussian historical school that took this point of view as a basis
and sought to ground it. As a single example there may be adduced here an
utterance of Droysen in his ``Geschichte Alexanders des Grossen''
(1833): ``The great right of victory is always victory for a higher right, for the
right that lies in the higher elastic force, in the superior evolution,
in the driving force of a new thought rich in future.'' Some French historians,
such as Augustin Thierry, have on the contrary shown an inclination to
side with the vanquished, to emphasize the value of the culture
% --- p. 60 ---
\opage{60}that perished as a result of the struggle. What points of view are taken as
a basis here will depend partly on whether the people of the historian concerned
has itself experienced victory or defeat, partly on the subjects he occupies
himself with, partly finally, and this is here of the greatest interest, on how
he conceives the relation between state power and culture. In his
``Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen'' the Swiss Jacob
Burckhardt places culture in sharp opposition to state and religion. The former represents
freedom; the latter are the realms of power; --- the former is the mobile,
the latter the stable. Burckhardt sees in history a constant conflict
between these three ``potencies'', a conflict that for him essentially takes on
a tragic character.

The historical conception and appraisal will naturally depend to a high degree
on the relation in which the historian himself feels himself to stand to
these potencies. National differences too will have influence.
They are traced right into pure sociology, which was nevertheless supposed to be independent
of definite historical events and conflicts. It has
thus rightly been found characteristic that Austrian sociologists,
especially Gumplowicz, conceive social science as a doctrine
of struggle of races, whereas English and French sociologists, such as Spencer
and Tarde, conceive it as a doctrine of the positive unfolding of social life. It must in any case be the task of sociological and historical
inquiry to find a continuity through and in spite of all
conflicts and catastrophes. A significant work in that direction
is Alexis de Tocqueville's work ``L'ancien Régime et la Révolution''
(1855), in which, in the words of a French critic, he did for history
what Lyell did for geology, in that he rejected the theory of catastrophes
in the historical domain and showed that what suddenly
broke forth as transformative in the French Revolution had been prepared
by the policy of the absolute monarchy through centuries.
Later Kropotkin (Mutual Aid 1902) has sought to show that the catastrophe
must in any case be dated back to the time when state regulation
begins to take the place of the involuntary adaptation through
interaction and mutual aid in the small societies, within which
the neighborly relation could act as a support and supplement and prevent the
isolation of the individuals.

In face of the emphasis on continuity in history the philosopher
Charles Renouvier has raised a criticism, in that he found in it a tendency
to embellish all that happens, by regarding it as the
only possible and finding it justified thereby. He holds that it is
especially Romanticism that has introduced this, in his eyes reactionary,
% --- p. 61 ---
\opage{61}way of thinking. In his remarkable work ``Uchronie\starnote{Uchronia means that which does not exist at any time, just as Utopia means that which does not exist in any place.} (``L'Utopie dans
l'Histoire'' (1902) he wishes to show that it was by no means necessary that
ancient culture should perish. From the second century after
Christ (the age of the Antonines) there could --- he holds --- very well
have unfolded other series of development than those that, through the dissolution
of the Roman Empire, the Middle Ages and Catholicism, led to the modern
age. Renouvier, to whom we shall return in another connection,
wished by this view to strengthen responsibility and the consciousness of freedom
