against reactionary tendencies that think they can claim
history for themselves. According to Renouvier too great a weight has been laid
on the opposition to the eighteenth century, the real period of breakthrough
of free humanity. The historical sense, which is praised as the
distinction of the nineteenth century, has led to one's entering into the past
to such a degree that one did not understand the present and the possibilities for
new points of development that it can present. And this whole historical
determinism redounds to the benefit of political and ecclesiastical reaction!
--- Renouvier takes his stand in opposition to a tendency that corresponds
to what in Germany was called the historical school. Here in
the North a similar criticism had already long ago appeared against
the historical school and its conservative tendency. It was in
the year 1838 that the Swedish historian and philosopher Erik Gustaf Geijer
broke with the historical school to which he had through Romanticism
come to belong. And he has himself declared that it was through history
that he had been freed from history, in that history equally
well shows us the new that emerges as the old that persists. He
saw the possibility of a generation's being able --- as he expresses
himself --- to ``walk away from inheritance and debt'' and try to strike out on new paths in
confidence in possibilities that were not yet realized. This break,
Geijer's so-called ``defection'', became of far-reaching significance for his
political, pedagogical and religious views, in that it led him
to the setting up of the so-called principle of personality, to which I shall return in
another connection. ---

From a quite different side the Romantic-historical tendency was attacked
by Karl Marx's so-called materialist conception of history.
The Romantic-historical conception laid the weight on the all-governing
influence of ideas and traditions. In opposition thereto
Marx (Das Kapital. 1867) maintains that it is economic factors and interests
that determine historical events and upheavals, however
% --- p. 62 ---
\opage{62}much the acting persons believe themselves guided by great ideas
surfacing in their minds or by venerable traditions. Both
cultural history and political history are determined according to Marx throughout
by economic causes. It is the laws of production
and distribution, in particular the constant conflict between capital and labor,
on which according to Marx it finally depends. In the section on leading
ideas in the domain of social life we shall return to
this point.

\chapterhead{6.}{PHILOSOPHY IN THE LAST PART OF THE CENTURY}
\sectionhead{a.}{Can Philosophy Give Closure to Thought?}

At the middle of the century it was really only in England that
philosophizing was done in an independent and free manner. It was Stuart Mill's Logic
and philosophy of experience that had the floor; he succeeded Comte as the spokesman
of positivism. After the collapse of Romantic speculation
there came in Germany a time of weariness, which was, however, filled out by
learned, in part monumental works on the history of philosophy. Hegel
had sought to demonstrate a connection within the history of philosophy,
and it was men of his school who took the lead in the great historical
orientation over the course of the development of philosophy, an orientation
which, moreover, in several respects led to a correction of Hegel's views.
In the first rank here are to be named Eduard Zeller, Kuno Fischer and
J. E. Erdmann. Many of the great figures of philosophy
now came to stand in a new light, and it was shown what significance
thoughts that are really grasped out of the innermost nature of the life of thought
and of experience can have for all times, even if the form in
which they first appeared is subject to perishability.
At the same time one had, through comparative historical study, to become
clear that there are, after all, different starting points for philosophizing.
Truth can and must be sought by different paths, and the difference
of points of view can be leveled out only gradually through
ever more deeply penetrating conceptions of the problems. A Danish philosopher,
in whose view the thought plays a leading role that all development
proceeds from scattered points in order then gradually --- under
favorable conditions --- to lead to a formation of a whole, has also
applied this thought to the working conditions of philosophy. Sibbern, who
in the Forties in various works, of which may here be mentioned ``Filosofiens
Begreb, Natur og Væsen'' (1843), summed up the principal results
% --- p. 63 ---
\opage{63}of his philosophizing, maintained that a complete systematizing of
philosophy was not possible. Our experience proceeds always from the first
sporadically. Existence opens itself to us from several points
at once, as the different methods and views of the individual sciences already show. And every individual philosopher begins
from his particular standpoint, --- indeed, philosophy itself is only one of the many
processes that unfold in the spiritual world, and it will always
have a struggle to sustain, not only with other scientific endeavors,
but also with the manifestations of spiritual life that appear
in art and in religion. And even if through the debate
of everything against everything, which is always necessary, a comprehensive
system should at a given time work its way forward, the work of thought must nevertheless
be taken up anew in every new age. For while the systematic
work is in progress, there will, since life never stands still, accumulate
a new material of experience, which will have to be taken into account. --- From
such a point of view Sibbern had already earlier (1838)
criticized Hegel's philosophy. In particular he saw clearly the untenability of
Schelling's and Hegel's philosophy of nature, which in its arbitrary symbolizing
did not let the lawlike connection that natural science demonstrated
come into its right, and he sought himself in his philosophical works to
acknowledge this right.

It was, as we have seen, especially two thoughts that marked a great contribution
to the conception of the world from the side of natural science, the principle of
the conservation of energy and the doctrine of the origin of species by evolution.
Two ingenious German thinkers, Gustav Theodor Fechner and Hermann
Lotze, sought to let the fixed order of nature, which expresses itself
in these doctrines, gain a decisive significance in their philosophy, without
thereby giving up the idealistic basic view through which
they felt themselves akin to the Romantic philosophers. Could the ideas
not well be effective, even if they cannot work magic? --- asks Lotze.
Because one is not permitted to explain the individual phenomena of nature
by appeal to ideas or any other form of spiritual intervention, it may
very well be that idealism is right in the last word that thought can
say. Even if a strict realism must rule in our attempts
to explain what happens in the world, it might yet be that this very
realism rested on an idealistic foundation. All science,
even the most exact, rests on certain presuppositions, builds on
certain basic thoughts, which by the nature of the case cannot themselves be grounded
by the realistic way of thinking that rests on them. Realism
ends in a limiting concept, in the thought of a rational
% --- p. 64 ---
\opage{64}connection in the world, a thought that is presupposed in all natural science, but
not itself exhausted in any single law. It is only by virtue of this
limiting concept that we can speak of the unity of nature. If one wishes to form
for oneself a closer representation of this unity, that is, of ``that which
holds the world together in its innermost'', then there is --- Fechner
and Lotze see this clearly --- only one way that stands at our disposal: the way
of analogy. We go this way when we believe that what underlies
existence is of spiritual nature; for we then assume that,
as a human body is related to the soul of man, so
nature is related to the Godhead. But the justification of such an analogy
cannot be demonstrated by the way of strict inference. Romantic
speculation, on the contrary, believed precisely that it was going the way of strict thinking
and would not admit that it worked with images
and analogies. It confounded identity and analogy.

Earlier in the century Schopenhauer and Beneke had maintained
that our concluding thoughts are built on analogy. And here too there is
a great predecessor in the seventeenth century, namely Leibniz, according to
whom all metaphysics and all religion builds on analogy, and who calls
analogy ``mon grand principe des choses naturelles''. Fechner
has expressed this thought in ``Elemente der Psychophysik'' (1860)
and in ``Die Seelenfrage'' (1861), Lotze in ``Mikrokosmus'' (1856---64).
What the two philosophers do not state with full clarity, any more than Leibniz, is where the boundary lies between the analogies they
make use of in the rounding off of their thought, and the purely poetic images.
Only when such a boundary can be determined will the way be
barred to all dogmatism.

It was this indeterminate boundary that made Wilhelm Wundt apprehensive
about the standpoint that Fechner and Lotze took up. Wundt, who
in various domains did great work to build philosophy
on firmer ground and give it systematic connection,
could not find that analogy was a sufficient support for the rounding-off
concept of unity that philosophy, in his view too, seeks.
We cannot, he holds, remain standing, as Spinoza does, at
a ground of unity whose constitution is not more closely determined. We
must investigate which of the concepts that experience has led us
to form is best suited to be an expression of the principle of unity in
existence. He admits that we have here the choice between thinking
it as material and thinking it as spiritual, and since spiritual
existence is the way of being that appears most immediately
to us, most resembles what we experience in ourselves, it is analogy
% --- p. 65 ---
\opage{65}with it that we must keep to. (System der Philosophie. 1889).
It is only a faith, but it is, Wundt holds, a faith whose necessity
we can prove. --- Wundt overlooks here that this necessity
would be present only if it could be proved that the essence of existence
was exhausted by the two forms of existence appearing in our experience,
the material and the spiritual, so that we had a forced
choice between them. But the difference between the spiritual and the material
is purely factual and therefore does not exclude, as Spinoza already
saw, the possibility of other forms of existence. Even if
an absolutely compelling counterproof against materialism could be
produced, idealism would therefore not be strictly proved. We do not stand here before a
strict either-or. Fouillée, Bergson and Spencer stand on a standpoint
similar to Wundt's.

That there cannot be proved to be a forced choice between the two analogies,
the author of this exposition has sought to show in the epistemological
part of his ``Religionsfilosofi'' (1901) and more fully
in ``Den menneskelige Tanke'' (1910).

--- When Spencer is named among those who go the way of analogy to the
last rounding-off concept, it might seem striking. In the first place
he stands nearer to positivism than any of the philosophers just mentioned,
and in the second place the essential task of his philosophy was
to demonstrate the concept of evolution as a basic concept in all domains.
He seeks to establish that there are certain features that recur in
all domains and that make up the content of the concept of evolution. Every
subject of experience presents, when we follow its coming to be, three
stages. In the first it appears as a collected and uniform
whole; in the second more and more differences appear,
and in the third these differences are ordered into a more or
less harmonious whole. The three stages may be designated as concentration,
differentiation and harmonization. Evolution in the sense
of a process that runs through these three stages can, according to Spencer, be
demonstrated in all domains (geological, biological, psychological
and sociological), and he has in a series of works sought to ground
this assertion. But beyond such processes of evolution appearing in experience we can, he maintains, have no grounded knowledge.
If we nevertheless seek out beyond them, we stand before the Unknowable
(the unknowable) (First Principles. 1861). In a more special
connection (the concluding section of ``Principles of Psychology'') Spencer
does, however, declare that, were he to choose between a materialistic and
an idealistic interpretation, he would prefer the latter.

% --- p. 66 ---
\opage{66}--- The conception of the limits of philosophical thought that emerged in the views discussed here received, as we shall see, a closer determination and grounding through the resumption
of the problem of knowledge that is characteristic of the last decade of the century.

\sectionhead{b.}{Division of Labor within Philosophy.}

Toward the end of the century a change made itself felt in the manner of philosophizing, apart also from the views just mentioned, especially in that the division of labor, which had already advanced far
in the domains of the individual sciences, now also appeared in philosophy.  For the Romantics, as for most older philosophers, there existed at bottom only a single problem, the problem of existence
(the cosmological or metaphysical problem), and all other problems were subordinated to it and solved in connection with it.
But now psychology, epistemology, ethics and philosophy of religion step forward with their particular tasks and methods, and the question then approaches, in what sense philosophy can still be said to constitute
a whole. --- Psychology has already been discussed.  Philosophy of religion will be discussed on occasion in a later section.  Here, therefore, only ethics and epistemology will be dealt with, and finally some
remarks will be made on the state of the cosmological (``metaphysical'') problem.

\sectionhead{α.}{Ethics.}

In the domain of ethics, two views stood opposed to one another at the beginning of the century, and their influence extended, despite
Romanticism and positivism, right up through the century.  They were Kant's ethics, grounded in the concept of duty, and Bentham's grounding of all morality in the desire for happiness.  Both theories had appeared at about the same time,
namely in the penultimate decade of the eighteenth century.
Kant proceeded from the view that when there is to be talk of general rules for human action, and moreover of rules that can come forward with authority in the face of man's individual drives and wishes, they
must have their root in reason, the same reason that in science leads man to cognize the lawfulness of nature.  That
an action is a duty can be grounded only in its answering to a demand that must be made of all rational beings in the same situation
as the agent.  The consideration of the action's effects, by contrast, has no ethical significance; such a consideration would make ethical
% --- p. 67 ---
\opage{67}evaluation dependent on experience.  According to Bentham, on the other hand, it is precisely the consideration of the effects of actions that grounds ethical
evaluation.  Only those actions are good which, directly or indirectly, in their more remote as in their nearer effects, lead to happiness or
utility for human beings.  Bentham combats the ``rights of man'' which the American and the French Revolution proclaimed
as self-evident.  There are no original rights.
A man's right rests on the effects of his actions toward happiness or utility.  But if man only rightly understands what can
bring him happiness now and in the future, he will act in such a way that
the true desire for happiness of other men too can be satisfied.
Well-understood self-interest is, according to Bentham, the foundation of all morality, and he was fully and firmly convinced that when all men
merely followed their own advantage with prudence, it would turn out that the interests of all were in mutual harmony.

To understand the position of the new century toward these views, it must be observed that both Kant and Bentham proceeded from presuppositions
that were given no place in their theories.  Kant had (as I have sought to show in a treatise on the course of his philosophical development) arrived at his ethical conception through the study of the struggle
that is carried on in the course of history between human interests, a struggle that can end only by means of a social order within which
the freedom of the individual is limited by the conditions of the equal freedom of others.  His ethics thus stands at bottom as an anticipation
of the goal of historical development, as an ideal we must follow in order to work in the direction of this goal.  Hence Kant could in his work of old age
``Zum ewigen Frieden'' (1795) maintain that moral evil
dissolves society and therefore must in the end dissolve itself, whereby it paves the way for the good.  It is thus the struggle for the
continued existence of a human society that is the real presupposition of Kant's ethics.  As for Bentham, his delight in the harmony of interests cannot be explained from a purely individual standpoint.
When the single individual has only the prospect of securing his own isolated interests, it may after all be a matter of indifference to him how it goes
with the interests of all others.  It is thus a social motive of evaluation that underlies the place the harmony of interests occupies in
Bentham's theory.  Bentham's German successor Beneke has already emphasized this.

Both of the two great ethicists thus point, without being
% --- p. 68 ---
\opage{68}aware of it, to social life as the foundation of ethics.  And it was precisely here that the new century took hold, as soon as it had
recovered from the great upheavals with which it was ushered in.
Both Hegel and Comte, both Romanticism and positivism, found here
their stage.  Their ethics is essentially social; the duties and rights of the individual are conditioned by their being members of a society.

When Hegel in his very first drafts proceeds from the people organized in the state as the presupposition of ethical ideas, there is at work in this
not only opposition to Kant's attempt at an ethics of pure reason, but
also, and especially, his studies of ancient culture.  The subjective, individual
ethical feeling, conscience, is really a product of dissolution,
which arises when advancing culture and critique abolish
the people's involuntary and in part unconscious adherence to custom
and usage.  The isolation of individuals thus arising is abolished
again when they freely see themselves as members of the great whole that the state
is.  (Phänomenologie des Geistes. 1807).  Hegel's ideas here recall
the thoughts that Fichte --- as mentioned in an earlier connection
--- had set forth shortly before in ``Grundzüge des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters''.
In Hegel's chief ethical work (``Philosophie des Rechts''. 1821)
the higher unity that comprises within itself both right and morality is
designated as ``Sittlichkeit'', which appears in the family and in civil
society (economic life), which in turn both find a higher unity in
the state, which is ``the reality of the ethical idea''.  Only by being a good
citizen in a good state does the single individual attain full value, not by
standing on his abstract right or by insisting on his conscience.


Like Hegel's ethics, Comte's has the character of a reaction.  The
``positive'' (scientific) way of thinking is, according to Comte, the
best safeguard against anarchistic excesses (divagations anarchiques).
--- ``Esprit positif'' does not, however, come into play only in science;
it is already at work in sound human understanding (le bon
sens universel) and in the experiences of which it is the expression.  All human
development takes place within a society, which binds the individuals
together, so that a feeling of solidarity becomes possible.  Thereby
there is gradually developed a disinterested sympathy, an altruism (a
word coined by Comte to designate the opposite of egoism).  The
stages in spiritual development that precede the ``positive'' each favored
egoism in its own way.  At the theological stage
everyone is absorbed in his own personal salvation.  And at the ``metaphysical''
stage it is the single self that believes it finds truth through its intuitions and
% --- p. 69 ---
\opage{69}speculations.  At the ``positive'' stage, by contrast, one follows with attention the influence
that every action, every need and every feeling has on private
or social life, and on the basis of such experience the
rules for human conduct are formed.  Society is not merely a product
of human calculation; in that case it would never have come into being.
But at the properly human stage (as distinct from the animal)
reflection and social need work together (combinaison de
l’intelligence avec la sociabilité constitutes the human attribute).  (Discours
sur l’esprit positif. 1844).  In contrast to Hegel, Comte lays little
weight on the social institutions, in particular on the state.  Once the
right reflection and the sound, involuntary social life have developed,
such institutions will easily come into being.  In Comte's eyes the
social questions, as they are discussed by men of science
(``philosophers'') in interaction with employers (``patricians'') and
workers (``proletarians''), stand above the political ones and will more and more push
these aside.  (Politique positive. 1851–54).

While Romanticism, in its conservatism, proceeds from the organized
society and its authority over the individuals, positivism
proceeds from the living forces which may gradually lead to social
organizations.  But according to both conceptions ethics is social
ethics from first to last.  In the face of what conditions the continued existence of society
the single individual's desire for happiness or his own convictions become
a vanishing element, a drop in the ocean.  Hegel's line of thought
lies in this respect at the base of Karl Marx's grounding
of socialism (Das Kapital. 1867), to which we shall
return in a later section.  In purely philosophical form Wilhelm Wundt in
his great work on ethics (1887; 4th ed. in three volumes 1912) has taken up
Hegel's thoughts again on the basis of what has emerged since his time
in the way of facts and ideas.  In his preface
Wundt expressly acknowledges this kinship with Romanticism, which he praises
because it --- despite all its fantasies --- has widened the horizon
and paved the way for ``the more universal conception of spiritual life,
which is now a common possession of all the human sciences.''  The French sociological school has worked in connection
with Comte.  Its first man, Emile Durkheim, regards the dependence of the individuals
on society and the moral feeling thereby conditioned in them
as the fact underlying all morality (le fait
moral, se Bulletin de la Société française de Philosophie. 1906) and
has especially illuminated the development of modern industrialism in its
% --- p. 70 ---
\opage{70}connection with the advance of the division of labor within society
(La Division du travail social 1893).  The ethical theories developed by philosophical thinkers stand for the sociological view as
various attempts to rationalize the moral process that prevails involuntarily (in the
time and people of the thinker concerned).  ``A man's
conscience, or his moral ideal, however high it may
stand, is so to speak never his own work, except for a vanishing
small part.  Like the language he speaks, the
religion he professes, and the occupation he holds, they are the
results of constant participation in a social reality which is infinitely
more comprehensive, which existed for him, and which will outlive him.''
(Levy Bruhl: La Morale et la Science des Moeurs. 3rd ed. Préface).

In the face of conceptions like these there naturally arises, however, the
question on what the value of society ultimately rests, and who is
to decide whether this value is present in the individual case.
The problem of value cannot be dismissed by however thoroughgoing historical
or sociological demonstrations of the individual's social dependence.
And history itself demonstrates (and has not least since the close of the century
demonstrated) that it always depends on whether there
is something in the inner life of the individuals that asserts or confirms
the value and significance of society.  Under primitive conditions the individual
involuntarily shares the lot of society and follows its demands; here
education, tradition and faith in authority prevail.  But both Romanticism and
positivism have themselves shown how in spiritual and social
development a critical stage naturally sets in (which is designated now
as negation, now as differentiation), where what has hitherto stood
as self-evident is put under debate, a debate which will precisely concern
the value and justification of that in which one has hitherto involuntarily rested.
In such a critical period the individuals compare the demands of society
with the conditions given in experience.  And to this is added that
different social formations may occur within the same people.  Thus
church and state may stand against each other, aristocracy and democracy,
intellectual and material culture, employers and workers.  How
can this debate end?  Is there a rational solution to it?
Not to mention that different peoples or states stand as the expression
of different, perhaps mutually hostile social formations,
and which ``society'' then has right (value) on its
side?  It is no accident that Hegel and Comte, Wundt and Durkheim
with predilection dwell on ``organic'' periods or look toward
such in the future.

% --- p. 71 ---
\opage{71}In ethics one cannot refrain from discussing the psychological presuppositions.
And it will be necessary to seek out constantly operative
motives, which can make themselves felt in critical no less than in organic
periods.  Comte here relied on the altruistic (sympathetic)
feelings and their growth in the race and found in them the foundation of all
social ethics.  He has here English philosophers from the eighteenth century
(Hume and Adam Smith) as his predecessors.  Stuart Mill subjected
(in his treatise ``Utilitarianism'' 1861) Bentham's doctrine of utility to a
revision which led him to emphasize the significance of sympathetic feelings
as an element in moral feeling.  Herbert Spencer goes further
in this direction, at first in connection with Adam Smith.  He finds
in involuntary sympathy a foundation which through reflection
and understanding can be developed into the feeling of justice which alone
makes true ethics possible.  (Data of Ethics 1879. --- Justice 1891).  In the same
direction goes my exposition of ethics (1887. 4th ed. 1913), which
at the same time, however, stresses the epistemological presuppositions of ethics, which
are presumably far too often pushed aside on account of the still prevailing
dogmatism in the ethical domain.

The point is that, just as in the face of a purely social ethics it can always
be asked why just the interests of this particular society are to be taken
as the basis, one can in general in the face of any motive of evaluation
always ask why just that one is to be decisive.  The psychological
basis of ethical judgments is, no more than the sociological,
the same in all men and at all times.  The sporadic,
of which Sibbern spoke so much, makes itself felt not least
here.  A motive of evaluation cannot without further ado be forced upon everyone,
as the first presuppositions of logical and mathematical
thinking can be (because they are contained in all thinking).  There is then
no other way to go in a scientific treatment of ethics
than to procure an overview of the essential motives of evaluation
that can make themselves felt, and to investigate to what extent the evaluations
that must be made on the basis of them can be brought into mutual agreement.
Here there will perhaps sometimes prove to be an irreconcilable conflict.
But often it will prove that what from one motive of evaluation
stands as an end (with immediate value), from another stands
as a means (with mediate value).  Perhaps such a result
of the discussion can then gain retroactive force, so that the fundamental motive
concerned is shaken in its full dominion.  Each single exposition
of ethics must of course proceed from a determinate fundamental value, but
there must then be an express consciousness that the fundamental motive thereby
% --- p. 72 ---
\opage{72}determined has a struggle to endure in the face of other fundamental motives
that come forward with their demands.  The significance of the single exposition
will then depend on the light which it, through consistent application
of the fundamental motive and through the abundance of experiences by which this
application can be confirmed, casts on the nature of the fundamental motive.  The
Danish exposition mentioned proceeded for its part from the
feeling of humanity (altruism, universal sympathy) which developed
toward the close of classical antiquity, was thereupon in part deepened, in part
limited by Christianity, and later in the eighteenth century
was asserted with full consciousness by French and English thinkers. ---
It was the application of epistemological critique that led to this
conception, in natural connection with the predominant significance
which epistemological problems on the whole acquired toward the close of the century, as we shall see
later.

It has on the whole been characteristic of ethical theories in the nineteenth
century that the question of the relation of ethics to strict science
was given special treatment.  This question appears not only
in the form just mentioned, that is, with regard to the possibility of rational
and universally valid grounding of ethical evaluation.  It also appears
in the form that it is investigated whether ethics should rest on
presuppositions that stand in contradiction to those otherwise taken
as the basis in science.  Can ethics be reconciled with the recognition of the
lawfulness of nature, when we take ``nature'' in the widest sense, so
that the human life of the will also falls under it? --- One
could here hold that a real proof of the principle of causality
is not possible.  Hume's problem still stands.  But the talk
here is of the presuppositions without which science, here science
of real subjects, would not be possible; and to this the
principle of causality decidedly belongs.  We also see that even those who maintain ``freedom''
in the sense of freedom from having a cause, the so-called indeterminists,
endeavor to restrict this freedom to the least
possible.  So modest one was not in the good old days.  Often one means
by ``freedom'' merely that something new is put into the world
through human actions.  William James's standpoint
is here characteristic.  The only ``free will'' he acknowledges rests
on the character of novelty which can arise in a situation
where we act.  (Pragmatism 1907).  All acknowledge that something new can
arise, in the domain of the life of the will as in all other
domains.  Actions can surprise both the agent himself and
others.  But this character of novelty by no means abolishes the
% --- p. 73 ---
\opage{73}possibility of afterwards finding the cause of the arising of the new.  It goes
here as with the so-called mutations in the biological domain,
which precisely set the task of finding the cause of them.  The need to
find a cause, the need without which science of real subjects
would not have come into being, is itself explicable only by the fact that something
stands for us as new and surprising, perhaps in decided contrast
to what precedes, and that we nevertheless seek to get beyond this
difference.  This need is closely connected with the
nature of personality, which precisely expresses itself in a striving to get beyond the
chaotic, the incoherent.  And where the talk is of human
actions, it becomes then of quite particular significance that they
can be understood in their place within the whole personality of the agent.
If indeterminism has had to restrict itself in the course
of the nineteenth century, this is undoubtedly connected with a
deeper understanding of personal life.

The pragmatic point of view which James adopts leads him
to complain that the question of ``freedom'' has been put in such close
connection with ``accountability'' (this contemptible right to punish
which has made such a noice in past discursions on the subject).
As a pragmatist James looks forward, not backward.  The old
doctrine of retribution, on the other hand, which underlies the popular
conception of ``accountability,'' looked only backward, looked only at what
had been done, not at what the effects of the action and of the punishment would
be.  Kant conceived of remorse as a retributive punishment.  Already
Fichte looks differently at the matter when he declares that we have not
time to repent, because new action is constantly required of us.  He overlooks
that remorse, the painful consciousness of having erred (``the painful
identity''), can be necessary as a spur to future action.
But even then it is the effects of remorse, not its causes,
that are decisive for the value that is attributed to it.  Utilitarianism
exerts its quiet influence here even on those who do not acknowledge
it as a theory.  And it makes itself decidedly felt in modern theories of punishment,
which have abandoned the theory of retribution and rely on the deterrent
and educative effects of the treatment of punishment in order to ground
the right to punish.

Even though the discussion will for a long time yet move forward and backward,
the general direction in which thoughts have moved
in the nineteenth century is clear and beyond doubt.  What matters
is to give both life itself and the understanding of life what is due
to each.  Life unfolds now with clear consciousness, now
% --- p. 74 ---
\opage{74}unconsciously, and by both ways it can bring forth what stands as new
and wonderful; but the need for understanding constantly demands its right
and sets reflection in motion as soon as the prehistory of the action
can be surveyed.  We live forward but understand backward, a
Danish thinker has said.  How far understanding can reach is a matter
in itself.

--- Not only the relation to scientific understanding in general has
posed problems for ethics.  Quite especially Darwin's doctrine of
the struggle for existence was bound to arouse the attention of those who thought
about ethical questions.  It is in this connection a matter of indifference whether
one attributes to this doctrine significance for the understanding of the evolution of the species
or not.  What is at issue here is the fact that all
living beings must satisfy certain conditions in order to be able to subsist,
and that they perish when they are unable to.  It then depends
not on the value of a form of life whether it can subsist, but on the
external conditions, independent of all value, in which it is placed.  Here is
no difficulty, when at every moment, particularly in such
moments as when one is about to succumb in the struggle, one can invoke
a supernatural power capable of upholding the values.  But
an ethics that takes its stand on the ground of natural human life and of experience
seems here to face insuperable difficulties.  Will
not brutal force, ruthless egoism have the greatest prospect
of victory, however ideal the conditions of life it comes
to trample underfoot?  Fr. Jodl says in his ``Geschichte der
Ethik'' that the modern doctrine of evolution brought the greatest crisis
that ethics has had to go through in modern times.  It will have
its interest to see to what extent and how the attention of the philosophers
has been aroused to this question.

The first to be named here is Friedrich Albert Lange, the
brilliant author of ``Geschichte des Materialismus.''  He saw clearly
the significance of the struggle for existence as the foundation of the great
social problem.  As a creature of nature man seeks to assert himself and
to fight his way forward to conditions that satisfy and secure the impulse of self-preservation.
This impulse one cannot get around.  It
yields only when either another, stronger impulse is raised against it,
or when it can be satisfied by ways that make possible the
satisfaction of other men's impulse of self-preservation.  All ethical and
social endeavors must therefore carry on a struggle for existence and
set a higher and better right in place of the mere right of self-preservation.
In this spirit Lange illuminated the social question in his writing
% --- p. 75 ---
\opage{75}``Die Arbeiterfrage'' (1865), a few years after Darwin's famous book
had appeared.  Darwin himself came upon the problem in his second
principal work (Descent of man. 1871).  He pointed out that the qualities
which the struggle for existence strengthens are not only those that are beneficial
to the single individual, but also those that are to the benefit of the helpless
offspring or of the group to which the individual belongs.  The sympathetic
feelings too have their natural history, not only the egoistic.  And
when the need to live together with others (sociability) and the capacity for
fellow-feeling with others (sympathy) are combined with memory and reflection,
there is a foundation for the development of ethical feeling.  Darwin
here stands at a standpoint similar to Comte's.  And he refers
to the fact that the qualities which men at different times regard as
virtues are closely connected with the extent to which men
come into contact with other men.  In a similar spirit Bartholomäus Carneri (``Sittlichkeit und Darwinismus'' 1871)
took up the question, though he emphasized more than Darwin the
power of thinking to raise man above the animal stage,
so that in spite of and through the struggle for existence there could take place
a growth in the direction of magnanimity, self-control and harmony.  For
my part I laid the emphasis, in a little writing ``Om Grundlaget for den
humane Etik'' (1876), on the fact that the struggle for existence always
means a struggle to preserve the determinate form or kind of existence
in which one lives.  It is not merely bare existence that is at stake;
man fights to exist in and for that which has the
highest value for him, whatever that may be.  Therefore the ethical
striving too is a struggle for existence.  Later (``Etik''. 1887) I have
shown more closely that self-assertion in and of itself is an ethical end, since
society consists of and in single individuals; self-preservation and self-development
are therefore a duty which the single individual has not only toward himself,
but also toward society.  And further, that devotion and
sacrifice do not stand in absolute opposition to self-assertion, but,
where they are genuine, are due to a surplus of energy that makes it possible
to fight for that which is not necessary for one's own, isolated
self-preservation.  And finally I have stated that ethics does not stand and fall
with faith in a progress within the world of experience, such
as many evolutionists have assumed.  ``Even if the victorious
tendency in the course of the world ran counter to ethics, the ethical principles
would not be shaken.  There would be greater use for pity
and resignation; but where the ethical disposition was present,
one would hold with the defeated cause, though the gods held with the
% --- p. 76 ---
\opage{76}victor.  Ethical value does not rest on mere might.  He who
follows his conscience can of course do so only because it is the
strongest thing in himself; but he does not do so because it is the strongest
in the world.''

The most considerable of the authors who have sought to make the concept of evolution
and the doctrine of evolution fruitful for ethics is Herbert
Spencer, whose ``Data of Ethics'' appeared in 1879 to be incorporated later
as a part of his comprehensive ``Principles of Ethics.''  I therefore dwell
somewhat more closely on him, without being able to go into the interesting
thoughts of Rolph (Biologische Probleme. 1880), L. Stephen (The
Science of Ethics. 1882) and Alexander (Moral Order and Progress.
1889).  Spencer criticizes utilitarianism, as Bentham and Mill
had conceived it, because in his opinion it was inclined to
keep to the nearest effects of actions.  Since mental life, like
everything else in the world, is subject to evolution, one will by attending to
the general law of evolution find the foundation of the ideal toward which
one can strive.  The perfect human life will present the picture
of a harmony between concentration and differentiation, like
every evolution that completes its course.  And in this harmony
self-preservation and sympathy are united, whereby the principle of welfare comes
into its own.  Spencer lays particular weight here on the fact that a man's faculties
do not come to full development when he limits his striving
to his own, isolated ends.  There are forces which only through
altruism come to full unfolding.  With this will follow a
limitation of one's own freedom where it would involve encroachment
upon the equally justified freedom of others.  To his surprise Spencer arrives
here (Justice 1891, fourth part of ``Principles of Ethics'') at the same
result as Kant.  But the existing society goes, according to Spencer,
in its demands far beyond the limit thus set, in that it
undertakes tasks that ought to be left to the free, altruistic
activity of individuals.  On the whole the existing social order satisfies
the demands of ethics far from adequately.  Militarism, which by compulsion bends man
to obedience and regards obedience as the highest virtue,
and industrialism, which demands work for the sake of livelihood, must
give place to a type of life in which work is practiced not merely for the sake of
the result, but because it is immediately attractive and satisfying.
A model of this we have in intellectual and artistic
work.  The time will come when the sense of duty is unnecessary,
in that there has developed an ``organic morality'' which makes right
% --- p. 77 ---
\opage{77}action as natural and involuntary as a mother's care for her
child and the artist's work on his work is.

--- The ``naturalistic'' character which an ethics built on the concept of evolution and
the principle of welfare acquires has provoked critique from the ``idealistic''
side.  As considerable works in this direction must be named
Guyau's ``La Morale Anglaise Contemporative'' (1879) and Sorley's
``Ethics and Naturalism'' and his ``Recent Tendencies in Ethics''
(1904).  The dispute here concerns mainly whether an inner connection can be demonstrated
between the stages by which, according to the doctrine of evolution,
life's elementary need and force can be converted into forms
that may rightly be called ``higher.''  It is at once a dispute between
continuity and discontinuity in the ethical domain (in that
``idealism'' will deny that connection) and an epistemological
dispute about the grounding of the standard according to which an expression of will
is called higher or lower than another.  Here, as in
other domains, subjects enough are left for discussion in the new
century.

\sectionhead{β.}{Epistemology.}

For the greater part of the century those who philosophized
had been concerned predominantly with winning a world-view.
Among positivists and Romantics alike a systematic
tendency made itself felt.  In the face of the cosmological (metaphysical) problem
the problem of knowledge had been pushed aside, if one disregards
Stuart Mill's energetic attempt at the middle of the century to let
Hume's problem come to the fore again.  But he did not see that the problem,
whether it could be solved or not, now had to be posed differently.
On the side of both of the two philosophical tendencies Kant had been regarded
far too much as a standpoint that had been overcome.  This
greatest philosopher of modern times had shortly before the beginning of the century
completed a profound investigation of human
knowledge, its forms, its presuppositions and its limits, and
had declared such an investigation to be the most important task of philosophy.
In urgent words he had impressed the importance of
what he called ``the scientific self-knowledge of reason.''  Both
Romantics and positivists saw a predecessor in Kant's philosophy; but
they thought they had given it all that was due to it, and had taken up
in their new views everything in it that had lasting significance.
Later in the century minds were occupied with the grandiose
extension and carrying through of the theories of natural science.
% --- p. 78 ---
\opage{78}The question must nevertheless naturally force itself forward: why did
Romanticism go too far in its speculations?  why did positivism
not go far enough?  by what right does natural science come forward with
a claim to universal validity?  It is one and the same question that
underlies these three questions.  And if it is raised in earnest,
it must lead to taking up the problem of knowledge again.  Epistemological
points of view had now not wholly vanished.  Fries
and Schopenhauer in Germany, Kierkegaard in Denmark and Renouvier
in France had maintained that Kant was no standpoint that had been overcome,
and that his way of posing the problem must still be of the greatest
importance.  And when the philosophical discussion in the last part of
the century apparently presents the curiosity that the philosophy of Romanticism,
in particular Hegel's philosophy, after having been driven from the scene
in Germany, gains diffusion and adherence in England,
America and Italy, a closer examination of the most important works
belonging here shows that the whole standpoint is rather
Kant's than Hegel's.  We meet thoughts from the concluding section of the ``Elementarlehre''
in the ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' (the doctrine of ideas as
ideals of knowledge, which cannot be shaped into strictly scientific
knowledge).  This holds of the most important work in this whole
group, Francis Herbert Bradley's brilliant work ``Appearance and
Reality'' (1893), which has rightly been called the book that in the
last generation has exerted the greatest influence on philosophical thinking
in the English-speaking countries.  Proceeding from the view that all thinking
sets its subjects in mutual relation to one another (the relational
way of thought), and that only complete experience can reveal
reality to us (complete experience the standard of reality), he draws
the consequence that a closure of our knowledge is impossible;
ever new relations need closer determination, and experience
can ever become more complete.  That he does not become a skeptic
is because he maintains (not always with full consistency)
that ``the Absolute'' does not lie remote, beyond everything limited, but makes
itself felt at every stage.  Every stage has its truth; no
province is severed from the whole realm of truth.  A kindred line of thought
is found in Josiah Royce in America (The World and the Individual.
1900) and in Benedetto Croce in Italy (Logica come scienza
del concetto puro. 2. ed. 1909 --- Ciò che è vivo e ciò ê morto
della filosofia di Hegel. 1907).  Croce has expressly declared (in a
``Critique de moimême,'' which was translated in Revue de Métaphysique et
de Morale. 1919) that when his conception has often been designated
% --- p. 79 ---
\opage{79}as neo-Hegelianism, one could with just as much right designate it
as neo-Kantianism or neo-positivism, and he rightly points out
that the features most characteristic of Hegel's system
are lacking in him.

Although Kant could thus not be said to have been forgotten, it was yet
natural that an endeavor stirred to take up Kant's
problem again.  In the last generation of the century the cry
accordingly also sounded: ``Back to Kant!''  At times this battle-cry perhaps became merely
the introduction to purely historical-philological studies of Kant's works;
but these too were necessary and had the significance of fixing attention
on the elements in his philosophy that were the most essential,
and which one had often lightly pushed aside.  For independent
thinkers the said watchword meant a resumption of the
problem of knowledge itself.  If a single work is to be named which can be said
to mark a turning point, it must be Friedrich Albert Lange's
``Geschichte des Materialismus'' (1866).  Aroused by him, but in turn acting
back upon him (as can be seen from the second edition of the said book)
Hermann Cohen began his ardent Kant studies, which first led
him to a thoroughgoing correction of the current conception of Kant
(Kant's Theorie der Erfahrung. 1871), later gradually to the development
of an independent epistemology (Logik der reinen Erkenntniss.
1902).  Cohen is the founder of the so-called Marburg school,
the most energetic and influential epistemological
tendency of the present.  Characteristic of this tendency is that scientific
thinking is set in sharp contrast to the ordinary life of consciousness,
as this involuntarily unfolds itself through
sensation, memory and spontaneous reflection.  Kant had shown that natural science
comes into being by the individual observations being shown to be
members of a great whole (``Nature''), whose individual parts are connected with one another
with logical-mathematical necessity.  He admitted,
however, that between the necessity of thought which strict science lays
at its base and the observations at hand there is only a relation of
analogy (cfr. the section ``Die Analogien der Erfahrung'' in ``Kritik der
reinen Vernunft''), not, as within pure logic and mathematics,
a relation of identity.  This concession to empirical philosophy
the Marburg school takes back, in that it regards it as an
after-effect from Locke and Hume, an after-effect that had hindered
Kant from solving Hume's problem.  The observations are, when they have
gone through the sharp examination of thought, to be able to make complete
confession of what they fundamentally contain, and this content
% --- p. 80 ---
\opage{80}comes into its full right through the equations in which natural science
expresses its results.  Differences of quality and time
have vanished without a trace in the scientific conception, --- and
vanished to such a degree that the founder of the Marburg school is not merely astonished,
but indignant that Hume could have found so great a difficulty
in the transition from quality to quality and from moment to moment.
--- As the Marburg school corrects Kant, it leads
not only back to Plato, but beyond him to Parmenides of
Elea, and it is with full consciousness that it acknowledges this kinship.

In a peculiar contrast to criticism, especially as
it was developed in the Marburg school, there appears the so-called pragmatism,
which lays weight on the fact that it is always determinate needs,
certain express tasks, that determine the forms and principles of our thinking.  We form, this tendency maintains, the concepts and
set up the maxims that we have need of.  The forms of knowledge
are determined by the tasks which the subjects set us, and are not, as
zealous Kantians hold, independent of these.  Pragmatism arose
at about the same time in different places.  The name is American,
derives from the mathematician and philosopher Charles Peirce, who maintained
(in a treatise of 1878) that in order to find out the meaning of a thought,
one must look to what action it leads to; if there is no
difference between two thoughts in this respect, then there is in general
no difference between them.  William James took up some years
later (1898) both the idea and the expression pragmatism.  For him it was
not merely a theoretical idea; not only intellectual, but also
practical needs condition our thoughts; not only our science,
but also our faith is always built up pragmatically.  The famous
physicist Maxwell (died 1879), who also left philosophical
treatises behind, saw the progress of the exact sciences as conditioned by the fact
that one could form conceptions of the subjects that could at once
represent every special subject and make rigorous inference
beyond the subjects at hand possible.  He too saw the significance of principles
in their being usable, in particular for directing definite questions
to the subjects at hand.  Maxwell arrived at this conception
of knowledge through his experiences as a working physicist.
But he was also influenced by his teacher in philosophy William Hamilton,
who precisely laid strong weight on the self-activity of thinking
as more important than all single results, and who even set up the
paradox that a living error was better than a dead truth.
% --- p. 81 ---
\opage{81}Through Maxwell Ernst Mach (from 1863 on) has come to kindred
ideas of knowledge and has found them confirmed by thoroughgoing
studies of the history of the natural sciences.  His concluding
work is ``Erkenntniss und Irrtum'' (1905).  He stresses particularly
(here in connection with Spencer) the development of knowledge as a constant
adaptation, which leads to thinking the subjects with the greatest possible economy,
which shows itself in our preferring the simplest explanations,
--- in our rather reshaping old thoughts according to the new subjects
than forming wholly new ones, --- and in our working with analogies in order to let
one domain of subjects illuminate another.  Richard Avenarius (1876) joins
the inquirers named, in that he had by his own way come
to conceive philosophy as ``the thinking of the world according to the principle
of the smallest measure of force'' (as the title of his habilitation writing runs),
a conception he later developed at length in his principal work
 ``Kritik der reinen Erfahrung'' (1888---90).
In the attempts at epistemology that have appeared in Danish literature,
standpoints are adopted which make it possible to let both
pragmatism and criticism come into their own.  Thus when
Kroman (``Vor Naturerkendelse''. 1883) declares the fundamental
principles of knowledge to be pure postulates, but at the same time teaches that
our impulse of self-preservation leads us to set up certain quite determinate
postulates and not others.  Likewise when the author of this exposition
in his Psykologi (1882) showed how the involuntary
need for action already leads to performing experiments which impress upon us
the connection of things, and how practical
needs thereupon awaken wishes and expectations, which are provisionally held fast
until experience either confirms or rejects them.  A germ
of the principle of causality lies already in the involuntary orienting oneself in
the world, which tacitly proceeds from the view that everything that exists must stand
in unavoidable connection with one another.  In ``Den menneskelige Tanke''
(1910) it is shown how the development of the forms of knowledge is conditioned
by the questions or problems that are posed, but how
already the fact that a problem, a question, can be posed at all
presupposes an energy which expresses itself through spiritual work in determinate
forms.  A problem arises only when there is either something in
our conceptions which needs to be filled out, or when there is
mutual contradiction between the conceptions we have formed.  In
both cases there is presupposed the capacity to combine and compare,
of which Kant had so clear a view, and which he called
synthesis.  The single forms of this activity of thought (the
% --- p. 82 ---
\opage{82}categories) come forth under the interaction with emerging subjects that
the history of science demonstrates, and can thereafter be ordered in a series advancing from the
general to the special. ---

Kant had sanguine conceptions concerning the possible completion
of the critical philosophy he had founded.  Not only did he think
he had set up a definitive list of categories, but he even stated
in the concluding words of the ``Kritik der reinen Vernunft'' (1781) that everything that
human reason could require for its satisfaction could
be attained before the close of the century.  The Marburg school, the
ablest reviver of criticism at the close of the nineteenth century,
cannot, as we have seen, be acquitted of a certain dogmatism either.
Pragmatism is a salutary counterweight on this point.  It points
(like evolutionism) to the possibility that the forms of thought
and presuppositions at which we finally stop, and which according to Kant
were to be the expression of the innermost essence of the human faculty of
knowledge itself, could themselves be derived in relation to more deeply lying
principles whose time has not yet come (if it ever
comes).  Epistemology would in this respect stand before
a situation similar to that of modern physics, which still recognizes
the maxims from which the physics of the seventeenth century
proceeded, but sees the possibility that they could be derived in relation
to maxims whose time is only now coming.  Criticism will
always retain the last word in the face of pragmatism, but when will
the moment come when it has said its last word?

\sectionhead{γ.}{Cosmology (``Metaphysics'').}

But now the problem which for the philosophers of earlier times stood as
the real, the central philosophical problem, and which one often believed
one could immerse oneself in without taking epistemological detours, ---
the problem of the ultimate ground of existence, the metaphysical, or as
I prefer to call it, the cosmological problem?  Can we
have a grounded thought (Logos) about the world as a whole (Cosmos)?
What fate has this problem had in the nineteenth century?
--- For Romanticism it stood as the only problem; for positivism
it was no longer any problem; for criticism it lies infinitely
far out on the horizon of thought; pragmatism holds (in
some of its forms) that it can solve it with a practical postulate.
Yet there also exist more thoroughgoing considerations on its
problem and its significance.

% --- p. 83 ---
\opage{83}It has been shown in the foregoing that eminent inquirers, to whom this
problem lay seriously at heart, had become clear that the only
way by which one could arrive at a conception of what holds
the world together in its innermost was the way of analogy.  One had
come away from the belief that a definitive result here could be reached
by the way of pure thinking, of strict deduction.  Only
one was not clear what the ground really is why one is forced out onto the way of analogy
at every closure or rounding off of knowledge.  Several inquirers have taken up this side of the question.  Thus
Fouillée (L’Avenir de la Métaphysique. 1889), the author of
the present exposition (Filosofiske Problemer 1902. --- Den menneskelige
Tanke. 1910), Dilthey and Wundt (Kultur der Gegenwart I,
6. 1907).  Among older inquirers Fries is especially to be named.

Analogy plays a great role in all science, in that inquiry illuminates
the one domain of experience or domain of thought by means of
the other.  Whether the chosen analogies hold, that is, whether they can
be carried through with full consistency (without ``the comparison limping''), one
will in the single, special cases be able to decide by testing whether
a series of subjects within the one domain corresponds point for point
to a series of subjects within the other domain, perhaps
even so that full proportionality obtains (not merely relationality,
but identity of relation) between the two series.  In the last
case one can apply what Mill has called the method of
proportional changes.  But in the case of the cosmological problem, which is to
concern existence (``the world'') as a whole, as comprehended into
a unity in a fundamental law or a concluding principle, one is cut off
from proceeding by means of such formations of series.  Existence
as a whole is not a subject for our thinking that could be compared
with other subjects.  It ``does not step forth as one object
among others, several.''  We know existence only through all the various
subjects which our knowledge can face, and in every group of subjects
existence reveals itself in a different way, without our
yet having any certainty that its innermost essence is exhausted by
the subjects that stand at the disposal of our knowledge.  Since it is now
--- in any case at the point of development which science has so far
reached --- not possible to lead all subjects back to a single
subject, a basic subject (``Urfänomen''), there will be no other
way than to use a single subject, or a single group of subjects,
to characterize existence as a whole.  And the different
sciences then contend for the right to be decisive for this
% --- p. 84 ---
\opage{84}characterization.  The history of the problem shows how one has constantly
gone the way of building on an analogy between the totality of existence and
a single subject, to which one, with clear awareness or quite involuntarily, ascribed
fundamental significance.  Thought (logic) or on the whole mental life
(psychology) as the characterizing subject leads to idealism; physical
and chemical processes (natural science), regarded as primal phenomena,
lead to materialism.  If one takes as basis the fact
that general laws prevail in the world, so that it thereby appears
as a unity, one gets a monism (which in turn can take on an
idealistic or materialistic stamp); if one holds to the fact that the subjects
are different, and that new, surprising subjects can constantly emerge,
one gets a pluralism (which likewise can in turn be either
idealistic or materialistic).  And to this is added the ethical
interest, which often leads to seeing existence as the home for the
unfolding of values, perhaps under hard opposition.  In the choice of a
characteristic subject which every cosmological attempt presupposes, it is
very often this interest that, with greater or lesser consciousness,
underlies it.  Fichte therefore declared in his time that the philosophy
one chooses depends on what kind of man one is.  And Jacobi
added that every philosophy has its holy place.

When clarity comes over this relation, it cannot arouse
surprise that philosophers more and more let the cosmological
problem lie and merely set it up as a limiting problem.  Those who
in our day venture with full confidence to give a positive answer are
for the most part not philosophers by profession.  If it is nevertheless maintained that
there is here a real problem, and that it is of importance to set it up
with full clarity, this is for two reasons, which Kant has already
pointed to. --- First, the human mind works in the face of
all subjects to comprehend them into a whole, and limits cannot
be drawn in advance for this striving.  There sounds here
an Excelsior, which springs from the innermost nature of thought.  When it
can no longer be heard, that means the death of the life of thought.  Even though
it is clear that an absolute closure is not possible here, there will
yet be a need for a provisional rounding off, even if this were to hold
only for a single generation or in the end only for a single
thinking personality.  And every serious striving
in this direction can have its significance, if not directly, then
at least through its side effects, through the light that is cast
on the nature of human thinking or on the nature of the single age
or the single people, or in any case on the character of the single
% --- p. 85 ---
\opage{85}thinking personality.  Even where it ends with a question,
this can be of great significance; the nature of human thought
shows itself no less in being able to ask than in
being able to answer, and the capacity to ask rightly is in the long run the most important.
If it is so that an absolute closure of knowledge is impossible, then the last word of thought must be a question. --- Second,
despite all critique there will again and again show itself an involuntary
tendency to conclude, in that now supposedly theoretical, now supposedly
ethical-religious or poetic motives lead to maintaining a
determinate light as that in which ``the world'' both can and must be seen.  Here
there is need of a vigilant philosophy, which can keep order in the
spiritual domain, so that immature conceptions do not obtain rank
as the highest wisdom.  Precisely because it is often ideal motives that
lead to cosmological speculations, what matters is a critique that
can distinguish between illusory satisfaction and the valuable
starting point.  What matters is to keep dogmatism out without, however,
hampering the constant striving after truth, which for great spirits
has had greater value than possession would have had.

Tegnér says in a letter (to Hagberg. 26 Nov. 1820) that poetry
is mankind's purest, highest, most human expression, and that
everything we regard as noble and high is nothing but modifications
of it.  Religion is a poetry limited on practical grounds, ``circumcised,''
and science, especially ``metaphysics,'' is ``castrated'' poetry.  There
is this truth in the remark, that man's great urge to expand,
his infinite longing, can be satisfied only imperfectly through
the conceptions of religion and the concepts of science and above all
must not be confused with them.  It is possible that a great and high poetry
will some day replace both religion and ``metaphysics,'' and that the boundary between
science and art will be able to be drawn with full definiteness,
without any spiritual loss being felt in observing this boundary.

% --- p. 86 ---
\parthead{II. SOCIAL LIFE}
\sectionhead{1.}{The Social Question.}

\opage{86}In the eighteenth century social and political questions had already
before the Revolution been discussed with great energy and ruthlessness,
but only within a small circle of free spirits, who were even
very apprehensive of the thought that these discussions should
be able to influence larger circles.  They felt quite sure, however, that
``enlightenment would not reach the suburbs''; free discussion
and the perspectives of the future to which it led were to and must be reserved
for ``respectable people.''  Although in the eighteenth century there stirred
a consciousness of the existence of the social problem, it was nevertheless,
until the Revolution had gained speed, limited to a few.  It
is Jean Jacques Rousseau who has posed the social problem through
his critique of modern culture, which by the division of labor in the
material domain makes the individual worker a machine or
even merely a link in a machine, and which in the spiritual domain
detaches the life of thought from its natural connection with instinct
and feeling.  The involuntary forms of life are threatened with dissolution.

The changed position which the social question acquires in the course of
the nineteenth century is conditioned first by the fact that the distress in the world of labor
increased or at any rate was felt more strongly, but second by the fact
that conditions in the domain of material culture became more sharply
illuminated through growing experience and more thorough reflection, a
reflection that was awakened in people in all strata of society.  The
decisive peculiarity in the appearance of the question in the nineteenth
century consists precisely in all classes of society
taking part in its discussion.  Of this one had as yet no examples
in history.  The obscure multitude that constituted the
lowest stratum of societies had hitherto made itself heard only through
revolt --- slave revolts,
peasant wars, etc. --- Now it itself came forward in order,
through its deliberations and resolutions, to help find
% --- p. 87 ---
\opage{87}ways out for the ailment of society.  The Revolution's proclamation of liberty,
equality and fraternity awakened the conception of an ideal in relation
to which reality had to come to stand in a harsher
light than as long as one had had no inkling of new possibilities.
``Enlightenment'' had reached the suburbs.  One got beyond the
eighteenth century's aristocracy of the spirit.  Among many in the better situated
classes an understanding and a practical sympathy made themselves felt
which had hitherto been lacking.  To a great extent it was also
men of these classes who took the lead in the discussion and directed
the work that led to progress.  It was of great importance that
the intellectual and the material forces could meet, so that the discussion
of the great problem could be undertaken, not only by those who
had time and capacity for carrying through reflection and thorough study,
but also by those who suffered directly under the conditions.

It was naturally not always an elite from both sides that conducted
the discussion, and not infrequently it was interrupted by violence and excesses.
During the class struggle that developed on account of the conflicting
interests, taunts were hurled from both sides --- at times
it was the same derisive designation that both parties used.  Characteristic
is especially the role that the word ``mass'' came to play.  From the
conservative side the workers were called ``the great mass.''  They
were in the first period of the century still unorganized, without firm order
and without clear conceptions of their own advantage as little as of the
conditions of social life.  Then there fell away, for an aristocratic view
(which was far from an aristocracy of the spirit), all awareness
that one stood in the face of personal, individual beings who wished
to live life in a human manner, and it was feared that
in the chaos one thought one saw before one, all culture, or at any rate what
one regarded as culture, would perish.  On the other side the workers
and their leaders used the word mass as a taunt against their
opponents from other social strata, whom they regarded as unjustified
enjoyers of what they had not themselves produced, and they had
no understanding of the inventiveness and energy, of the work in
the service of inquiry and progress, which the third estate
had rendered.  Both parties were moreover inclined to think that the problem
was wholly new.  And yet it is a question that under various
forms runs through the whole of world history, and which --- strange
as it is, but psychologically understandable --- presents itself especially just
after certain advances have been made in the direction of emancipation.  As long as
bondage or serfdom lasted, the single bondman
% --- p. 88 ---
\opage{88}or serf still belonged to the house or to the estate, could feel solidarity
with its interests and have his existence secured by belonging
to this determinate, narrow circle, just as the master's self-interest
had to lead to providing help and protection.  But when the patriarchal
order had led to abuse, and when the relation of dependence therefore
loosened or was dissolved, this emancipation led to the single
freed man being isolated and referred to fighting the battle of life on his own
account.  Then a social question arises.  Protection has disappeared,
and no new refuge, no new support is to be found.  Poverty
developed in the Middle Ages especially after the cessation of personal slavery,
and a similar increase of distress arose with the cessation of serfdom
and with the abolition of the guilds.  The abolition
of the old forms was in each of these cases an act of justice
on account of the great abuses that had taken place, but
at the same time posed problems that could be solved only by new expressions of the
justice that had led to the emancipation.  These new expressions were slow
in coming, for a historical view on account of shortsightedness
on both sides.

Were a determinate point of time to be indicated as decisive for the
social question of modern times, the German economist Lujo
Brentano has presumably rightly emphasized the turn which was brought about
by world trade from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries on gaining decisive
influence on production, so that this was not, as hitherto,
predominantly determined by domestic or local need.  Exchange value
now gained predominance over use value.  More capital
and more workers were now needed than the localized turnover had
required.  And the new hosts of workers came from the country, in the beginning
especially freed or fugitive serfs.  Thereby began the influx
from country to town, which in the eighteenth century Rousseau and
other authors complained of, and in which they saw a phenomenon of dissolution.

It was thus not a wholly new problem that the nineteenth century had
to wrestle with, but a problem that had developed through centuries,
although it now acquired a quite peculiar sting, partly on account
of the development of economic conditions, partly on account of the most immediate
preceding age's critique and revolution.  No wonder that
it has weighed upon many, and not the least, of the century's
people like a nightmare, and is directly or indirectly connected
with the pessimistic current that again and again surfaces in
the course of the century.  Nor any wonder that the century, despite
much good will and great ability, comes to leave the problem
% --- p. 89 ---
\opage{89}to its successor or successors.  But the consciousness of its
existence is awakened as never before, and through the discussion in science,
in the press and in the popular assemblies provision has in any case been
made that it will not so easily vanish.

\sectionhead{2.}{Practical Progress.}

Even though there were some who already at the beginning of the century
saw the difficulties for social life that lay in the labor question,
there prevailed nevertheless on the whole in the first decades a confidence
that one was on the right path.  Both personal freedom
and freedom of trade had after all been proclaimed!  Now everyone could take hold according to
his ability and his inclination.  In economic activity one saw either, with Adam
Smith, a need laid down by Providence in human nature, whose
effects were bound to be to the benefit of society, if it were only
allowed to move with full freedom, and that it could now, --- or
one saw in it an expression of a natural law, which worked with necessity
and would surely be able to heal the ills it might for a time
bring with it.

It must surely be maintained that the conception that proclaimed free
enterprise as the one thing needful and trusted the impulse of self-preservation
in the individuals as the best guide, arose among the spiritual leaders of the age
either from religious presuppositions or else from the conviction
that the one right way to general welfare was for everyone
to look after himself.  Jeremy Bentham, the most considerable philosopher of law of the age,
saw in the prudence with which individual men work
each for his own happiness the sure foundation of right and morality.  He was
himself guided by sympathy with men.  It was by virtue of this sympathy
that he rejoiced in the harmony of interests which he
was sure would reveal itself when all followed their
self-interests with prudence. --- Naturally there were not a few for whom this
faith in the harmony of interests was a welcome ground for isolating
themselves, looking after their own advantage, baking their own cake, and so letting
the others look after themselves, whether they had a cake to bake
or not.

For the workers, on the other hand, it was bound to appear as if
it were a wholly strange world into which they had come.  They had their
freedom, but they also had their empty hands, and the increasing
use of machines seemed bound to diminish the use there
could be for human labor.  What were they then to use their
% --- p. 90 ---
\opage{90}freedom for?  In the face of the absurdities, incomprehensible to them, that they
encountered, despair and defiance often found vent in the destruction of machines
and in other disorders.

Thus on the one side one trusted in the blessed effects of
freedom, on the other side one did not see what one was to use freedom
for. --- It turned out, as a Danish author has expressed
it, that the goddess of freedom did not, as many believed, heal all
wounds, but that she only laid them bare.

The principle of freedom had in the American and French Revolutions been
proclaimed as a self-evident truth.  But the proclamation itself
had been called forth by the experiences that had been
had of abuses and oppressions to which old, self-outliving
institutions gave occasion.  Since the associations of the past,
in particular the guilds, had led to abuses, one went in one's zeal
so far as to forbid all associations, both among employers
with one another and among workers with one another.  This prohibition
stems from Turgot's ministry.  It was repealed at his
fall, but issued again during the Revolution (1791), and a corresponding
law was issued in England (1799).  Later too the theorists
long regarded industrial associations as pernicious,
because they hindered the ``free'' use of forces.  And the workers themselves
were long in realizing that the prohibition of associations was the
most important obstacle on their path.  Even the radical English politicians,
who worked for the repeal of the prohibition, because it conflicted with
the principle of freedom, which must surely also comprise freedom to join
with others, --- even they thought that the repeal of the prohibition
would have no essential effects.  It was to turn out
quite differently.

In spite of the prohibition the workers had formed associations, which were
persecuted (while no action seems to have been taken against the employers'
associations).  But the most important workers' associations held
the struggle out.  And when the prohibition was repealed in England (1824), on which
occasion Francis Place especially, who later played a great role
in the first parliamentary reform, was active, association took
speed.  Craft unions were formed and joined together (into Trade
Unions), and there now showed itself a great solidarity within the working
class.

The development in England became a model for the course of things in other
countries, and we need not follow this in detail.  With the great
associations --- besides craft unions: producers' and consumers'
% --- p. 91 ---
\opage{91}cooperatives --- a new social and political power had entered the world.
It was then a wholly new principle that underlay it, for the right to
association was, as the radical English politicians saw, a
consequence of the principle of freedom; association was a continuation of
emancipation.  At the same time association was a preparation for the
brotherhood that, though proclaimed later than freedom,
was thought to belong closely together with it.  This association
within the working class is the greatest social event of the nineteenth
century.  It came into being after much groping and amid much envy.
--- I permit myself to repeat here what I said on this in
a speech at the University in my last lecture hour in the nineteenth
century (19 Dec. 1900).

``A social movement like that which has taken place in the nineteenth century
no earlier age has been able to show.  Hitherto history had
moved over the heads of the great mass.  The historical
struggles were fought out between the higher strata of society, and the obscure
multitude took no active part in them.  At first slowly, but then
with increasing speed the emancipation and organization of the working class
has advanced, and it has become possible for it in an independent
manner to take part in the public discussion and in the work of legislation.
Immature humanity has not waited for the ideas to come
