to it; it has grown up, so that it could itself catch sight of the ideas
and become receptive to them.  For with the advancing organization
and the increasing independence the need for participation in ideal culture
has also risen in the great multitude ..... Never
in history has ideal culture had so broad a basis in the human race
as now.  Its finest works will always be born in solitude,
and it will for the present, perhaps forever, directly and with full
understanding be able to be enjoyed by only few; but through intermediaries and
many conversions it can now come to the benefit of ever growing circles.
Whatever difficulties may remain, --- the time of dullness and
blindness is past.''

--- As long as the associations comprised only the skilled workers,
they signified an aristocracy within the working class.  It is
now once and for all so that development proceeds by strata, and the difference, in part
the contrast, between the various strata of workers constantly makes itself felt,
milder or stronger, in the subsequent history of the social question.
But the socialist ideas, which more and more gained scope,
led to a widening of the framework and to the organization of the
unskilled workers.  The whole movement is, however, not merely an
% --- p. 92 ---
\opage{92}application of the principle of freedom to ground the right to association;
for through the associations the self-esteem of the individuals grows, the horizon
of their sympathies is widened and the need for knowledge is awakened.  And
the struggle did not concern merely the assertion of a human standard of living;
they strove for a shortening of the working day, so that there might be
time and strength left over for participation in spiritual culture.  The worker
felt himself to be something other and more than a mere means for production and
was himself recognized as one of those for whom production was to
come to benefit.  What a great moral philosopher had stated toward the close
of the eighteenth century, --- that every human being is to be regarded as
an end and never merely as a means, --- that now moved toward its realization.

Of great importance it also became that a regular negotiation
with the other classes was now possible, partly through the overview of
economic conditions that the workers themselves could now more easily gain,
partly by courts of arbitration now being able to be established, before which the
interests of the various groups can be weighed, and their conduct attacked
and defended.  Through this the other classes of society are educated
no less than the workers; they learn that there are other social worlds
than their own, and they learn to know the limits of their
own justified demands.  In the negotiations that were conducted it has
often turned out that it was two ethical systems that stood opposed to each other.
There was often a lack of presuppositions recognized by both parties.
Often it was external compromises that for a time halted the struggle;
but through the whole course of the strife it could yet be traced that the presuppositions
approached one another.

\sectionhead{3.}{The Struggle of Theories.}

As can be seen from the practical development characterized in
the foregoing, this development takes place involuntarily and often unconsciously
under the influence of certain presuppositions, which either are due merely to
the experiences of the past or also contain germs of new directions of thought.
Thus the principle of freedom led beyond the limitation
that for a time one had wished to set for its application; free association
was its inevitable consequence, and this in turn led to new
relations of power within society.  The organized workers stand
now as a power in the state.

With this another point was also connected.  The principle of freedom
had had its significance in opening the possibility of initiatives, of
% --- p. 93 ---
\opage{93}new directions of work and new institutions.  It became of significance for
production.  The older political economy (Adam Smith and his
successors) was essentially a theory of production and its conditions.
But gradually the question of distribution pushed itself
to the foreground beside the question of production.  It
turned out, namely, that the law of the harmony of interests did not in fact
hold for the existing economic society.  Production itself
suffered under the workers' unfortunate economic circumstances, and the producers
too came to suffer more thereby than they were aware.  When
the social utility which Bentham had demanded was to supply the standard,
then the distribution of what is produced must also become
an essential point of view.  The eminent position that Stuart Mill at
the middle of the century occupied in the history of the social question
is due especially to his clear distinction between the conditions of production,
which can in part be formulated as natural laws, and the conditions
of distribution, which are essentially connected with social relations of power.
(Political Economy. 1848 --- but especially in the 2nd and 3rd editions).
By this distinction Mill at this time thought he could
mediate between capitalism and socialism, which more and more came
into opposition to one another in theory as well as in practice.

Socialist theories had long since made themselves felt, in the age of the Renaissance
for example in two brilliant works, Thomas More's ``Utopia''
and Campanella's ``Solstat.''  In the nineteenth century they swarmed
forth in manifold forms.  One can, as I have sought to show in
my ``Etik'' and still maintain, distinguish between four main forms of
socialism, the utopian, the philanthropic, the speculative and the
empirical.

Utopian socialism springs from the imagination, which is set in
vibration by the distress of the time and driven to shape pictures of the future
that depict a harmonious society in which remedy has been found for
all social ills.  Such depictions (in Danish literature
Sibbern's may be mentioned) have their significance, partly as expressions of where
one at a given time thinks the shoe pinches, partly as symptoms
of the direction in which one imagines the help to lie.  A characteristic
feature of most depictions of ``Utopia'' (``a land
that lies nowhere'') is the weight laid on men
getting sufficient leisure, so that their spiritual faculties can be developed
outside the domains in which their special work lays
claim to them.

Philanthropic socialism, which in the nineteenth century is
% --- p. 94 ---
\opage{94}represented by St. Simon, Owen and Fourier, springs from love of mankind
and appeals to the feelings of men.  It conceives free associations
as the way to the goal and trusts that employers and workers
will be able to work together without compulsion by the state.  In England, France
and Switzerland, and thereafter in other countries, this tendency has exerted great
influence through the establishment of producers' and consumers' cooperatives.

Speculative socialism, whose chief man is Karl Marx (Das
Kapital. 1867), looks with scorn on the fantasts and the philanthropists.  It
maintains the possibility of a purely rational demonstration that the course of
history leads in the direction of a concentration of capital in very
few hands, while at the same time the distress of the workers rises in an ever
stronger degree.  When the workers, driven forward by distress, then unite
and seize political power, it will be an easy matter
for them to expropriate the few capitalists and thereby get the means of production
into their power.  It is not, however, the single workers
who will come to own the means of production, but the state, whose policy
the working class will then come to determine.

Empirical socialism, whose chief work is Sidney and Beatrice
Webb's ``History of Trade Unionism'' (1894), demands that it be investigated,
particularly by way of experiment, which domains are suited
to communal or state operation, and which must for the time being or perhaps
forever be left to private enterprise. ---

Another division of the socialist theories has been attempted by Werner
Sombart (Kapitalismus und Sozialismus) and after him by Muckle
(Geschichte der sozialen Ideen im 19. Jahrhundert).  These authors
distinguish between rational socialism, which holds that a certain
determinate social order is a necessary consequence of the very nature of man,
and evolutionary socialism, which does not assume unalterable
norms for social order, but maintains that the social forms of life
undergo constant changes, whose goal and direction thought
is to find in order thereafter to determine what the necessary
course of things must bring in the direction of social order.  I cannot
see that all the views mentioned above can find a natural place
when the contrast between an unalterable human nature and a
constant process of evolution is taken as the basis.  Neither utopians nor
philanthropists need regard the nature of man as given once and
for all.  And for the very significant empirical socialism
there is no place at all, although it seems to acquire greater and greater
significance.  The four kinds I find stress respectively imagination,
feeling, thinking and experience.  But since these mental elements
% --- p. 95 ---
\opage{95}never work isolated each by itself, but always in connection with
one another, there can be no sharp boundary between the
four kinds.  In the present the greatest weight is to be laid on the contrast
between speculative and empirical socialism.  It is
really between them that the battle now stands.  It will therefore be of interest
for our task to characterize them somewhat more closely.

Speculative socialism as Karl Marx, after several preliminary works,
had presented it in ``Das Kapital'' (1867), became in the
last part of the century of overwhelming significance in the social struggle.
It did not recognize Mill's distinction between production and distribution.
The state ought on behalf of the workers to take over the means of production
and the whole work as well as the distribution of the proceeds of labor.
Material labor is the source of all value.  Social development,
especially the division of labor, has led to the means of labor (the land
and the tools) having gone out of the hands of the workers and come into
the hands of a few capitalists, to whom then the greatest part of the proceeds
falls.  But future development will lead to the power of capitalism
being broken through the political power of the workers, and the state then takes over
the management.

Marx's theory is a theory of catastrophe like Cuvier's geology.  Concerning
the state of things that will set in after the catastrophe, he
expresses himself in his later writings very indefinitely.  He and his followers
think that it is early enough to speak of the future state
when the catastrophe is over.  Here the speculative
construction thus fails, which was applied with self-assurance as long as
the talk was of the past.

While older economists thought they could demonstrate eternal
laws of labor, social laws of nature, Marxism maintains that all
social laws are conditioned by the economic relations which at
a given time obtain.  And that holds not merely for the laws of the ordering of labor.
The whole life of the state, as well as all science, art, morality and religion,
is derived from and conditioned by the economic relations existing at each time,
is really only a reflection of these.  It is not
men's thoughts that order their life, but the practical,
economic conditions of life that condition their thoughts, their imagination
and their feeling.  Therefore the whole of history is a series of class struggles.

The grandiose picture that Marx has sketched of the course of development in
history is, however, not, as he thinks, the fruit of pure objective, intellectual
investigation, without all moral or ``ideological'' presuppositions.
Marx is a great ethical idealist and speaks in the end in the name of
% --- p. 96 ---
\opage{96}justice.  Thereby is understood the indignation that breaks forth
between the lines of his book, which according to the program was to be a
logic on an evolutionary basis.  In a single place he even
directly expresses a principle that directly recalls Kant's moral principle.  He
declares, namely, that the worker does not exist for the sake of economic products,
but that conversely they exist for his sake.  This ``exists''
must mean ``ought to exist,'' for according to Marx it is precisely not
so.  And this very moral principle expresses the idea of humanity
that has worked its way forward in modern times, particularly through the
discussions of the eighteenth century.  Here again one of the significant thoughts of
the nineteenth century proves to be a working out and
application of the thoughts of its predecessors.  Whereas Kant applied
his moral principle in particular against serfdom, it was by Marx directed
against the social and economic dependence of the workers, which still
persisted despite the proclamation of personal freedom.

What according to Marx was to bring on the catastrophe was the concentration
of capital in a few hands, and at the same time the increasing
distress among the working population.  The prophecy in these two respects cannot
be said to have come true.  And to this is added what experience shows,
that the value of the product of labor rests not merely on the labor it
has cost, but also on the use there is for it, and which neither
the worker, the capitalists nor the state controls.  Finally experience
also shows that personal genius and energetic initiative are of such
essential significance for production, both in the material and in
the spiritual domain, that the material worker can no more be
said to be the real cause of the yield than the bellows-treader
could be said to be the real cause of organ music.  On such
experiences empirical socialism lays the main weight,
particularly in the face of the question whether collective production in the
individual domains can take the place of individual production.  It
lays weight on the experiments in this direction being made first in smaller
circles, thus in the communes, before they are made in the larger.  It seeks
above all to improve the hygienic, domestic and intellectual
standard of living of the workers.  It begins from below, while speculative
socialism begins from above.  It is characteristic that while
Marxism stems from Germany, where the idea of the state in theory and in
practice stands exalted above the ideals and initiatives of the free society of culture,
empirical socialism is at home especially in England.  The very expression
``empirical socialism'' is due to Sidney and Beatrice Webb.  The
conception this expression denotes is, moreover, not very different from
% --- p. 97 ---
\opage{97}that which Stuart Mill in his time maintained, when he e.g. declared
that we know as yet neither what free self-activity in its highest
form can accomplish, nor what a carried-through socialization of all
relations of production would be able to bring about.  And he sees (as he has especially
stated in his Autobiography) that there is an inner connection between
these two sides of the problem.  True individual freedom for all becomes
possible only through far-reaching social reforms, which can give
the individuals such training and instruction that they can come
to use their natural faculties on an equal footing with others.  But
on the other hand freedom and spiritual development are not merely results
of social conditions, but are themselves a condition for social
development to become possible and lead to the right goal.  Herein lies at the same time
a constant reciprocal relation between spiritual and material culture.
The sting, the constantly working sting in the social problem, lies precisely
in the contrast between the individual and the social and in the contrast
between spiritual and material culture.  There will here always
make itself felt an irrational relation, however many
intermediate links are found.

Socialist ideas did not, however, come to be all-ruling within
the working class.  Already earlier in the century there had arisen
an individualist reaction against socialism in the so-called
anarchism.  The word anarchism was used by Proudhon in its original,
negative meaning ``absence of all dominion.''  There
can well be connection between men without compulsion and without
sovereign power.  What leads the anarchist into community with other
men is partly the need to be helped by them, partly the need
to help them.  In men like Proudhon and Kropotkin this
side of anarchism stood in the first rank.  They laid particular weight on life
in the narrower societies, where neighborliness already develops a feeling of community
and the ``mutual aid'' which Kropotkin in his interesting
writing ``Mutual Aid'' 1902 set in sharp contrast to
the state's regulation of all relations, supported by might.  But there were
anarchists whose whole life went into struggle with all authority in the world,
in whatever form it then appeared.  Bakunin was a type of
this sort of anarchists.  He fought first the old state society,
the corruptness of which his experiences in Russia had opened
his eyes to, but later he fought no less energetically
organized socialism and Karl Marx.  To an even higher degree
than Marxism he had to content himself, as regards the future,
% --- p. 98 ---
\opage{98}with indefinite hints of what was to come after the
chaos he wished to bring about.

In France there appeared toward the close of the century the
so-called syndicalism, a social philosophy that more than any other
social theory has developed within the circle of the workers themselves,
though philosophers by profession for a time joined it.  Syndicat is the
French name for craft union.  Various syndicats in the same town
join together into a labor exchange (bourse de travail); syndicalists
of the same trade in a district into a fédération régionale; the various
regional associations have in turn formed a Conféderation nationale
(1895), and the various labor exchanges have finally joined together
with the national confederation into the Confédération générale du
travail (1902).  Within these associations the theory of syndicalism has
developed.  The most important representative of it is the worker Ferdinand
Pelloutier, who has developed it in several writings.  (In a treatise
``Le Syndicalisme revolutionnaire'' Challaye in ``Revue
de Métaphysique et de Morale,'' 1907, has given an interesting exposition
of the theory of syndicalism.  Besides revolutionary syndicalism
there is also a Syndicalisme reformiste and a Syndicalisme
jaune, which in this connection have less interest).

What binds the syndicalists together is the common interest of the trade.
What is aimed at is the establishment of free workshops, where personal
sense of duty and joy in work take the place of the masters' authority
and create a mutual sympathy between the individuals that makes all compulsion
superfluous.  Not a mechanical necessity, as Marx believed, but
free labor itself brings forth the new society within which
the right distribution of the yield can take place, as the state never
could bring it about.  A society of free men can, according to
Pelloutier, be viable only through an education that goes on
in the moral, the administrative and the technical domain alike.
Admittedly most workers do not yet possess the economic
insight which is the only sure guide for the workers' associations,
but Pelloutier hopes that through the labor exchanges experience will be gathered
and an intellectual sense provided which in due time
can enable the just sovereignty of labor to replace capital
in the management of human interests.  The philosopher Sorel, who
for a time joined the syndicalists, expressed this thus (in
a certain connection with Bergson), that there would develop an intuition concerning
social ends and means, and that by the instinctive,
% --- p. 99 ---
\opage{99}riddles could be solved which modern understanding, isolated from all immediate need and feeling,
sought in vain to guess.

In the motives to which it refers, and in the ideals it sets up,
syndicalism is of a positive character.  The critique of the existing society
it borrows from socialism.  But it disagrees with the latter in that
concepts like state and nation are wholly rejected.  No
historical development is recognized, for there is no difference between the
wage laborer of recent times and the serfs and slaves of earlier times.  Democracy
is rejected because it mixes different classes together
in struggle for common political ends.  There are to be in general no
political parties any more, not even any socialist party (which
indeed even harbors millionaires in its midst).  Syndicalists in general
will not take part in politics, since all politics must amount to a provisional
recognition of the existing society.

If one now asks about means and ways to make this free, ideal
society possible, the syndicalist theory presents two peculiarities.


In contrast to democracy the syndicalists insist that it
cannot do to wait until a fully conscious majority joins
the new ideas.  Pelloutier, who has been called the father of syndicalism,
admits, as we have seen, that most workers do not yet
have the economic insight that is required to be able to take
a stand from reasoned conviction.  Therefore a small circle of
intellectually developed syndicalists must take the lead, an elite, which
acts on behalf of the multitude and for its good.  What is aimed at
will be for the good of all workers, also for the ``yellow'' syndicalists,
who regard peaceful cooperation with the employers as possible.
Such a new aristocracy is necessary, because one must act
quickly; the right moment for demonstrations and strikes must be seized.
Therefore syndicalism is also an enemy of arbitration, which leads
to drawing out the time by negotiations and formalities, and which in the
end demands a vote of the whole multitude.  The leaders must of course
have the multitude with them; but it can be won by brisk action
in an assembly where voting is by a show of hands and in
enthusiasm, while secret individual voting dissolves solidarity
and easily lets the individual in his solitude forget what he
owes to the whole class.
In contrast to parliamentary negotiation about new laws and to
peaceful negotiation with employers, direct action is set

\whiteline

% --- p. 100 ---
\opage{100}(action directe) in various forms, such as street demonstrations,
work stoppages, destruction of machines (sabotage), boycotting
of workshops and shops, and finally, as the last great
means: the general strike.  A general cessation of all work
is to be sufficient to put through everything one desires.
By this economic, not political revolution the old social order
will vanish at a single stroke and the new justice take
its place, with happiness and freedom for all. --- The philosopher Sorel, who for
a time joined Syndicalism, regarded the general strike as
a myth, whose significance lay in giving the imagination a great picture
of a catastrophe that opens the glorious realization of the
great ideals.  But the workers themselves hardly understand it so;
it exerts its alluring and attracting power and can easily come to
push all other striving and activity aside, just as (to use
a comparison suggested by Challaye) the faith of the first Christians in
the near coming of Christ proved stronger than the interest in family life,
culture and the life of the state. ---

Here we are concerned merely with Syndicalism as a theory, and it is
easy to see the inner contradictions from which it suffers.  There may lie in it the possibility
of a tyranny in the ancient sense, in which a single intelligent
leader rules with the involuntary adherence of the great mass.  And
how the use of force could then be excluded is not easy to
see.  The old state will, in one form or another, only not the democratic one,
stick its head out again.  At any rate, a great
work of education is presupposed on the part of the leaders toward
the mass, a work that makes great demands on the patience, the
capacity to wait, which the Syndicalists expressly disclaim.  And
no less contradiction than between the free leaders and the passive
multitude is there between Syndicalism's ethical ideal of joy in work
and fellow-feeling on the one hand, and the sharp and destructive means
to which appeal is finally made, on the other hand.  Will it be possible to return
to quiet, uniform work after sabotage and general strike?
Will the new society stand there spontaneously when the work of destruction
is completed? ---

These questions had naturally to present themselves in a purely theoretical way.  It
lies outside our task to speak of how the idea of
Syndicalism has worked in the chaos which the end of the World War called forth in
large parts of Europe.  In wise words the English labor leader
Arthur Henderson has said how the war has accustomed the peoples to
thoughts of violence and made it natural for the great masses to apply force
% --- p. 101 ---
\opage{101}in order to reach their goals by short cuts, and how it will especially be
men of uncertain temperament and impatient mind who will attempt
to go such ways.  Only history will one day be able to show what
role ideas that already appeared in the last decades of the 19th
century have played in the events that --- as this account
is being concluded --- have not yet completed their course.  Then it will
perhaps also become clear how ideas that had their home in
France could suddenly pop up in the Slavic, Magyar and
Germanic world.

--- The 19th century's thoughts on the social question have passed through
a series of phases, from the conservatism of the historical school and the Hegelian
doctrine of the state, through the faith of Liberalism in the harmony of
interests and the faith of Socialism in the state as economic
leader, to the free workshops of Syndicalism, led by a labor aristocracy.
Yet the word ``pass through'' is not apt.  For there is no doubt
that all these different points of view are still nourished and
maintained, even if it is in silence.  At any rate they have all set
their stamp on the course of development.  It must be left to those who have
the gift of prophecy to say how the social problem will present
itself when there is again time and quiet for factual discussion and for the
honest work in the individual circles of society that must always
form the solid foundation for further development, in whatever direction
this may then go.

\sectionhead{4.}{The Principle of Nationality.}

Social life takes shape in every single people in a peculiar
way, even if the social problem everywhere appears with certain
general features.  And the consciousness of such peculiarities
has in the 19th century found expression with greater force
than in earlier times.  Besides the various other names one can
give it, one could also with justice call it the century of nationality.
Never has national feeling intervened so strongly in
the course of events as here.  There may perhaps in earlier times
have stirred a more violent instinctive rage at violations of common
laws, common gods, a common ruling house.  But under ordinary
conditions the instinct did not account to itself for its origin or its right.
Conquests could therefore be carried through comparatively easily, or by
other ways, e.g. by princely marriages, a union of different
nationalities be effected, without any stronger and more lasting resistance
being offered.  One had no clear consciousness of what danger
% --- p. 102 ---
\opage{102}might thereby be brought upon the individual people, its language, its memories,
its whole way of taking life.  Observers as different as
Bluntschli (Politik als Wissenschaft. 1876) and Bryce (Studies in History
and Jurisprudence. 1901) have, on the contrary, declared that the idea of nationality
in the 19th century has had greater influence on the life of the state
than in any earlier time.  If we seek the grounds for this, they lie
in various circumstances.

True culture is present only where the demand made on human
capacities agrees with the peculiar nature of human beings,
and especially when these demands spring from this very nature in immediate
interaction with the conditions of life.  This holds for the individual,
and it holds also for peoples.  Rousseau's critique of modern
culture was grounded precisely in the consideration that for most people
it had been transferred from outside or from above, not sprung from
self-activity or at least won by independent appropriation.  He especially
protested against the idea that culture could without more ado be transferred
from one country to another.  It is characteristic of him that when
he received from Poland the naive request to write the country a constitution,
he answered that if he had lived ten years in the country, he might
perhaps write its history, but a new constitution for it
he could not have written even then.  What Rousseau here said
holds for all sides of culture.  Foreign
influence is not thereby excluded; but what is foreign must first be tested and appropriated, cannot
without more ado gain admittance, and it works best when it serves
to awaken the people's own powers.  Even translations succeed best
when they are re-creations.  The significance of language one becomes
conscious of altogether only gradually, as development proceeds.
The presupposition will be that there is not merely a need for a spiritual
content, but also for this content to find expression by the same
means that one involuntarily uses to give vent to one's experiences
and to communicate them to others.  Language struggles play a great role in
the nationality struggles of recent times.  It is felt as an impediment and
an insult when it is made impossible to use the mode of expression that
involuntarily lies nearest, and by which the difference between thought
and word becomes for the individual the smallest possible.

Together with culture and language there operates local belonging together,
neighborliness.  It has asserted itself at all times, among the nomadic
hordes as in the Greek cities.  But under the conditions of earlier times
there often arose isolation and a limitation of the feeling of belonging together
to circles that were far narrower than the people as a whole.
% --- p. 103 ---
\opage{103}A Danish author who has examined the difference between peasant life
formerly and now shows how the feeling of belonging together was naturally
and remained limited in earlier days, especially in remote regions.  One did not
see beyond one's own fields, or, at the most, beyond one's
own parish.  There was no view of the larger society, of people and
state (H. F. Fejlberg: Dansk Bondeliv, saaledes som det i Mands
Minde førtes, særlig i Vestjylland. 1889).  The isolation and the limitation
were removed by better means of transport, by increasing enlightenment
and by participation in political life.  Free constitutions
brought the right and duty to take part in deciding the great decisions
about the people's conditions of life, so that these no longer simply came to
stand as inexplicable fates.  Thereby the feeling of solidarity and
community was developed.  Common hopes and common fears can arise,
consciousness of a common soil, common memories, common fates.

Besides such conditions determined by the people's inner development,
the struggles through which the peoples of Europe in the first part
of the century had to assert their existence have also been of great importance,
in that they brought about both a firmer cohesion inwardly and
a sharp common opposition outwardly.  The feeling of brotherhood which the Revolution
awakened in the French people found expression in the Marseillaise's
call to ``Enfants de la Patrie'', just as the feeling toward foreign
attack found its expression in the summons ``Aux armes, citoyens!''
And when the wars of the Revolution and the Empire led far beyond
the right of self-defense and brought with them the oppression of other peoples, a
corresponding feeling was thereby awakened in those who had not at first hand
taken part in making the Revolution.  It became Napoleon's Nemesis that he,
who had been borne forth by the wave of the French Revolution and of national feeling,
himself fell by reason of his contempt for the freedom
and nationality of other peoples.  Later too it has been shown that a national breakthrough
can so dominate and blind the mind that one does not
discover that other peoples too have a need for unity and freedom.  Just as
the individual human being's drive of self-preservation can develop into
an egoism that knows no consideration, so national feeling can lead
to national egoism.  And with this there is often joined a sentimental
self-contemplation, an enjoyment of one's own supposed excellence.

In the case of Germany, the feeling of nationality that developed
under Napoleon's tyranny found a great and beautiful expression in
Fichte's ``Reden an die deutsche Nation'' (1808).  These addresses, which
were delivered in Berlin while the city was still occupied by a French
% --- p. 104 ---
\opage{104}army corps, may be regarded as a principal work in the philosophy of nationality.
The same thinker who a few years before had characterized the preceding century
strongly and penetratingly has also said a decisive word on the feeling of nationality,
which was to play so great a role in the new century.

Fichte begins by asking whether there still exists at all
a German people, and whether its continued existence deserves, if so, to be
secured.  After the Peace of Tilsit the German people is cut off from every
independent action outwardly.  The victor determines its policy and
decides how large an army it may keep.  There are now perhaps those to whom
it will be most agreeable to make themselves slaves and to put up with the deprivation of freedom.
And there are no doubt also those who feel admiration for
the conqueror's genius, for his superiority, for the mighty power his
thought can set in motion.  But it will be most worthy to maintain
inner freedom, now that outer freedom is lost.  And above all it is a matter of
holding fast to the true standard of what is great and noble,
and not letting oneself be dazzled by mere power.  True greatness must
now as before be ascribed only to those who foster ideas that lead the peoples
forward, --- and over the living let us leave the future to judge!

The conqueror has thought only of outward oppression.  Intellectual life,
and especially the education of the young, he has in his arrogance left unheeded.
In this, the freest domain, there is still work to
be done.  And the right foundation for a pedagogy that can serve the development
and consolidation of the independence of spirit and character has been
given by Pestalozzi. --- Fichte then, following Pestalozzi,
the German-Swiss reformer of education, gives his ideas
on a national pedagogy. ---

The hope that along this path a future may come for
the German people Fichte grounds on this, that this people has since time immemorial
dwelt on its own soil and spoken its old language.  And then it is a
people from which men such as Luther, Kant and Pestalozzi have come forth,
men whose whole direction of spirit bears witness to a deep sense of originality,
inwardness and personality!

A people, Fichte maintains, is never wholly expressed in the state that it
forms.  People and fatherland extend beyond the state in the narrower sense of this word.
What makes the individual a member of his people never becomes wholly the object of his own clear
consciousness.  Through invisible threads he is bound to that which also forms the ultimate
foundation of the people's rise and existence, --- the divine
source of all life.  No political order can let this inner
% --- p. 105 ---
\opage{105}coherence come into its full right; the state is only the social order
that secures right and peace and makes trade and handicraft possible;
it is only means and condition for the spiritual content that lives
in the people and conditions the feeling for the fatherland.  A universal state is impossible,
because it would not let the innermost peculiarity of the individual peoples,
as it expresses itself in spiritual life and language, come to
its full right.  It is a divine law that the essence of humanity
can come to revelation only in a wealth of individual and
national forms.  Therefore it is a contemptible consolation for the loss of one's own
nationality that can be sought in being absorbed in a universal state.

--- Yet it was not these thoughts that for the time being became decisive
for the conception of the relation between people and state, not even in Fichte's
own fatherland.  The reaction after the Revolution and after the Napoleonic era
put what was historically handed down in the first rank, forgetting the
living forces that had in their time produced what was now tradition.
It was the heyday of the ``historical school''.  All present-day movements
stood as insignificant in comparison with the legacy of the forefathers.
In conceptual form this line of thought was developed in Hegel's
``Philosophie des Rechts'' (1821), which throughout the whole century,
and beyond it, came to stand as the German conception of the
relation between people and state.  Fichte's great thoughts, which had come into being
in a time of need, were forgotten, like the promises that the princes of Germany had
given of popular freedom when the struggle against the foreign conqueror had been
carried to its end.  When in 1824, ten years after Fichte's death, a
new edition of the Addresses to the German Nation was contemplated, it was forbidden by the censorship.
But when in the second decade of the 20th century a new world war
had brought new distress upon Germany, then Fichte's addresses were cited
by the Imperial Chancellor from the rostrum of the German Reichstag.

Hegel saw in the historically developed state a work of a thousand years of
labor, a labor in which the single individuals and peoples with
or against their knowledge and will have taken part, and by which there
has been produced a world order before which all individual interests
and ideals pale.  A higher power has worked through the
human passions in the course of history; the world spirit has
used the conscious aims of historical persons as means and ways
for something that lay beyond their horizon.  It is God's march in the world
that expresses itself in the existence of the state.  In the state the individuals now find
their tasks, which are determined by their position within it.  They
need not work out by speculation what their duty is, still less that they
should have any right to make their supposed ``Besserwissen''
% --- p. 106 ---
\opage{106}count.  For Hegel, as once for Hobbes, the state is a mortal
god (mortalis deus).  And it is not a mere ideal of a state that Hegel
is thinking of here.  In the preface to the ``Philisophie des Rechts'' there occurs
precisely the famous proposition that what is rational is also actual,
and what is actual is also rational.  In the state --- and especially
in the Prussian state --- Hegel saw a rational reality or the
realized reason.

Hegel nevertheless finds a difference between his concept of the state and the ancient one
in that he lets individual freedom and conviction come to
recognition.  The modern state is precisely to be the organization of freedom.
The freedom of the individual has its sphere of action within the state
and under its laws.  And the state cannot reach its goal without the adherence
of the single individuals and of civil society, which through
trade and industry procures satisfaction for the economic
needs.  But this adherence must be regarded as given once
for all, and it cannot be taken up for renewed discussion.  There can
not even be any talk of a faith in the state among the single individuals; for faith
presupposes that there is a relation of opposition which must constantly be overcome,
whereas the whole being of the individual is --- insofar as it has any
justification at all --- once for all a member of the state and takes part in its
life.  Where this complete unity does not prevail, the individual stands,
however much he may appeal to his good conscience,
on the brink of evil.

The people can be recognized only as organized in the state.  But then
the people as state is also the highest power on earth.  That this power
is in fact exercised by the bureaucracy is in Hegel's eyes no objection:
``es sollen die Wissenden regieren!'' --- That in the July Revolution in
France and in the agitation for the English Reform Bill there stirred elements
in the peoples who did not think themselves to have come into their
rights in the modern state did not trouble Hegel.  His last work
before his death (1831) was a critique of the English reform bill.  What
people in the West European countries were now working for, that, the philosopher
held, had long since been attained in his fatherland, and in a more perfect
form!

Hegel's theory of the state made itself felt in the course of the century
not only among philosophers, but also among jurists and historians, especially
of course in Germany.
In his great work ``Das Selfgovernment in England'' (1860) Gneist regarded
the whole recent social and political development, especially in England,
as a great process of dissolution, fostered by the fact that civil
% --- p. 107 ---
\opage{107}(economic) society has pressed into the state and wants to use its
power for its interests.  Quite in Hegel's spirit he teaches that ``what
the strife between duties and impulses means in the life of the individual, that means
in the life of peoples the eternal struggle between state and society''. ---
Beforehand, then, right is to be on the side of the state when civil
society appears with its demands for a reorganization of the state,
because the involuntary and unforeseeable development of life is no longer
satisfied within its framework!  Yet it is precisely through labor
for material culture that the people's most elementary forces stir and
its practical thoughts develop, and if the state is not to hover
over the working society without regard to it, and thereby
in the end become powerless, it must try to give these forces room
within its framework as active members.  It is in that direction the West European
ideas of the state point.  How far state organization of the
free forces can go is, as we have seen, still an open question.
--- In German historiography the conception maintained by
Hegel appears, as we have seen, in the aim which the Prussian historical
school sets for historical inquiry, in that it declares the state
to be the proper subject of history and will include the history of culture only
insofar as it acquires significance for the state.

Even if it were possible to make material cultural work a
mere means for the state, it will not succeed with regard to spiritual cultural work.
Already in the former the need and capacity for independent
activity and for striking out on new paths will resist
absolute systematizing, --- that maintained by Marx as well as
that maintained by Hegel.  But spiritual culture cannot, according to its whole
essence, be made a mere means.  Language, e.g., goes its own ways,
and in vain will the power of the state at the present day hinder a subjugated people
from using its language.  Fichte already in his time pointed to language as
the expression of a people's peculiarity and as withdrawn from a conqueror's
dominion.  Since his time conquering powers have nevertheless held
that the unity of the state requires a unity of language carried through by compulsion, ---
a progress in brutality in comparison with the Napoleonic age. --- What
holds of language holds of all spiritual culture.  It must be
national, insofar as it must lay claim to all inner forces,
also to those through which the individual is connected with his
people and his race.  The national character of culture has therefore inner, not
outer grounds.  Sentimental national feeling sometimes demands that
art shall set itself national tasks, draw its subjects from the people's
nature, life and history.  But art must itself set its own
% --- p. 108 ---
\opage{108}tasks, and it has its own immediate relation to life.  If its
tasks are solved with originality and passion, the artist's nationality
will also involuntarily show itself; it will express itself most healthily
and most deeply the less the artist himself thinks of it.  Julius Lange
has aptly expressed this relation thus: ``The condition for outstanding
and thorough art rests more on the nation's learning to enter
into the peculiar tasks of art than on the demand that
art shall enter into those of the nation''.  (Sergel og Thorvaldsen. 1886).
Far from the national significance of art being diminished by this consideration,
it becomes precisely greater and deeper.
In peculiar contrast to Gneist's conception of the state, developed in Hegel's footsteps,
stands the view which the Swiss scholar Jacob
Burckhardt has put forward in his ``Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen'',
whose first draft dates from the years around 1870, while
the book first appeared in 1905, after the author's death.  Burckhardt was in
the enviable situation of belonging to a small people and yet of
having a world language for his mother tongue.  As belonging to a small people
and as a historian of culture he naturally arrives at a different point of view
from the legal philosophers and historians of a great power.  He saw clearly
that the concept of the state in the 19th century has been placed in a crisis, which is called forth
by the question whether the state is to determine the direction of culture, or
culture that of the life of the state.  That this problem
has first arisen in the 19th century he derives from the fact that culture
has only then reached such a development that it can strive to take
the state into its service.  We see throughout the free society of culture
grow at the expense of the state and at the same time demand of the latter what it
is not itself able to do.  All culture cannot be left to the free
forces, since they may work unsteadily and one-sidedly; but the condition for
beneficial influence here on the part of the state is that the independence of culture
be recognized.  Burckhardt is against the cult of the state, its
unity and its power, which quite naturally develops in great states.  It
will in the long run be at the expense of culture.  It is by no means only among
those in power that the lust for power develops such a cult; it is also
among individuals, in that their self-esteem is satisfied by belonging to
something great. ---

The relation between state and culture is again one of the great problems
which the 19th century leaves to its successors.  And by reason of
the tension that at the transition to the new century
prevailed between the great states among themselves, as well as within each
of them, the problem presents itself more sharply than before.  The World War
% --- p. 109 ---
\opage{109}will perhaps through its outcome and through its side effects lead to
a new phase in the interminable history of the great problem. ---

But however it may go with the relation between nation and state,
the principle of nationality will not vanish and will perhaps even outlive
the principle of the state, in that it stands in a closer relation to the involuntarily
working forces in the world than the principle of the state does, so true is it that the content
of life is more important and more original than the forms of life.

An eminent French sociologist, Émile Durkheim, has (at the
philosophical congress in Bologna 1911) singled out as the value-creating (and at the same time
consciousness-of-value-creating) times such times when
human beings for one reason or another are brought closer to one another, are led
to express their thoughts about common conditions and thereby become conscious of
common aims.  These are the great periods of fermentation, in which life
is lived with special intensity, and in which individuals forget
their particular interests in face of the great currents that sweep all along with them.
These are the times fundamental for social life, which are later commemorated
in national and religious festivals and customs.  Even if the mood of such
great moments is not preserved when one returns to
the tasks of daily life and the interests of private life, they will nevertheless not
vanish without a trace.  They are at any rate symptoms, and that which
makes itself known in them may later emerge under other, perhaps
unforeseeable forms. --- What the French sociologist points to here
throws light on the development of national feeling, but at the same time presupposes
that blind urge, mere instinct, no longer prevails.  Mighty and sweeping events
may pass over a people without
a clear consciousness forming of the common values around which
one gathers.  Ideas must be able to form both of what
one possesses and of what one desires, in order for national feeling to
come into being. --- Already earlier Bryce (American Commonwealth.
1885) had put forward a similar view to Durkheim's.  He
found it characteristic of the Americans that, in spite of all apparent
preoccupation with individual interests, they in serious moments
push everything aside for that which socially and politically is the one thing decisive.
Most of those who speak about the Americans take account only of
their business life and their preoccupation with it.  But in the decisive
moments the idealism that dwells in them reveals itself. --- Bryce
has here pointed to the opposition which in psychology is called
the opposition between disposition and emotion, and to the importance
of observing human beings in both states.  In disposition what may
be hidden and potentially present, in emotion steps
% --- p. 110 ---
\opage{110}forth in full clarity and actuality.  In and by itself, to be able to be seized
by strong emotion when one stands before great and significant
events is a good testimony, and Kant, who otherwise
had difficulty in looking brightly on human beings, was within his right
when, in the enthusiasm which the French Revolution awakened, even where
the expression of this enthusiasm was bound up with danger, he saw a
testimony that human nature, in spite of ``the radical
evil'' (propensity to sensuality and egoism), harbored good and noble
elements in it.  It is naturally a task for the psychologist and the historian
to find the bond and the interaction between disposition and emotion;
only then can he rely on the testimony that lies in this
latter.

The testimony to which Kant pointed, the enthusiasm for the French
Revolution, pointed beyond the limitation that may lie in national feeling.
When culture comes to consciousness of its value, independent of
all factors of power, there will arise the idea of a society
beyond the boundaries determined by nationality and state.  Already at the
close of classical antiquity such a thought was present.  It was especially
Stoic philosophy that developed ideas of a universal human society;
Plato had prepared the way for it by demanding a pan-Hellenic
consciousness, a feeling of humanity, which was to prevent the Hellenic states
from treating one another as barbarians.  In the Christian church
the universally human consciousness assumed a religious character, and the
science, art and humanity of modern times brought new points of view
and a new foundation for it.  In the 19th century an international
community begins to assert itself in the case of the
industrial workers, and Marx in his Communist call
turned to the proletarians of all lands to unite.  Both material and ideal
culture make it possible that a group which within one people has joined
together around a common aim can feel itself most closely related to a
group within another people that has formed around a similar
aim.  If one imagines this carried through in all domains of culture,
one approaches the thought that the time of nationalities might be
past.  Practical difficulties, however, arise on several sides
against this.  With state socialism the disappearance of nationalities cannot
be reconciled.  Marx appealed confidently to the proletarians of all lands.  He
believed in the harmony among the well-understood interests of all proletarians.
But when the state is to organize labor, the opposition
between the different states will assert itself, in that the economic
interests of one country cannot without more ado be reconciled with those of the others.
% --- p. 111 ---
\opage{111}It is not merely with regard to the circulation of goods that this question
emerges.  It presents itself also as far as the workers themselves are concerned.
Are Polish workers to be allowed to undercut the workers of the Nordic countries, or Chinese workers the American, the Italian
the Swiss?  The economic oppositions that existed between
the old states, and which there often, if not always, lay at the root of
the wars, will not have vanished between the new, socialist states of the future.
And according to Marx national feeling is in the end occasioned (like
every other ideal feeling) by economic interest.  The ambiguous position of the Social Democratic
parties during a world war finds its explanation herein.
According to Hegel, whose concept of the state Marx has taken over
(only with the change that the relation between state and economic
society is reversed), the states are ``absolutely independent totalities'',
which can indeed enter into agreements with one another, but always stand
above these agreements, so that in relation to one another they are in the state of nature.
--- Syndicalism, which wants to abolish the concept of the state entirely,
is here more consistent than Socialism.  There will be easier forms of
intercourse and interaction between the free societies of culture that are to
replace the states than between the ``absolutely independent totalities''.
And with the centralization to which state socialism pays homage there follows naturally,
perhaps unavoidably, a certain feeling of power and an isolation of the
interests of the individual country.  A feeling of power stirs, as Burckhardt rightly
has seen, not only in the leaders, but also in private persons in
a great state.

The inequality in culture which conditions the immigration of workers from
countries with the lowest wages or with fewer needs and
demands poses a new problem.  How is a country with supposedly
higher culture to place itself toward a country with supposedly lower
culture?  Is it merely to depend on the power which a country with
``higher'' culture may possess?  Or will one in the future
have the great pedagogical patience that lets the peoples whose
culture is still at what Europeans call lower stages follow
their own natural development, provided only that care is taken to keep external
hindrances away?  Hitherto the peoples of Europe have not followed this procedure,
not even toward one another.  It has essentially
been the relation of power that has been decisive, and nations with
fewer soldiers and cannon have been declared ``underweight''
(``minderwertig'').  Toward the peoples of other parts of the world, whom by
European standards one might call ``primitive'', no respect for human beings has been shown.
Religiously they have been regarded as material for
% --- p. 112 ---
\opage{112}conversion, commercially as subjects for exploitation and militarily as
objects for conquest.  Here lies a problem which in the 19th century
was touched on by a few authors (very energetically by Herbert
Spencer), but which has not found any solution in principle.  It
remains to be seen whether the ``League of Nations'' contemplated by the world peace
can take up the question in earnest.

--- It is material culture and its tasks that Socialism and
Syndicalism especially have in view, and it is indeed here that the shoe first and foremost
pinches.  But, as already indicated, behind the demand for wages and what
it sets in motion there stirs more and more a need for participation
in ideal culture.  And it is here that the last and greatest resistance
will be made against the obliteration of nationalities.  For here one notices
especially that an element of life would fall away with them.  Language and memories,
life of feeling and cast of thought make their involuntary claims felt, and
spiritual works would with the disappearance of national relations lose
a great part of their peculiar timbre.  If it is said to this
that spiritual culture is accessible only to a few, this holds certainly
of the full understanding of the greatest works, especially at their
appearance as something new for the age.  Art and science are born
in solitude.  But it is a social and national work that they signify;
the artist and the man of science are as it were the people's chosen scouts,
who at their lonely posts are to greet the new that is breaking forth.
Art and science follow their own laws, which do not without
more ado favor accessibility on the part of large, unprepared circles.
But it is then precisely the task of a peculiar art, a distinctive
sagacity, to find intermediate links and intermediate forms through which the new
can become generally accessible, so that the self-activity without
which no ideal culture is true can be awakened.  Own experiences
and moods, one's own involuntary mental work must be met with that
which is communicated from outside.  The task must not be solved by dragging down
what stands higher, but by finding in the primitive, unprepared
sense germs of a striving after truth and beauty and releasing it,
a striving which in all its meanness can be akin to the
spiritual forces that produce the greatest works.  In scientific
respect there will here be use for what is called a ``noble
popularization'', which gives the most important results of investigations in such a way
that a labor of thought is thereby called forth in the readers.  In
artistic respect people have taken up the idea of a close connection
of art and labor, so that labor itself can be practiced as an art.
And it has been thought that for the future socially organized society
% --- p. 113 ---
\opage{113}architecture, music and drama will become the most important fine arts.
On the other hand, people are so optimistic as to think that the time of the novels will
be past, as there will be a lack of material!  (Morris and Bax: Socialism, its
growth and its outcome. 1893).

--- In an effort in the direction here indicated it will be a matter of
getting removed the practical dissatisfaction that hampers the sense for
what the nation has in store of ideal culture.  The French
philosophical world has had a clear eye for this.  In an interesting discussion
in the French philosophical society (1907) it was debated
whether and how it was possible to awaken understanding of and
love for nationality in working-class circles.  Various speakers
who had moved in such circles, especially in Syndicalist circles,
had had the experience that it was impossible to get anywhere
by way of discussion when one wanted to convince a Syndicalist
worker of the significance of national culture.  The sociologist Bouglé
expressed this by saying that he had often found in Syndicalist circles
that he and his opponents did not agree in any
evaluative judgment (jugement de valeur).  The workers felt themselves ``desolidarized'',
and they had more interest in foreign events
and endeavors than in those at home, when these did not particularly
concern their own conditions.  In this philosophical circle there was agreement
that the only way to go was to get the existing state
to satisfy, to a far higher degree than hitherto, the demands of justice
in all relations: Le patriotisme ne peut se maintenir que par
un réformisme décidé.

% --- p. 114 ---
\parthead{III. RELIGION}
\chapterhead{I.}{THE RENAISSANCE OF FAITH IN AUTHORITY.}

\opage{114}In the religious domain the opposition to the 18th century is
far greater than in other spiritual domains.  The revolutionary
movement in France within literature and politics and the
great humanistic Renaissance in Germany had pushed religious
questions into the background, indeed might seem about to shove them entirely
out of the realm of spiritual interests.  Free inquiry and free conscience
had been proclaimed as guiding stars, and among the proclaimers were
great personalities, some of the greatest of mankind, highly superior
to those who maintained that human life would dissolve into bestiality
if the rules of thinking and acting were not laid down by
superhuman authorities.

But, as was already remarked at the beginning of this account,
precisely the 18th century's most important men in the century of thinking
and poetry pointed beyond what in the
broad circles must be said to be the distinguishing mark of the 18th century, a
dryness and sobriety in the course of thought, an overvaluation of the understanding
at the expense of feeling and imagination.  The Romantic need,
the need for fullness of content and for being absorbed in great and captivating
conceptions, which stirred at the beginning of the century, benefited religion
too.  Religion was recognized as poetry before it was
recognized as authority.  In the Romantic spiritual tendency
poetry, science and religion were in the end to be one.  The development in the first
decades of the century is marked by the fact that religion breaks out of
this harmony and in ever sharper forms resumes its old
points of view.  In the religious domain, as in the social,
the oppositions are sharpened in the course of the century.  After the
great apostasy there was felt a violent need to bow again to supernatural
powers as ruling over everything in life.  The principle of authority awakens to
new life.
In French literature De Maistre is the most important spokesman for this
% --- p. 115 ---
\opage{115}tendency.  He pointed with full right to the fact that
``the syllogism, the scaffold and the epigram'' --- the 18th century's
three chief weapons --- had proved powerless against the need for
absolute support and refuge.  The power of the Church had asserted itself in
secret.  And besides --- De Maistre maintained --- the terrible
times one had lived through had furnished proof that human reason
has no power to guide life.  It is of no use to appeal
to science.  The so-called laws of natural science are mere dogmas
and do not teach us to know the real causes.  Only a divine
will can be the true cause of what happens in the world.
And to find out what is right and good, human reason
is not sufficient.  To solve this task there is required
a spiritual authority which only the Catholic Church possesses, and which
presupposes infallibility in the ruler of this Church.  (Du Pape. 1820).
In the following period De Maistre's line of thought is continued under various
nuances by a series of gifted spokesmen for the ever more powerful
Catholicism in France.  The new constitution after
1830 was used to demand elbow room for the Catholic faith.  ``We are'' --- said
Montalembert in the Chamber of Peers --- ``the sons of the Crusaders, and we will
not yield to the sons of Voltaire''.  Lacordaire worked for the revival of
monasticism.  Whereas even under the Restoration no
monk's habit had shown itself on the public street, Lacordaire appeared
publicly in his Dominican habit, even at a minister's table and in
the National Assembly in 1848.  The times had changed; in the
first years after 1830 clergymen had been able to visit
the dying in the hospitals only in civil dress.

Whereas De Maistre gave his principle of authority political, intellectual
and religious significance alike, John Henry Newman, the spokesman
for the principle of authority in England, was a purely religious figure.  From his
youth he had felt ever more strongly the Anglican Church's
wavering between authority and freedom, and it finally came to stand
clear to him that it had failed in its task, because it had not
the courage to assert its divine authority, although it strictly
maintained its unbroken continuity with the original Church.  It
was in England not, as in France, an external revolution that one had
to combat; but the line of thought of the 18th century had in many
ways penetrated into the Church itself, supported by its Protestant
character.  What Newman attacked first and foremost was the right to
follow one's own personal conviction (private judgment).  The consequence
of this must be skepticism.  And how then can
% --- p. 116 ---
\opage{116}remedy be had for the anguish that has so deep a root in human
nature?  Only the Church is capable of this, and capable of it only by virtue of
the holy authority on which it builds.
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``The Church'', says Newman
(Apologia pro vita sua. Being a history of his religious opinions.
1865), ``has the task of delivering human nature from its misery
by lifting it up onto a higher foundation.  The Church recognizes
human nature in its real, moral loftiness, in spite of its degradation;
but it cannot free it from the earth except by raising
it to Heaven.  To this end a re-creating grace is laid
in its hands''.  And in order that the Church may administer this gift of grace,
it must possess absolute authority. --- In the ``Apologia pro vita sua'', one
of the most remarkable books of the 19th century, Newman describes
how the necessity of absolute authority step by step dawned
on him amid heavy inner struggles.  As so often the real
decision had in fact been made long before he with full consciousness undertook
the transition to the Catholic Church (October 8, 1845); it has
probably been said with right of him that from childhood he was a Catholic by
instinct.  For him there was in the end only a choice between Catholicism and
atheism.  The middle way (via media) that the Anglican Church, and
Protestantism generally, would go was for him a wrong road.  As early as
1841, thus four years before his transition, he designates Lutherans and
Calvinists as heretics.  Of interest for the history of religion is the fact that the
living expectation of Christ's second coming was a main point in his
religiosity.  Christianity, he says somewhere, ever since it came
into the world, has always been on the point of going out of it again.  The
great expectation that gives primitive Christianity its stamp must always
live in the Church --- ``else the New Testament is not written for us!''
And Newman found in the monk and the nun the only ones who strictly followed
the commandment to have one's treasure in heaven.  This he expressed already in
his Protestant time. ---
In Germany and in the North the countermovement against the 18th century's
Rationalism came in the form of a return to the old Lutheranism.

The Holstein pastor Claus Harms issued on the three-hundredth anniversary
(1817) of the beginning of the Reformation 95 theses, the same number as
Luther's.  But whereas Luther had spoken against papal power and indulgence,
Harms spoke against reason and conscience.  He found the beginning
of Rationalism in the distinction Calixtus had introduced in the
17th century between dogmatics and ethics.  Thereby the throne was
set up before conscience, and later on Kant let it be ascended
% --- p. 117 ---
\opage{117}by his doctrine of the self-legislation of conscience, which made
it independent of faith.  One must choose between the Bible and reason;
the so-called rational faith is either bereft of reason
or of religion or of both.

--- Even before Harms appeared, Grundtvig, who from Rationalism
and Romanticism through hard struggle of soul had been led back to
the old faith of the Church, had rejected the independence of science --- toward
H. C. Ørsted the independence of philosophy and natural science,
toward Chr. Molbech the independence of historical inquiry.  He
demanded that all inquiry should bow to the word of the Bible.  But he later became
doubtful about the scholars' investigating, by the way of science,
the origin of the biblical books and the manner in which they must be
interpreted.  An independent opinion about these things requires a learning
which not every layman can acquire.  He sought then
another authority than that of the written word.  He could not conceive
that it had been God's meaning ``to bind the faith of the unlearned to the
testimony of the learned''.  And he found then (1825) in the apostolic creed,
which from ancient times is heard at baptism, the right norm
for the Church's faith as well as for the interpretation of the Bible.  Here there
was a testimony accessible to all, and which could stand
firm, whatever results the learned might arrive at in their investigations
of the authenticity and interpretation of the Bible.  The creed stood in close
connection with the Church's cult, and in what Grundtvig called his discovery
there expresses itself a sense for what the history of religion shows
to be fundamental for all positive religion, --- the close connection
between cult on the one side, myth, legend and dogma on the
other side.

--- It was thus the same principle in different forms that people in the
Catholic and the Protestant world appealed to.  Whether
authority is to be sought with the Pope, in the Bible or in the creed,
it demands obedience and submission of all one's own thought and feeling.
In the course of the century the opposition between the different
confessions emerged ever more sharply.  There was still at the beginning of the century
good and cordial understanding between Catholic and
Protestant clergy; even Jewish clergy were counted as colleagues.
Here there still operated the long-prevailing rationalistic line of thought,
for which confessional differences were in the end insignificant.
Later in the century it became otherwise, especially on
the part of the Catholic Church.  A Catholic bishop in Switzerland thus declared
that the Catholic Church cannot exercise any tolerance toward
% --- p. 118 ---
\opage{118}Protestants, for it is, after all, the only true Church, outside
which no one can be saved; the Protestants, on the other hand, are obliged
to exercise tolerance toward the Catholics, for the Protestant Church
dare not claim to be the only true Church.

--- In the Catholic Church, however, the principle of authority did not come to stand
alone.  A passionate or emotional need for absolute support
in life and faith was for the leaders of the Catholic Church not a sufficient
foundation to build on.  It was too personal and too subjective
a stage.  The decision about the value of faith in authority for life would then be
left to the single individuals!  For the time being one gladly made use of the
support that authors like De Maistre could give in awakening the need
for a firm foundation; but one wanted this foundation to be built up
with rational theology.  Renan's teacher at the theological seminary
of St. Sulpice said to him, when they read De Maistre together: ``Ah,
comme on voit bien, mon cher, que M. de Maistre n'est pas théologien!''
It was and is not enough for Catholicism that reason is taken
captive under the Church's doctrine as under a paradox at which it basically
takes offense.  Reason is by the way of thinking itself to be compelled to
recognize the Church's doctrine.  One is not to begin with faith, but
with reason; for by what other way than that of reason could one
demonstrate that faith is right?  One therefore does not put up with it that
reason's capacity to prove the existence of God is denied.  Once
this proof is carried out, theology can build further, in that it infers
that the God thus proved must have revealed himself in a reliable
manner, and that this revelation is present in the Church's doctrine and through
the Church as organ becomes the share of each individual.  The Catholic Church
rejects decisively the more recent philosophy's treatment of the problem of knowledge
and in opposition to it goes back to the Scholasticism of the Middle Ages.
Thomas Aquinas is set over against Kant.  It was the grand-scale
Catholic thinking of the 13th century that people renewed --- or rather: tried
to repeat.  Whereas within Catholicism there had earlier
prevailed a certain freedom in the philosophical respect, so long as the dogmas
themselves were not touched, it now became otherwise.  In the ``Syllabus errorum'' issued by Pius IX in 1864
the principles of scholastic philosophy were declared
to accord with the interest and progress of science, at the same time
as the view was condemned that moral doctrine and philosophy might
be cultivated without regard to supernatural revelation and ecclesiastical
authority.  In the ``Vaticanum'' (1870), by which the Pope's infallibility
was established as dogma, those were anathematized who denied that the existence of the true God
can be proved from human reason, as well as those who
% --- p. 119 ---
\opage{119}thought that one could come to faith by the way of personal experience
and feeling.  Leo XIII, who already as a Cardinal had proposed
that Thomas Aquinas, doctor angelicus, should be the patron of the universities,
declared in 1879 his philosophy (``Thomism'') to be
the best philosophy.  And later, under Pius X, there was condemned in a papal
bull (1907) the so-called Modernism, which wanted to introduce a psychological-historical method into theology and to base faith on experiences
that perhaps were not even had with full consciousness.  The bull, which
is a very interesting document and gives a thorough and expert
characterization of the modern methods of psychology of religion and history of religion
which it rejects, finds the cause of the heresies
that show themselves in the use of these methods in spiritual
corruption, untimely curiosity, arrogance and ignorance.  As means
against this it names the subordination of all science to
Thomism and a prohibition against Catholic students' attending lectures
on philosophy at other than Catholic universities.

The Catholic Church is thus not afraid to make ``the faith of the unlearned
dependent on the testimony of the learned.''  From laymen
it demands only childlike and undeveloped faith (fides implicita) that the Church
possesses the gift of grace of truth.  But this position
it then maintains through sharp and firm rejection of the intellectual striving
and spiritual demands of the age.  In the course of the century a whole series of
Catholic thinkers have been condemned, now because they gave reason
too much influence, now because they gave it too little influence.  Abbé
Bautain thus had to recant his doctrine that reason could not
prove the existence of God.  According to the Vaticanum it is a matter of faith
that such a proof can be given.  It is a two-edged sword that the Catholic
Church has here armed itself with, in that a critique of the sanctioned proofs
must lead to doubt about the Church's authority.  About his theological
period of study at St. Sulpice Ernest Renan says in his memoirs of youth:
``Sous le couvert de réfutations faibles, tout l'ensemble des idées
modernes venait à nous. ---

So consistent a return to the stage of earlier times
Protestantism was not able to carry through, to say nothing of daring to
ascribe to the Church authority to establish new dogmas, as
the Catholic Church did twice in the course of the century (Mary's
immaculate conception 1854 and the Pope's infallibility 1870).  Nevertheless
the Protestant Church exerted itself to maintain the concept
of the Church, its cult and its tradition as standing above all
individual striving and conviction.  But it became ever more difficult
% --- p. 120 ---
\opage{120}for the Protestant Church to explain on what this authority
really rested.  It was not able with decisive authority to
interpret its own cult and doctrine.  On this rest both the strength and the weakness
of Protestantism.  It is strong when it rests
on the self-acquired conviction of free personalities; but it will
always fall short when it is a matter of setting up a systematic concept of the Church.
It would not be of great interest for cultural history to follow the
Protestant Church's concept of authority through the different forms
and degrees in which it has been maintained in the course of the century.
It is, on the other hand, of great interest to see what motives on the whole
operated in the return to positive religion and Church that
characterizes the first half of the 19th century.  These motives
come forth, by the nature of the case, most clearly and strongly within
Protestantism.

First of all it must be noted that the general characterization one
can give of a century does not without more ado hold for all strata and
all circles, to say nothing of all individuals.  There live at every time great
masses of human beings who are very little touched by what for a
historical view gives a time its stamp.  Even in the century of ``the Enlightenment''
many lived in quiet in the old faith and stepped forth only in
a warding-off manner when the new thoughts became too pressing, and it
was then no wonder that the old thoughts came up again when the movements
of the time subsided.  The changes which these old thoughts have undergone
in the meantime and later undergo by meeting
the new circle of thoughts within which they emerge again,
were not always the object of clear consciousness.

In the very circles that were animated by ``the Enlightenment'', there must
naturally come a certain lassitude or weariness and with it a need for nourishment
or movement of another kind.  Where the Enlightenment was more than a
passive fashion, it demanded exertion, active use of the faculty of thinking,
constant self-activity.  There was then gradually engendered a need
for relaxation, for rest in the simple and unadorned, for devotion
to forms that one did not need to produce at the same moment
that one had need of them, --- for going by ways that did not first have to be
cleared.  And such forms and ways were in ecclesiastical religion laid
ready through the experiences of centuries.  ``The faith of our fathers'' stood
then as an inheritance one could enter upon without more ado, not a capital
one first had to produce.

Besides, it was, as Rousseau had already maintained in the midst of the Age of Enlightenment,
a very one-sided culture that the 18th century
% --- p. 121 ---
\opage{121}represented.  There were deep spiritual needs that did not come
into their own, especially the need for immediate living in imagination and feeling,
for following one's longing in its free course, unconcerned about all manner of
criticism.  The great labor of thought that had already been accomplished, and which was continued
by the century's greatest spirits, had not yet exerted its
effects on the dark strata of mental life, had not been deposited in the life of feeling
and will, and had therefore not yet become full personal
property.  Such a penetration takes time, and it occurs essentially
by indirect ways.

With this it is connected that the Enlightenment of the 18th century
had a character of aristocracy of spirit; it was, and wished only to be,
accessible to a small circle.  But the Revolution had called forth a
new social stratification, and besides, the strong flaring up of national feeling
had awakened a need for community, for sharing the spiritual
life of one's people.  There stirred a growing need for forms of spiritual life which
--- in a literal or figurative sense --- could be common to
