all.  All were to have access to the highest spiritual life.  Now, as
we have heard, the demand was made that the faith of the unlearned should not be
dependent on the testimony of the learned in the most important matters of life.  And
ecclesiastical faith and cult seemed to satisfy this demand.

Finally, the so-called Enlightenment had an abstract and at the same time a
dogmatic character.  It built on a series of general principles
that were regarded as secure results of thinking and science.  But
it turned out that these principles, even where they were correct, needed
closer carrying through and confirmation.  And the 19th century was
precisely, if the characterization given in the foregoing is correct,
the century of carrying through and of confirmation by experience.  Its natural science,
its historical and philosophical inquiry had the chief significance
in the particular of confirming and limiting what the preceding
centuries had initiated.  But it now turned out that a distinction
had to be made between the ideal of knowledge and the knowledge actually won,
and that it was still a long way to the time --- if it should
ever come --- when life could be conducted on thoughts that
were fully carried through and tested through.  The question of knowledge
and faith turned out to be more complex than people had
thought.

All this had to bring it about that people stood differently toward the
spiritual inheritance of the past than before.  They needed it, understood it better and
had better spiritual room for it.  The Romantic movement worked
here together with the religious reaction.  Poetic and historical
% --- p. 122 ---
\opage{122}sense and personal need for support and refuge worked for a time
hand in hand.

It had, in the case of Protestantism at least, not
merely been outside and against the Church, but also within the Church, that
the Enlightenment (Rationalism) ruled, and the history of the Church in the first
decades of the century is the history of Rationalism's successive
retreat.  An excellent church historian, Karl Hase, who was far from
belonging to the orthodox, has in his time (Theologische Streitschriften.
1834) shown that the Rationalism which had penetrated into the Church and long ruled there
met resistance in the new century on three different
grounds. --- It lacked historical sense.  It wanted to put its inferences of reason
in place of the peculiar forms in which spiritual life has clothed itself
in the course of history.  Every age has its natural and popular
ways of expressing its highest truths, and where there is a sense
for the original, for that which really issues from life, one will
not try to put self-made, abstract forms in their place.
--- In the second place Rationalism proceeded from the idea that one can act on feeling
only through the understanding, and it shrank from the purely involuntary outbursts of
religious feeling and from the images in which it
found expression. --- And in the third place Rationalism understood by ``reason''
really only common sense, as it
had developed in an age that regarded itself as educated and enlightened.
Every age has its common sense, which rests on the
experiences it has had or believes it has had, on the traditions
it takes for good wares, and on the scientific results
that are accessible to it.  Common sense can never
be the highest judge.  It must be tested by the highest scientific
insight the age has at its disposal, and in this respect
ecclesiastical Rationalism had settled down much too early. ---

If we now look at what position religion, after the struggle with Rationalism,
takes up in the spiritual life of the century, two main points will
emerge.  The one concerns religion's relation to culture, the
other the psychological foundation of religion itself.

There were times when religion was the highest, indeed the only
measure of value.  It then determined the place of every spiritual or material striving
within the world of spirit.  Spiritual life was judged by its
relation to the ideals and interests of religion.  This is, even after religion's
awakening to new life and new recognition, no longer so.
It is now conversely religion whose value is measured by its significance
for a rich and deep spiritual life, by a standard that is not
% --- p. 123 ---
\opage{123}given with religion itself, but is drawn from what, according to the testimony of
experience, promotes unity and fullness, inwardness and depth in the minds
of human beings.  It has become one element among many, and even where
one puts this element in the seat of honor, the standard is drawn from the connection
among all elements, not from this particular element
alone.

That religion has at all become an essential element in the spiritual life of
large circles, after it for a time seemed about to be eliminated from
this, is due to a personal need, in relation to which the content of religion
plays a subordinate role.  If one examines religious discussions
from the 19th century, one will notice how this
personal, subjective moment gives the whole its timbre.  Even
where the principle of authority (whether it is represented by Pope,
by Bible or by creed) is stressed with force, the main motive is
the need for support and refuge.  Religion has, as Pius X rightly
saw in the bull against Modernism, become pragmatic.  It is by no means
essentially objective grounds that condition man's faith.  Comte is
certainly right that when we no longer believe in Apollo and Diana, it is
not because the existence of these gods has been refuted, but because there
no longer stirs any need to believe in such gods.  Throughout
the whole history of religion it is in the end a mental need that
is the foundation of religion; but this foundation lies hidden under
the overwhelming and captivating power of the content of faith.  It is precisely characteristic
of the 19th century that the foundation is consciously drawn forth
and used as an argument.  It is a turn in the whole position of the religious problem
which Rousseau and Kant had prepared in the 18th century.
We therefore see also that clear-sighted religious thinkers
in the first place stress honesty and integrity in the religious respect,
warn against supposing oneself in possession of a faith that is not in reality
grounded in a living need.  The center of gravity has decidedly
shifted from what is objectively, historically given to the innermost part of
personality itself.  We shall have occasion to return to this
point.

--- Old and new always collide with special force in the
religious domain, and the reappearance of religion did not take place without
sharp frictions both in public life and in narrower circles.
The renewal of the old faith often assumed forms which for those who
had grown up in the spiritual sphere that the humanism of the 18th century
had formed might well arouse offense and concern.  In the
year 1799 Schleiermacher had published his book ``Über die Religion.
% --- p. 124 ---
\opage{124}Reden an die Gebildeten unter ihren Verächtern''.  When in the year 1821 he
issued the third edition he declared in the preface: ``The times have
changed so strikingly that the persons to whom these addresses
are directed no longer seem to exist at all.  When one now looks around
among the cultured, one would far rather find it necessary to
write addresses to mopers and slaves to the letter, to ignorant and
uncharitably condemning superstitious people.''  In a similar direction H. C.
Ørsted expressed himself in a university address (1826), where he alluded to ``certain
proud and harsh men of our time, who in the name of Christianity break the
staff over the 18th century's boldly inquiring men.''
The philosopher Rudolf Haym tells in his autobiography that his father,
a rationalistic teacher, saw him with concern choose the study of theology.
``Some coarse word from the orthodox camp must
have roused his anger.  If I knew, he then said, that you would some day
come over in that direction, I would rather see you dead.''
--- Toward the end of the century it was conversely orthodox
fathers who with concern saw their sons walk --- in their grandfathers'
footsteps.

\sectionhead{2.}{Philosophy and Religion.}

As philosophy's representatives toward religion there stand in the first
third of the century Hegel and Schleiermacher.  They both seek
to show that religion, especially Christianity, is an essential and indispensable
component of the human spiritual life.  But the ways by
which they arrive at this result are different.

It was, as we have seen, Hegel's conviction that the actual and
the rational are one.  Toward religion, as it has historically
developed, he therefore seeks to take up a standpoint that is
raised above the opposition between Orthodoxy, which holds to the
literal reality of what dogma teaches and cult would express,
and Rationalism, which puts its supposed reason in place of
the historically developed doctrine of faith.  Orthodoxy does not see that the literal
expressions and formulas are more or less figurative, and it
does not examine what spiritual significance they have in a deeper
appropriation.  And Rationalism applies a prosaic, intellectual
consideration to the living spiritual content that religion has to offer;
it places itself in a purely external relation to this.  ``Now it is,''
says Hegel (Philosophie der Religion. Einleitung), ``certainly not
the business of philosophy to lead a man to religion. .... He whose heart
% --- p. 125 ---
\opage{125}has not reached beyond all finite being, --- who has not raised
himself above himself in longing and presentiment or in a feeling of the Eternal, has not
cast a glance into the pure ether of the soul, --- he does not know the subject
that philosophy here wants to comprehend.''  What philosophy has to do with is,
according to Hegel, religion's relation to the whole remaining conception of the world of man.
The religious problem arises from the fact that there may be
an opposition present here.  Hegel demands here, as in the doctrine of the state,
that philosophy shall enter into the historically given, into what reality
offers, and here this is positive religion.  If he does so,
he will --- of this Hegel is convinced --- find that what lives and breathes in religion is the same as what lives and breathes in
true philosophy.  Man has not needed to wait for philosophy
in order to find truth; it is already given in religion.  But
it is given there in the figurative language of imagination, and philosophy cannot
stay with the figurative form thus created.  The content
must be translated into thought's own language.  It is peculiar to
imagination that it views as different things what yet
belong intimately together.  It forms, namely, an image for each single
member of the whole that is basically what it wants to express.  Thus
it represents God to itself first as Father, then as Son, and then
as Spirit, and yet the meaning is that there is only one God.
It is
furthermore peculiar to imagination that it views as a historical event
taking place at a given time and in a given place what
is basically an eternal truth, valid at all times and in
all places.  Church theology presents it as an event
that God created the world, and as another event or series of
events that he became man, suffered and died.  But for philosophy
it is an eternal truth that the Eternal and Infinite reveals itself
in and through a finite world, and that it can therefore reach fulfillment only through
impairment and downfall.  Despite this difference
between religion's imaginative and philosophy's conceptual
language, the content is nevertheless the same.  It is the task of philosophy to
justify religion from the thinking consciousness.  Childlike
piety does not need such a justification; it takes
truth on authority and feels satisfied and reconciled in its faith.
Only in the face of doubt and critique is a justification by thought
necessary.  But even if religion and philosophy, faith and knowledge, can be
reconciled, this reconciliation holds precisely only for the thinking consciousness.
If the people no longer rest securely in faith in the truth of
religion, and if it cannot attain to a philosophical
% --- p. 126 ---
\opage{126}understanding, --- why, then there is a split in the spiritual life.  And Hegel
concludes his presentation of the philosophy of religion with the declaration that
how our age is to find its way out of this split, that one must
leave to it itself; philosophy has nothing to do with this practical task.
Hegel thus saw, what has as a rule been overlooked, a constant
thorn in the problem, despite the harmony he has proclaimed.

--- Schleiermacher's standpoint in the philosophy of religion is determined by
his course of development.  He was brought up in the educational institutions of the Moravian Brethren
and was later strongly influenced by Kant's philosophy.
An extraordinarily rich and deep personal life was in him combined
with the sharpest critique, a critique that exercised its force both toward
the historical and the philosophical foundation of theology.  It was
the side of feeling in religion that he laid weight on first and foremost.
Only that can have religious significance for him which appeals to feeling.
But the conceptions in which feeling, in times of devotion and rapture,
procures expression for itself, reflection must afterwards test.  Reflection
seeks to follow the oscillations of feeling and to cut away everything
that is not an immediate and necessary expression of the real
experiences of the inner life.  Schleiermacher had learned from Kant that we can form no
well-grounded thoughts beyond possible experience.  Religious conceptions,
formulated as dogmas, have then only the justification of being
expressions of what is experienced in the religious life of feeling; it
is then a matter of drawing the boundary between dogmas in this sense of
the word and mythological fantasies, which go far beyond and outside the
immediately experienced.  In this distinction Schleiermacher saw theology's
proper task.  In his already mentioned ``Reden über die Religion''
(1799) and in his ``Der christliche Glaube'' (1821) he has developed
this conception.  The concept of God is for him the thought that
corresponds to the feeling of absolute dependence, which is the characteristic
mark of religion at its culmination.  The thought of Christ
as redeemer and exemplar corresponds in the same way to the
feeling of peace and reconciliation that participation in Christian congregational life
brings about.  But from such thoughts no theoretical inferences
can be drawn; they can acquire only symbolic significance.

Hegel too basically conceived all dogmas as symbolic.
For Hegel's as well as for Schleiermacher's philosophy of religion there had to
arise the question whether the practical consciousness can let itself be
content with a symbolic expression of truth instead of the complete
solution of the riddles of life that religion in its classical
times had given or at any rate promised.  As we have seen,
% --- p. 127 ---
\opage{127}it is Hegel's last word in his philosophy of religion that this question
remains standing.  It also emerges even among those who do not know
what philosophy is.  Where does the figurative in religion begin, and where
does the literal cease?  From the side of the Church no clear answer
to this has been given.  There is, however, hardly any question that many
people who adhere to the Church in reality embrace the
symbolic conception.  Hegel and Schleiermacher have, without knowing and
willing it, set the century one of its most important problems.

Common to the two thinkers who gave Romanticism its most clarified
expression was the belief in a harmony of the oppositions that life
presents.  A younger contemporary of theirs, Arthur Schopenhauer,
stepped into sharp opposition to them by putting disharmony in the first
rank.  Inner experiences and outer observations had early made
him feel life's contradictions and pain.  In the innermost of everything living, and
in the end of all existence, he found a never satisfied, painful
striving, a ``will to live'', which never found rest.  Therefore all
attempts to demonstrate the harmony of existence, whether they appeared
in philosophical or in religious form, aroused his indignation and his scorn.
When with zeal and enthusiasm he immersed himself in the source writings
of the great religions, it was their emphasis on life's anguish, sin and
pain that captivated him.  He admired primitive Christianity by reason of
its opposition to natural human life, and he scorned
modern Christianity, which thought itself its continuation.
But most he admired Vedanta and Buddhism, and as
the highest there stood before him the complete abolition of life's blind,
restless urge, the annihilation of ``the will to live'', which Buddha
had called Nirvana.  No positive expression can designate the state
that is thereby attained, and which lies beyond every possible experience;
but it is not therefore to be equated with sheer nothing; no more
than that which lies beyond every possible knowledge
becomes nothing because it cannot be known.  It is nothing only for
him who regards the world of the senses as one and all.  But it is only a few
who attain the full abolition of the will to live, and Schopenhauer
was well aware that he did not belong to them.  He regarded it as the task of
his life to open the eyes to the abysses and to the heights
between which life moves, and which the prevailing optimism does not
let us catch sight of.  For his own part it was the aesthetic-intellectual way of taking life
that helped him beyond its unrest.  His thoughts exercised in the second half of the century great
influence in wide circles.  They express a basic theme in Richard
% --- p. 128 ---
\opage{128}Wagner's great art, and they gave Friedrich Nietzsche the problem
that became the fate of his life through a convulsive attempt to
overcome pessimism in its innermost root.  By his clear and brilliant
style Schopenhauer became accessible to larger circles than Hegel
and Schleiermacher, and he became fashionable.  His significance lies in
the fact that he drew attention to other sides of the religious
problem than those usually noted.  And he was
aware that the relation between philosophy and life is more
complex than people thought in the Romantic period.  His relation
to Buddhism had a counterpart in Kierkegaard's relation to
primitive Christianity.

\sectionhead{3.}{History of Religion and Psychology of Religion.}

Romantic philosophy of religion had already set itself the task
of examining religion in its relation to the human
spiritual life.  But although it often by a stroke of genius cast light on
individual elements in the nature of religious consciousness, it had nevertheless
not been able to make it emerge in its whole composite
essence.  Hegel proceeded from religion as fully complete, with systematic
dogmatics and developed cult; it was for him in this shape
a reality whose rationality was to be demonstrated.  The difference of form
that he found between religion and science was in his eyes unessential,
although he conceded that for non-philosophers it might be very
essential, perhaps insurmountable.  Schleiermacher and Schopenhauer
went more into the practical and complex character of religion,
and their contribution to its psychology is of lasting significance;
but they did not pay sufficient attention to the historical character of religion.
In the course of the century people have sought to remedy this
one-sidedness through an objective, historical study of the religions
as actually given spiritual phenomena.  The science of language
gave here the solid foundation, and for the first time the great
religions of the peoples now came to be present in their characteristic peculiarity
and in their historical connection.  The history of religion became a
distinct science, which applied the same method as all other historical
inquiry.  Every religion is regarded in relation to its time and
to its material and spiritual culture, and through comparison
between the different religions one seeks to find the mental elements
and tendencies that mark the peculiarity of religious phenomena
in relation to other spiritual phenomena.  It then turns out
% --- p. 129 ---
\opage{129}that besides the historical connection, which assigns each single
religion its determinate place, there are also certain basic motives, which
in different degrees and forms again and again recur in all religions
from the lowest to the highest.

Whereas people were agreed that the lower religions' own account
of their origin could not count as real history, the matter stood
differently in many people's eyes with the biblical books' account
of the origin of Christianity.  Rationalists and Supernaturalists
had been agreed that here there was real history;
their disagreement concerned only whether the events that were presented
were of a supernatural character, or whether the accounts of
them could be interpreted so that the miraculous disappeared.  Into this
dispute David Strauss intervened with his book ``Leben Jesu'' (1835).  In the
choice that the Orthodox maintained, when the talk was of biblical accounts,
that they must namely be either historically correct or invented,
Strauss finds a false dilemma.  Historical events are always reported
in such a way that the narrator's presuppositions, moods, wishes,
and ideals determine both the choice of what is communicated and the
light in which what is communicated is seen.  The New Testament authors were guided
by faith in an expected Messiah; Jesus made on them --- or
on their informants --- such an impression that they saw in him
the one who was to come and bring the consummation of all things.  An account
in which events are involuntarily interpreted through conceptions
and moods in the narrator is called a myth or a legend.
Supernaturalism is then in the wrong when it takes the account
of Jesus as literal history, and Rationalism is in the wrong when
it explains away the supernatural in an artificial, often smugly prosaic manner.
Both parties overlook religious imagination's capacity and need
to form myths and legends.  If it is asked what we then know about
Jesus of Nazareth, the answer was: we know what effect he had
on the people who stood near him, and from whom the accounts
of him derive, perhaps through several intermediate links.  It is
``the Christ of faith'' we know, not ``the Jesus of history'', --- thus
Strauss later expresses (Der Christus des Glaubens und der Jesus
der Geschichte. 1865) his conception.  Besides the emphasis on the concept of myth
against the Orthodox's prosaic literalism and the Rationalists'
prosaic reinterpretation, Strauss has the merit of emphasizing
that the founder of Christianity saw himself as the one with whom
a new, supernatural world order was to take effect.  It is the expectation
of the last things (Eschatology) that is the basic thought
% --- p. 130 ---
\opage{130}in Jesus' proclamation and marks his position in the history of religion.
It is to this main point that the most recent historical inquiry too
has come around, after the so-called liberal theology had
made a series of attempts to present Jesus as a prophet of
humanity, an ethical exemplar.  The eschatological conception of Jesus
as the one who through mighty visions announces himself as
the founder of a new, supernatural kingdom, which was already near, at the point of
immediate breakthrough, has also the advantage that
from it one can understand the New Testament ethic in its direction
toward the one thing needful, in face of which all purely human relations
become indifferent, insofar as they are not hindrances.  One understands
that he who put the commandment of love at the head of his
ethic also had to enjoin that it might become necessary to hate
one's nearest, when the relation to them hindered the full devotion
to the Great that was to come.

Whereas in earlier times the problem of Christianity stood as a metaphysical
problem, in that it was asked how God could become
man, it now approaches more and more to being a psychological
problem, in that it is asked how he who in his addresses and
parables set forth the mild and consoling thoughts and proclaims the ethic of humility
and love can be the same who in mighty
visions sees himself as the one who is to come on the clouds of heaven
as judge of the world and savior of the world.  The paradox passes over
into becoming a psychological problem.  Whether this is insoluble cannot be
examined here.  I shall only remark that it is in and by itself not incomprehensible
that precisely he who leads his life and finds his task under the shelter
of great visions and in living expectation can feel pity and inward
compassion for human beings, especially when an inward and loving
mind stands as the best condition for being able to concentrate on the
one thing needful.  But it also becomes clear that of human tasks
in the long run, beyond the life of the single individual and of the contemporary
generation, there can be no talk.  The primitive Christian ethic could
not acquire any positive relation to the great labor of culture that has
been the nerve of human development in the following times.

The discussion of the problem of primitive Christianity continues unabated.  Orthodox
theology has not left the field.  But from its side too it is recognized more and more
that the problem, viewed purely historically, collects
around that psychological question.  It is a vindication
of Strauss in his grave that it is admitted from very opposite sides
that he nailed down the decisive point.  Later investigations
% --- p. 131 ---
\opage{131}have, even though in many respects they shared his points of view, at
several points had to dissociate themselves from him.  He undertook no
thorough investigation of the origin of the individual New Testament
books.  He himself recognized that this investigation was first properly
taken up by F. C. Baur, the founder of the so-called Tübingen school.
This school has set up, constructed according to its opponents' assertion,
a hypothesis which historical critique has since
abandoned.  But the Tübingen school has with energy spoken up for the application
of general historical method to the question of Christianity's
origin and first development.  Thus Baur says
(Die Tübingerschule und ihre Stellung zur Gegenwart. 1859): ``Christianity
is once and for all a historical phenomenon, and as such
it must put up with being regarded and investigated historically.  It:
appears in a historical connection, which it can in no way
deny ..... How can one know what it is, how
it arose and entered into the world, except by going back to the
ways by which it was introduced and prepared, to the causes that
cooperated in its origin, and then from all these moments together
explaining its origin and essence, so far as that is at all
possible.'' --- The Tübingen school's solution of the problem has no doubt been
abandoned by most.  But scientifically viewed the task still stands
firm of understanding Christianity as a member of the whole historical development.
In the end there is only a single historical method, and if one does
not follow it, one does not get history in the scientific sense of the word.

As to method, there has for other religions been no
doubt in this respect.  The study that has been applied
to historical elucidation of the different religions has been extraordinarily
instructive.  An essential side of the human spiritual life
has hereby been illuminated.  Tylor, Frazer and Durkheim have cast
light on the primitive religions, Burnouf and Oldenberg on the
Indian religion, Erwin Rhode on the Greek, Goldzieher on the
Muhammadan, --- to name only a few individual names.  The
historical sense, which is one of the peculiarities of the 19th century,
has found here an exceedingly important application.  We are led beyond
mere polemic and criticism, to say nothing of mockery and scorn, and
are led into directions of life and thought that would be wholly incomprehensible
if one stood before them as fully complete systems, but
which become comprehensible when one sees them in their development and in
relation to what otherwise stirs in human life.  Of special
importance for the understanding of the development of religions has been the
% --- p. 132 ---
\opage{132}elucidation of the relation between cult, legend and dogma.  Sometimes,
as in the worship of the Madonna, legend can lead to cult,
and cult in turn (by virtue of the presupposition that one can worship only
one who is of supernatural origin) to dogma.  Or cult can
itself be the immediate source of dogmas, as when in the Brahma doctrine
the need and longing that lead to cult itself becomes the highest
god.  Or cult can call forth legend, as in the mythical explanations
of why human sacrifices were replaced by animal sacrifices.  One of the
most important results of research in the history of religion is this, that cult
--- however it may have arisen --- is the central thing in all positive religion.
It can even be said to be a definition of positive religion
that it finds expression in a determinate cult, around which legends and
dogmas gather.  Cult stands as a firm point of departure, exerting
its power over all who take part in it.  Dogmas can be refuted, cult
not; it exists or it does not exist.  Through the power it exerts,
it is the most important foundation for the existence of religion.  Many who
cannot reconcile themselves with a religion's dogmas, and perhaps still less
with the sermons that are built upon them, find enrichment
and peace in taking part in cult.  Whether it can be justified to
speak of religion where cult is either not practiced or is regarded as
symbolic action is a question that leads over from history of religion
to psychology of religion.

The boundary between historical and psychological investigation of religion
is not easy to draw once for all.  The historian must be
psychologist, and the psychologist must here be historian.  This latter needs
no further explanation.  As for the former, it is
often overlooked, and the history of religion thinks itself strictly scientific
when it holds to the dogmas, legends and forms of cult
present at each time and in each place.  But the real significance
of these religious phenomena can be discovered only when one goes
back to what stirs in the minds of the people who take part
in cult, listen to the legends and believe in the dogmas.  One must go
back from the objective to the subjective; one must seek to determine
in what the religious value of the given forms consists.  At the same time
the historian of religion cannot avoid making a certain evaluation
of the religions in relation to one another, or of the different
stages of development of the same religion in their mutual relation.  When
a religion or a stage of development of a religion is called higher or
lower in relation to other religions or phases, there is thereby presupposed
a standard, about whose justification questions must be asked.

% --- p. 133 ---
\opage{133}Schleiermacher was already engaged in a psychological investigation
of the foundation of religion in the human mental life, and his reference
to the feeling of dependence is of lasting significance, although it
needs closer determination, especially because dependence presupposes
that there is something one wills or strives after, something to which
one attributes value, and whose attainment meets with obstacles. Schopenhauer
had already emphasized the element of will, and later Ludwig Feuerbach
maintained feeling, need and wish not merely as the psychological
foundation of religion but as the causes that produce religion.
While he has very little respect for the dogmas, he
has great sympathy with the mental foundation in fear and hope, longing
and need, from which they ultimately spring. In religion man beholds
his wishes and hopes as fully realized. Hence
one can study in the different religions the most secret striving
of the human heart in its manifold forms. It is, after all, this
foundation that bears life outside religion as well, and that stirs
in us all. (Wesen des Christentums 1841. --- Theogonie 1857).

The difference between the free-thinkers of the nineteenth and those of the eighteenth century
shows itself clearly when one compares Feuerbach with Voltaire.
Feuerbach is more radical in his outlook than Voltaire, but has a
sympathy with the foundation of religion that Voltaire, who regarded
religion only from the intellectual side, could not have. At the same time
Feuerbach stood toward religion as the natural scientist toward nature;
he is intent on explaining the religious phenomena by
means of causes that prove to be constantly at work in the human
mental life. Just as Lyell explained the geological processes of the past
by forces that are at work in nature to this day, Feuerbach seeks
to find the key to the understanding of religion in forces that psychological
experience constantly demonstrates. The dogmatic element in Feuerbach appears
when he flatly asserts that all theology is psychology.
That is as unwarranted as it would be, at the present stage of
research, flatly to say that physiology is nothing but
physics and chemistry. But just as modern physiology recognizes
no other manner of explaining organic phenomena than to trace them
back to physical and chemical laws, so there is for the science of religion
no other method than the psychological-historical one,
without our being able for that reason to assert in advance that everything can be explained
in that way. Feuerbach's method is, moreover, abstractly psychological
and often unhistorical. The great period of development of the history of religion
also lies after his time. ---

% --- p. 134 ---
\opage{134}Right at the turn of the century the American William James
applied the standpoints of the newer psychology to the understanding of religious
phenomena, having laid particular stress on what works
in us without entering across the threshold of consciousness. (Varieties of
religious experience. A study in human nature. 1902). James has paid special attention
to sudden and seemingly
unmotivated changes in the mental life; it is especially in such cases that it shows
itself, in his view, that what he calls ``the ultramarginal'',
that which lies beyond the margin of consciousness (margin), can
be a source from which new and perhaps higher directions in the mental life
well up. Under religion James counts every emotion that
becomes of significance for our full reckoning with life and with what it has
brought us, and that at the same time brings unity and concentration into our being.

--- It is the pragmatic tendency in epistemology that here
finds a counterpart in the psychology of religion, which is all the more
natural since pragmatism has on the whole the significance of illuminating
the problem of knowledge from a psychological standpoint. A complete
philosophy of religion will include not merely a psychological investigation
of religious topics but also an epistemological and an ethical
investigation, since the relation of religion to science and to morality will at
all times be a main point in its characterization. James
goes very little into this point. In my Religionsfilosofi, which appeared
the year before James's book, I have sought to bring out all three
standpoints that can here be in question. The philosophy of religion has
no special method but is an application of epistemological,
psychological and ethical standpoints to the religious problem.

The more the philosophy of religion distances itself from dogmatic theology,
the more it gives up every attempt to ground the content of religious
faith, and its main topic becomes the psychological motives
that in the past and present have sustained, and in the future may be assumed to sustain,
religion (in a narrower or a wider sense). On the philosophical side
one has often held solely to the negative side, to the unknowability
of the religious content, the scientific impossibility of grounding the
validity of religious representations. Herbert Spencer distinguished
between science and religion, so that the object of the former was the
knowable, of the latter the unknowable, and he saw the essential in
religion in its acknowledgment that what underlies all
and moves in all is a mystery, an acknowledgment he found increasing
in determinateness as one passes from the lower religions to the
higher. (First Principles. 1861. Ecclesiastical Institutions. 1885).
% --- p. 135 ---
\opage{135}For such a conception Spencer's friend the physiologist Huxley coined
the designation agnosticism (doctrine of non-knowledge), because every presentable
doctrine about such things had to be designated by a word ending
in -ism. Spencer, however, asserts an all too external relation between
the unknowable that is supposed to underlie all and the existence
we know, and he overlooks the conditionedness of the religious feeling by
definite wishes and interests, which are not satisfied by the mere
knowledge that there is a mystery. Comte's English disciple Frederic
Harrison maintained, in opposition to Spencer, that religion presupposes
an object of reverence, and like his master he found
this object in humanity. (Harrison's cult of humanity has
later been presented at length in his ``Creed of a Layman''. 1907). To this
it must be remarked, however, that what can make humanity an object
of reverence is that in the course of its historical development it
has fostered the spiritual and material goods that make life valuable
for us; hence we feel the best we know to be conditioned by its continued
existence and development. But this existence and development are in turn conditioned
by the course of nature constantly bringing with it the possibility of a
development in the direction of the ideals that are occasioned by human feeling of value,
--- a direction that is hoped to continue beyond the point where
our ideals have either been attained or have shown themselves limited and provisional.
In the widest sense religion must have not merely a humanistic
but also a cosmological character.

--- Theology as such cannot attribute decisive significance to historical
and psychological standpoints. It must always proceed from a definite
religion as the true one, and it thereby has a standard that
excludes the universal character that a historical psychological outlook
can acquire. As we have seen, various paths point
to cult as the central element in the positive religions, and every
theology must in the end become an attempt to justify a certain
cult. But it becomes more and more difficult for theologians
who have any contact with the scientific development of recent times
to meet the demands that the congregation, i.e. the circle that
gathers around a certain cult, makes. A modern theologian, Troeltsch,
has aptly said that the church can neither do without theology
nor put up with it. The church must have a coherent doctrine,
but every attempt in this direction contains a danger of reinterpretation
or of consequences that lead beyond the ideas bound to the cult.
It is a fine insight that expresses itself in Schleiermacher's proposition
that ``no dogmatic proposition has its ground in another, but
% --- p. 136 ---
\opage{136}every single such proposition must be found by contemplating the
Christian self-consciousness.'' Merely by being brought into logical
connection with one another the propositions may come to stand differently from when
they are drawn each by itself from life's own experience; the psychological
totality that a man's faith must always to a certain degree constitute will
be more or less different from the logical totality that reflection
could build up from the single components of the content of his faith.
Changes will occur still more readily when one tries to
bring the dogmas into connection with thoughts that have their origin
in quite other domains than the religious. And yet in the long run there
can be no complete opposition, nor a mere relation of indifference,
between religious representations and the thoughts that men
form in the course of life and in the work of scientific
understanding of life. A religious problem arises when
a circle of such thoughts has formed, and when the relation between
this circle and the circle of the religious representations presses
for clear determination. The difference between churchly
laymen and scientific theologians will essentially rest on this, that the former
do not have the need, which the latter must have, to find logical connection
between the single members of the content of faith and to find a certain connection
between the content of faith and the rest of the intellectual content that
is at one's disposal. Now it is precisely laymen who in the course of the century have come
to play a greater role in the life of the church. The church has become more
democratic; that was, as we have seen above, a condition of its
renewed life. This entails a decentralization, against which Pius X in his
bull mentioned above protested, particularly when it was sought to make
the laymen a factor of progress. For the time being the laymen
nevertheless stand as a good support for the church. A Catholic theologian, the former
Imperial Chancellor von Hertling, has thus stated that our century has
called laymen to the defense of Christianity in a manner that was not
known in earlier times. This movement leads, in any case
for the time being, to a sharpening of orthodoxy. It is easier to hold fast to
the letter than to enter into the relation between image and thought.
But the support that laymen can give becomes at the same time a control, and
the situation becomes, especially in Protestantism, which has no fixed
concept of authority, more and more this, that it is not the proclaimers
who come with message and instruction that are followed,
but that it is the laity who decide how the message and the instruction
are to sound. The position of theology nowadays rests more on its
position toward the laity than on its position toward science. It is
% --- p. 137 ---
\opage{137}after all also in the end by the experiences that individuals have as to what can
sustain them in life's struggle that the future of the religious problem
will be conditioned. This leads us over to one of the significant thoughts
that the nineteenth century has fostered.

\chapterhead{4.}{THE PRINCIPLE OF PERSONALITY}

When the nineteenth century is characterized as the century of confirmation by experience,
this characterization holds also for the religious
domain. It has shown itself in three different respects. The justification
of the religious reaction that marks the age (rhythmically alternating in
the course of the century) must be sought in this, that one turns back to
the old faith in order once more to test its carrying capacity, or, as
one of the most brilliant spokesmen of the reaction has expressed it: ``to read what is
Old, Familiar, handed down from the Fathers, through once more,
if possible in a more inward manner.'' It was a matter, in the second place,
of determining the place of religion in relation to the spiritual life that
has developed independently of religion, and that cannot and will not
be sacrificed for it. It was a matter, finally, of investigating the historical
and psychological foundation on which religion builds, and on whose
continued existence the existence of religion also depends.

But there is yet another very important side on which the said
characterization is seen to hold. Eminent spokesmen
have pointed in an energetic and brilliant manner to the individual human
personality itself --- ``the single individual'' --- whose interests and needs religion
(whether this word be taken in a wider or in a narrower sense)
is to satisfy. Here the real verification takes place in
the religious domain. Churchliness and theology, philosophy, history and
natural science cannot in and for themselves tell the individual anything about
how he --- with his nature, his circumstances, his experiences --- is to
take his stand in religious respects. And no faith, no way of taking
life (be it religious or not) has any real value
unless it has proceeded from one's own experience of life and corresponds to the
personal need awakened through the experience of life. It is the principle of personality
that expresses itself herein, and which the nineteenth century has
established with greater energy and with clearer consciousness than any of
its predecessors. Thomas Carlyle is the best known representative
of this line of thought, which was soon proclaimed in his footsteps by his
American friend Emerson and independently of him in the Nordic countries
by Erik Gustaf Geijer, Frederik Christian Sibbern and Søren
% --- p. 138 ---
\opage{138}Kierkegaard, and then toward the end of the century to stream from new
sources.

Carlyle turned, after a severe crisis in his inner life, both against
the claim of science and against that of the church to determine a man's
whole faith. (Sartor Resartus. 1833). Each individual must find his
own religion, just as each must find his own task in life. What matters
is not confessions and articles of faith but what a man
practically believes, perhaps without being conscious of it. What is decisive is
what really stirs in a man's mind in face of the existence
of which it is a member, but which it is not able to survey
or to see through. Traditions and churchly customs contain
a great deal that the individual will not be able fully to make
his personal property; what matters then is to become clear about what of
all this handed-down material one has really appropriated and holds fast in
one's faith. Most important in Carlyle's eyes is the eradication of the dishonesty
that prevails in the religious domain, and which led Carlyle
in a conversation with Emerson to declare that there was no longer any
religion in England. That an end be put to dishonesty is the
first condition for the real spiritual values that the past has handed down
to be preserved, and for new values to unfold
in silence. In silence --- for all that is great happens in silence, because its first germ
forms deep within the sanctuary of the personal life.

Independently of Carlyle similar thoughts arose in the Swedish historian
and philosopher Erik Gustaf Geijer. He had belonged to the Romantic
school and had long shared its conservative conception in
the religious, the pedagogical and the political domain. But the historical
study itself freed him from dependence on the historically
handed-down. His ``defection'' from the Romantic-conservative
tendency (1838) was connected with the principle of personality (an expression
he created) dawning on him. Some years later (1844) he writes:
``Our age has been remarkable more than any other for great
changes. Yet that is not what distinguishes it most, but
rather this, that these unheard-of changes more distinctly than ever
spring from inner causes. It is the inner world that is failing
in its foundations, in its faith, its conviction, its knowledge. Our age
is an age that suffers from its own thoughts. And if one would seek a name
for the basic and mother thought that here is pressing forward and making its way, it
is none other than the principle of personality, whose penetration into
general political life we have witnessed.'' And when Geijer some years later
(1847), shortly before his death, casts a glance back at his own life,
% --- p. 139 ---
\opage{139}he declares: ``There lies a basic thought in my whole life, which emerges
ever more distinctly; it is not my own work, but it has led
and guided me right up to this day. Were I to give it a name, it is
none other than the much disputed principle of personality,
whose prophet I have almost against my will become.'' Of the application
of this principle to the religious domain he says in a letter from
1843: ``I am neither a Church Christian nor a Bible Christian, though so much
of a Christian that I can find edification both in church and in
Bible. Thousands are in the same case as I, --- all who
cannot be content with a mere faith in authority, but are compelled to build
their own religion on the basis of their own experience and reflection.
This individual element, which is now the only living thing in religion, points
--- however scattered it may seem --- nevertheless toward a common goal.''

Geijer's statements about the individual as the only living thing in
religion correspond to Carlyle's declaration that what matters now
in religion first and foremost is honesty. Both statements point
in the same direction. And Sibbern meets, without knowing it, the
Scottish and the Swedish thinker. His plea for what Geijer called
the principle of personality is built not merely on a critique of faith in authority
and on a warm feeling for the worth of personality, but (as
we have already touched on) on a whole world-view, whose main principle
is that all development and all life, spiritual as well as bodily, proceeds
from separate points of departure, and that the general and common forms
come into being through union and interaction between the sporadically
emerging moments. From 1828 on Sibbern is engaged with these thoughts.
In university programs from 1846 to 1849 he applied
them to the religious and the social domain. According to his
conviction a domain in the human spiritual life where general
rules do not reach, and where one must await what individual
development brings with it. He objects to anything
being valid merely because it is asserted and acknowledged in wide
circles and formulated in doctrines handed down from generation to
generation. And this very common and general element had in its time its first
origin in the inner life of single personalities. Everything spiritual that is to
come to dominion in the world must go the way of subjectivity, must stir
with gripping and captivating power in single individuals. Through
mutual conflict between different personalities and tendencies
the religious life advances. For the time being every strong and living
faith is justified as a forceful outcome of life's inner power.

At about the same time as these statements of Sibbern brought forward here
% --- p. 140 ---
\opage{140}Kierkegaard set up his famous proposition ``Subjectivity is
truth'' (Uvidenskabelig Efterskrift. 1846). Truth was for
him not an object one could go and behold, not a content given once
for all. It comes into being only by being produced
and held fast with energy and inwardness. Whether the God
to whom a man prays is the true God thus depends on whether the man's
mind is honest and earnest or ruled by habit and superficial. He
who worships an idol nevertheless prays to the true God when there is honesty
and inwardness in the worship. Already as a young man Kierkegaard
wrote in his diary: ``What good would it do me if I found a
so-called objective truth, when for myself and for my life it
had no deeper significance.'' Kierkegaard speaks only of
truth of this latter kind, object of what he calls ``essential''
knowledge. ``Inessential'' knowledge is that which consists in
logic, mathematics, natural history and historical knowledge; all such
knowledge has, according to Kierkegaard, no significance for the personal
life. As regards religion, he declares, like Carlyle, honesty
to be what is first and foremost needed. When in his last
great polemic against the official church he was to say what he actually
wanted, he answered: ``Quite simply, I want integrity.'' And by
integrity he meant that one becomes conscious of where one stands
in the world of spirit, not least in what relation one stands to the
great models one acknowledges as one's own, --- whether one's own, personal
way of taking and conducting life covers the faith one thinks
one is building on.

The thoughts mentioned here belong to the middle of the century,
to the remarkable years between 1840 and 1850, when so much was being
prepared in silence. While Newman in his parsonage fought the last
battle to reach Catholicism, Ernest Renan fought his
battle in the seminary of St. Sulpice to work his way out of the faith he
had brought with him from medieval Brittany. At the same time
Geijer, Sibbern and Kierkegaard broke with Romanticism; the harmony it
had hitherto brought them now stood before them as a great, perhaps pernicious
illusion. Toward the end of the century the principle of personality comes to expression in somewhat
different forms, especially as a reaction
against the increasing division of labor in the spiritual domain. Emphasis
is laid on the immediate and involuntary craving for life and fullness of life,
which can never quite find expression and come into its own within
any of the rubrics into which spiritual life threatens to be parceled out.
Guyau maintains the involuntary urge to unfold, the
% --- p. 141 ---
\opage{141}overflowing
and yet unified energy, in contrast to the special
aims to which the practice of life leads one to set, and to the division and limitation
that reflection brings with it. A kindred thought has found
expression in Bergson's emphasis on instinctive intuition in
contrast to analysis and abstraction (Les données immédiates de
la conscience. 1888). In Nietzsche the involuntary power and fullness of life
are placed above all the forms that art and science command. In his
symbolizing thinking he expresses this valuation by
setting Apollo above Socrates, but Dionysus above them both.

Whereas for the thinkers who toward the middle of the century
worked their way out of Romanticism what mattered was self-reflection, honesty
and, as a consequence of this, limitation, for their successors
toward the end of the century (Guyau, Nietzsche, Bergson) what mattered
was to counteract the mechanization of life with which modern
experimental science and philosophical criticism seemed to threaten,
and which was favored by the magnificent development of industrial technique.
It holds of both groups of thinkers --- the anti-Romantic
and the anti-realistic --- that they draw too sharp a line
between personality and science. Science is itself a work of
personal labor and bears the stamp of the human spirit. And
one cannot distinguish once for all between the knowledge that
is of essential significance for the personal life and that which does not
have essential significance for it. The fact that scientific
understanding of existence is possible to as great an extent as
it proves to be the case is of great significance for a man's
personal faith, which after all must be conditioned by the relation to existence
as this, after the most exact investigation, shows itself to be
constituted. Thus the Copernican hypothesis and
the expansion of the picture of the world to which it led have also exercised great influence
on the conception of life of modern times, and the science of the nineteenth century,
which both in extent and in depth has continued the transformation of
the picture of the world, cannot without more be counted as inessential knowledge.
Moreover, science cannot renounce the right also
to draw the personal life itself under its investigations, even
if it here comes to stand before one of its most individual and
complicated subjects. --- In a series of lectures on the principle of personality
in philosophy (published in Swedish 1911) I have sought
to assert the significance of the principle of personality in such a way that the view here indicated
of the relation between personality and science
nevertheless came into its own. ---

% --- p. 142 ---
\opage{142}It is a very essential trait in the characterization of the nineteenth century
that a line of thought such as that which the anti-Romantic and
anti-realistic authors just mentioned represent has found such energetic
expression. In an earlier connection (the section on psychology) we regarded
some of these authors as remarkable subjects for psychology,
for which they were suited by the powerful, contradiction-laden character
of their personalities. Here we have drawn them forth again as
spokesmen for a principle that they, precisely on account of their own subjective
peculiarities, were suited to assert. The principle of personality,
as they conceive it, is in the first place a means of purging
all that is spurious, external and habitual. But it contains
at the same time the truth that everything that is produced or appropriated with
personal force and depth thereby already gets its value, quite
apart from what a closer testing leads to. And it opens finally
the eyes to the richness of human life, to the many individual points of departure
for spiritual life. It removes perhaps for the time being the prospect
of fellowship and unity in the domain of spiritual life, but opens
in return the prospect of richer and more manifold forms of spiritual life.
There may come a new grounding of what one can call in the widest
sense the religious life (whether this name be retained
or not), when the foundation becomes the real
life-experiences of men, interpreted according to each one's personality, and when
it is not the experiences and interpretations of earlier generations that are without more
laid to the foundation. It is the honor of the nineteenth century that it has had
an eye for the necessity and the possibility of such a renewal,
although the goal is great and distant.

\chapterhead{5.}{RELIGION AND MORALITY}

As mentioned above, in the tercentenary after Luther's
appearance protest was made from a churchly standpoint not merely against the
free reason but also against the free conscience. It will now have
its interest to see how the relation between religion and morality
shaped itself in the course of the century.

After the Revolution and Napoleon had been struck to the ground, the Holy
Alliance proclaimed Christ as head of the state, the princes as
his delegates and the Bible as the guiding principle for internal and external politics.
But apart from the fact that the princes, after the way they had acted
toward one another at the Congress of Vienna and afterwards toward their
subjects, were not exactly suited to be divine delegates, the
% --- p. 143 ---
\opage{143}whole idea so conflicted with the character of modern
state and national life that it was and remained a dream, even where it was meant seriously.
Not even the theological ethicists who sympathized with
this dream ventured to go so far. The German philosopher of law Stahl nevertheless
set up the idea of a Christian state. In such a state the Christian
church is the only church that is protected; the Christian law of marriage
holds; the school is directed by the church, and Christian confession of faith is a condition
for access to offices and for eligibility to popular assemblies.
Later in the century Martensen too in his
``Christian Ethics'' spoke up for a Christian state; but then the demands were
considerably lowered. He demands merely that the state shall be built
upon a religious foundation, since it would otherwise have no ethical
authority, for all ethics rests on religious authority. Fundamentally
only Christianity can provide the foundation for such authority; but it
is not required that all in the nation be Christians, only that the nation bow to
the authority of the Christian conviction. The Christianity of the state shows itself
in its supporting the church, upholding Christian custom and usage among the people and
letting its legislation be animated by Christian presuppositions.

It was, as Stahl and Martensen are examples of, especially speculative
theology and the High Church tendency that asserted the Christianity
of the state. When, on the other hand, one lays the weight on the people's free
association around a cult and the confession of faith attached to it,
one will naturally come to look differently at the relation between
people, state and church. Grundtvig, who after his visit to England had
won a free and natural view of human and civil relations,
realized that social relations must be ordered according to the experience
of human nature that history reveals at every given place
(the preface to ``Mands Minde''. 1838). Social ethics, and indirectly
all ethics, was thereby placed on an independent footing.
In conscious opposition to every theological grounding of the order of moral
and civil life stood the so-called doctrine of utility (utilitarianism),
which in Bentham's, James Mill's and Stuart Mill's hands
became a mighty reformatory organ, while the attempts at a
speculative grounding of morals as a rule had a conservative
character; the Hegelian philosophy of right, which was mentioned in an earlier
connection, is a classic example of this. But whether one
conceives of ethics as a strictly rational science, or considers
it necessary to build on the continually growing experience of
the effects of actions and institutions, there has in the century
stirred a decided endeavor to assert the independence of ethics, and thereby
% --- p. 144 ---
\opage{144}of social life, from dogmatic presuppositions. (See
above the section on ethics). In the practice of life it is, however, not always necessary
to go back to the ultimate principles. What in the individual
case springs from confessional motives may in its effects
very well agree with what from a rational or utilitarian
standpoint would have to be required. The motive of valuation need not always
coincide with the motive of action. A great example is the
way in which churchly philanthropy has in many respects
paved the way for the humane. Already Vincent de Paul in the
seventeenth century expressed the most important of the main ideas of modern philanthropy.
Whether one proceeds from religious motives of action
or not, a humane mind will be concerned that
something be accomplished of real benefit to the suffering, so that the motive of valuation
in the end becomes purely human.

It is, then, not in the philanthropic domain that the difference between
religion and morality needs to come forward. All will agree
that things are bad when men hunger, thirst and freeze. It will
be otherwise when it concerns the whole work of human cultural life,
--- the significance of work in and for science and art,
civil freedom and technical development. Can all this be grounded on
strictly churchly presuppositions? --- We stand here before a problem
that has occupied thinking spirits in the nineteenth century in a more
decisive manner than in earlier times. It is of course not for
all men that this problem has been able to arise. In practice most
live on an involuntary fusion of tradition, experience
and reflection, without becoming conscious of the ultimate sources of their
views. That the problem has come forward is due partly to a
historical comparison between primitive Christianity and the Christianity of modern times,
partly to an ethical investigation of how the modern Christian practice
sanctioned by the church stands to primitive Christian
ethics. It is more philosophers than theologians who were led to raise
these questions and thereby led to point out the
opposition in principle between original and modern Christianity
in ethical respects. Schopenhauer and Feuerbach saw this opposition clearly,
and from their very different standpoints Kierkegaard
in his polemic against the existing church maintained that the Christianity of the New
Testament --- by which he thought especially of the New Testament
ethics --- did not exist. The decisive point for these
thinkers was precisely the relation to the higher human culture, to
work for science and art, for political life, social progress and
% --- p. 145 ---
\opage{145}personal freedom. Such work has no root in primitive Christian ethics.
And the more recent historical investigation of primitive Christian literature has
(as already mentioned above) demonstrated the great influence that the expectation
of Christ's near return, and with it of the conclusion of
all human striving, has had on primitive Christian thought.
Everything came to depend on one's living with one's whole soul in this
expectation and in preparation for what its fulfillment was to
bring. Work toward the continued development of human culture and
human conditions of life could then not become of decisive significance.
It is on its own responsibility that the church has later sought to draw
the whole humane culture under the standpoints that its dogmas indicated.
Several eminent theologians have felt the difficulty that here lies
for Christian ethics. A letter from the church historian Hase from his
youth is in this respect so characteristic that it must be quoted.
``When I,'' he says, ``take Christian piety in its
peculiar historical character as the exclusive striving after
the Eternal, as an otherworldly longing, for which earthly life is only
a pilgrimage to heaven, then I understand such a mood well enough
and know how to respect it, as I respect everything where only one single
thing is willed with vigor, one single thing loved above all things; but in myself
there is also a good bit of paganism, which holds the world
dear and dives down into its beauty and into its pain, --- and not,
as the pious so often do, involuntarily and half with a bad conscience,
but without feeling remorse, with conscious purpose and in full
consciousness, because I regard the counterpart as a one-sidedness, however
exalted this has often been.'' What in the spirited church historian
comes as a sincere self-knowledge, later theologians
have wished to set up as a churchly theory. Ritschl thus distinguishes between
a wider and a narrower content of the New Testament. To the
narrower content he then counts what no longer corresponds to
the needs of the congregation, among other things ``das Detail urchristlicher Hoffnungen''.
Harnack wants to separate the actual ``Evangelium'' from the whole primitive Christian
content, and to this ``Evangelium'' he does not count the proclamation
of the literal nearness of the Kingdom of God. But Harnack has seen so
clearly that when one takes eschatology (the belief in the imminent conclusion)
away, the basic motive in Christian ethics falls away too,
and that an ethical principle is lacking which can orient toward the
civil life and modern culture, and he therefore wants to supplement
the ``Evangelium'' with thoughts drawn from the Greeks and from Goethe.
The highest would, in his opinion, be attained when one could ``combine
% --- p. 146 ---
\opage{146}Augustine's piety, inwardness and absorption with the openness of antiquity
toward the world, with its calm, vigorous activity and its clear
and bright mood.'' Also among theologians who are far from agreeing with
Ritschl and Harnack the problem comes forward, thus in the remarkable
correspondence, remarkable for the history of the time, between two Danish clergymen (Otto Møller
and Skat Rørdam). The content of the Christian faith stands for them
as given once for all, and the conclusion of all earthly existence
may come at any moment; they look with heartfelt longing toward this
conclusion --- but what if Christ now comes before the completion of
the national and cultural development to which they too had bound their heart
and their hope, and which requires the work of unforeseeable ages!
---

The problem that here arises concerns at one and the same time the relation of modern
Christianity to primitive Christianity and the relation of Christianity
in general to the culture which it has not itself produced. Alongside
the previously mentioned problem of the relation between the
literal and the figurative in the religious representations, this is
a main question, the practical answer to which will be of great significance
for the spiritual development in the new century.

\chapterheadii{6.}{THE RELIGIOUS PROBLEM AT THE TRANSITION TO THE}{TWENTIETH CENTURY}

There was a time in the seventh and eighth decades of the century when
many were inclined to believe that the religious problem had once
for all been put aside and would die a quiet death, like so many
other problems that in their time had occupied the minds of men
but rested on presuppositions that no longer existed. It
was especially the effects of the vigorous upswing of natural science at
the middle of the century that now exerted their influence on larger
circles. In the Nordic countries this influence united with the
movement that a vigorous Renaissance in the poetic and aesthetic domain
had awakened. One felt a new enthusiasm for spiritual freedom and deep
aversion toward the Romantic epigones, who did not understand that their
time was past. Philosophically considered the whole movement was not very deep.
One rejoiced, like Faust's famulus, over how splendidly
far we had come. Faust himself was after all not as glad as Wagner. And
the real inquirers did not share the confidence, frequent especially in literary
circles, that everything was now settled and done. It was the time of positivism,
but neither Comte nor Mill, neither Darwin nor
% --- p. 147 ---
\opage{147}Spencer believed that all riddles were solved, however sure they were
that science on the whole was on the right way, and however firmly they, as
honest inquirers, believed in the justification of their own hypotheses.
Just as toward the end of the eighteenth century one often had
an exaggerated confidence in the ``enlightenment'' one had attained, so
now in a more realistic form a corresponding trend of mind was fairly widespread
in the said decades of the nineteenth century. There can now
also be no doubt that very much in the current religious representations
could not subsist with the secure results of science or
be reconciled with its standpoints, let alone be demonstrated by its methods.
And it was especially the fact that there was so much one could no longer
believe in that occupied the minds of many. It was the negative side of
free inquiry that people came to lay most weight on. I wrote about it
in my Etik (1887): ``Only if our thought and our feeling
have really been expanded does the liberation from the doctrines of positive religion
have any ethical significance. Not to believe anything is about
the least that can be said of a man, and cannot
give him any positive value, especially since a negative creed
can be adopted in just as unindependent and thoughtless a manner as
the positive can be adopted.'' But even among those who were not content to
become clear about what they did not believe in, and who also did not
care to appear as emancipated schoolboys who make fun of
their catechism, even among them there prevailed a more or
less complete indifference toward religious questions. The
spirit of realism that prevailed may even be said to have seized theology
itself, which now, after the dying out of philosophizing theologians,
sought a purely positive ground in a sharpened faith in authority. The Catholic
Church proclaimed the infallibility of the Pope and the sole legitimacy of
medieval theology; the Protestant church held to its confessional writings,
made use of the word ``positive'' as a slogan and of a reference
to ``the congregation'' as the final argument.
In the last decade of the century, in the nineties, a new current is traced in the various
countries outside the church and an increasing self-confidence
within the church. Some years ago I expressed myself on this
in the following manner, and cannot now express myself better.

It is evident to every unprejudiced observer that there have been
spiritual needs which the preceding literature and currents
did not satisfy, and which now make themselves felt more and more strongly.
And since the world now, as Luther already experienced, is like
the drunken peasant who, when one has helped him up on one
% --- p. 148 ---
\opage{148}side of the horse, falls down on the other side, so this new
tendency, which like the preceding one talks much of ``what
moves in the age,'' becomes, for its part and in its own way, often guilty
of corresponding errors to its predecessor. Its language is often marked by
even greater arrogance than its predecessor's, which is connected
with its not, like the latter, having the feeling of being a militant
church, but without more ado thinking it can appropriate the traditions
of millennia.

Such a movement is to be traced in all countries, both as regards what is natural and
legitimate and as regards what is overstrained and superficial. It is particularly prominent in France, as a counter-wave
after the victory and excesses of anticlericalism. The remarkable thing is first and
foremost that the movement cannot be traced back to new thoughts and
points of view. No superior personalities appear here as
leaders, and no new solution is given of the old difficulties of dogmatism.
One has learned nothing and forgotten nothing. At most one goes around
the difficulties. As regards the motives, it is difficult
to decide to what degree personal need of refuge, of calm, help
and comfort is the determining factor, and to what degree, particularly in the case of the many,
need and desire for spiritual fellowship and comradeship,
thus a social element that does not wholly coincide
with the religious element, make themselves felt. An old Kierkegaardian
cannot help shaking his head at the frequent
talk of ``the numerous Christians of these times,'' which has replaced
the previous times' ``little flock''.

One thing there is, however, that even Kierkegaard, if he could still walk
among us, would have to acknowledge, and that is the great work that
the church and its men have set in motion to bring help and comfort
out there where it is most needed, to those ``who sit in the corners
and slink about on the roads.'' The church here makes use of its hold on
the people and of its great organization to practice philanthropy on a large scale,
and certainly with more discretion than formerly. This deserves all honor.
But the church must not forget that it has an intellectual account
to render, which it does not settle by reference to its edifying
and philanthropic activity. When Scipio Africanus was accused in
the popular assembly of disorder in his accounts, he said: ``On
this day I defeated Hannibal at Zama; let us go to the Capitol and
thank the gods!'' The people followed him. But it is not reported whether it
helped the accounts.

--- The movement may recall the one that arose at the beginning of the nineteenth
% --- p. 149 ---
\opage{149}century, except that it has not so far borne such rich fruit
for spiritual life on the whole as that one. We still lack material to
form a clear understanding of the real causes of the movement, whereas
such material for the movement of a hundred years ago
is available in fairly rich supply. If, as investigation seems to establish,
four elements chiefly cooperate in the origin of a religious faith,
--- the influence of venerable tradition, one's own reflection, the results of
knowledge by experience, and the innermost need of the heart, --- then it has
now been the first and the fourth element (tradition and personal
need) that have played the main role, whereas the second and the third
(reflection and experience) were effective in the first line in the immediately preceding
time.

It will be of interest to hear a testimony in this matter from
a thinker who had to a high degree contributed to determining the line of thought
in large circles in the seventh and eighth decades of the century.
Herbert Spencer in the year 1893 (in his seventy-third year) wrote down the following remarks
in his autobiography.

Spencer first mentions a change that has taken place in his
older days in his political views.
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``While in the days of youthful enthusiasm I thought that all would go well when the form of government
was changed, I now think that changes in the form of government
can only be of benefit insofar as they are expressions of the citizens'
changed nature.'' He then remarks that a corresponding, perhaps
somewhat less pronounced change has taken place in his conception
of religious institutions.
% translated from Høffding's Danish
``While the current faith slowly lost
its hold on me, the only question seemed to me to be that of the
truth or untruth of the special doctrines in which I had been
instructed. But gradually, and especially in the later years, I became
clear that this was not the only question. This was in part caused
by the more comprehensive acquaintance with different
human societies that I had gained ..... So striking is the evidence
that among races in different parts of the earth without mutual
connection progress in civilization has gone together with the
development of a religious system which was absolute in its dogmas,
terrible in its threats of punishment and led by a mighty priesthood, that
one must necessarily conclude that without such a factor the maintenance
of social subordination would have been impossible. One may well
feel much astonishment at the slight effect that threats and promises
supposed to stem from a supernatural source have had. The history of Europe,
which is bathed in crimes throughout, seems to show
% --- p. 150 ---
\opage{150}that fear of Hell and hope of Heaven have had little influence
on men ..... But they must nevertheless have had some influence, and had they not been, things would surely have been
worse. And in any case the right grounds for good conduct lie
too remote and are too obscure for people, as people have been and are,
for them to be able to exert any effect ..... Furthermore it shows itself more
and more clearly that real faith is constantly different from literal faith
and adapts itself to new social and individual conditions ..... In modern
sermons theological dogmas recede more and more into the background
and ethical doctrines come to the fore, so that we may
think that in the course of time we shall reach a stage of development where it is acknowledged
that the riddle of existence is insoluble, and where religious institutions
will then be placed in the service of ethical culture. By these
paths I have come more and more to look with calm on forms of
religious faith toward which in younger days I felt a decided aversion.
Believing that they are on the whole naturally formed in relation to the
different peoples and times, I consider it good that they each
live and work as long as the conditions permit, and also that
sudden changes of religious institutions will surely be followed by
reactions ..... But to a large extent, perhaps chiefly, this
change in my feeling toward religious faith and the institutions that
sustain it has sprung from an ever deeper conviction
that the place in mental life which it has occupied can never stand empty, but
that the great questions about ourselves and about the existence of which we are a
part must constantly arise anew, and that, even if no
positive answers to them can be found, there must nevertheless constantly assert themselves mental states
(modes of consciousness) that can take the place of
positive answers .....  Religious faith fills a place in mental life which
thought strives to fill, but without being able to do so, --- and is able less
and less to fill, the more it strives for it.
I have therefore come to regard it with a sympathy that has
its origin in a need I also feel. My divergence from it comes
from my not being able to accept the solutions it brings, but
I cherish at the same time the wish that a solution might be found!''

--- Spencer is certainly right that knowledge of the history of religion must
