work in the direction of understanding the place of positive religion in practical
human life. It makes it easier for us to feel our way into the disposition
on which the historical religions rest. And when to this is added the
reawakening insight into the nature of the problem of knowledge and into the limits
of its solution, it is understood that one comes to look
% --- p. 151 ---
\opage{151}differently at religious questions than before. The old objections to
religious doctrines now lie so near and have become so trivial that
an aversion naturally arises to bringing them forward, little as they are
answered and can be answered. It is a criticism any child can practice.
But for him who has a sense for the jubilation over the sustaining powers of life
or for the anxiety about what may threaten the values of life, as well as
for fidelity to that to which one has bound one's heart, --- feelings
which have all found expression in the cult of the religions, their legends
and their dogmas, --- for him criticism will never have the last word, but will be followed by a hope of new spiritual forms of life that
can lead beyond the disharmony to which the history of the religious problem
in the nineteenth century also bears witness.

How the mighty experiences of the second decade of the twentieth century
have worked and will work in the time to come must be left
to be answered by those who have prophetic ability. It is conceivable that
these experiences have brought many men into an immediate relation
to the most elementary opposites of life, pleasure and pain,
joy and sorrow, jubilation and anxiety, life and death, --- and that it will lead to
men's building their personal faith on that whose power they, as
standing nearer or farther, have tested in life's struggle. Whether this then
again leads back to an old faith or over to quite new thoughts
about life, time will show.

% --- p. 152 ---
\unnumhead{CONCLUSION}

\opage{152}There is hardly any age that has thought more about itself and about
its relation to its predecessors than the nineteenth century.
Other ages have thought they had the right to feel their opposition to
the past with pride or at least with the certainty of faith of being
on the right way. This holds for Greek antiquity in relation to the barbarians,
for Christian faith in relation to paganism, for the age of enlightenment in relation to
the darkness of the Middle Ages. To be sure the nineteenth century too has
had its self-esteem. It has at times regarded its science
as a consummation, in relation to which the intellectual
striving of earlier ages stood as a series of preliminary stages, or it has been
glad in the consciousness of the manifoldness of its external culture, also
in the thought that knowledge is now spread in far greater circles than
before. But by virtue of its historical sense the nineteenth century has an
understanding of the culture of earlier ages and of its justification as
an expression of their life, an understanding that was formerly lacking, and which
had to lead to circumspection in self-appraisal. The great question
had now really to become whether what one called one's science,
one's art, one's religion, one's culture really stood as form
and expression of an energetic inner life, of depth and earnestness in relation
to the tasks. There had come forward --- and this decidedly redounds to the
honor of the century --- a standard that made it more difficult
than before to have an undivided feeling of one's own excellence. There were many
discontented spirits in the nineteenth century, and there were especially many
who missed the fullness and power of life which all intellectual progress
and all perfecting of the external apparatus of life ought nevertheless to
serve. And if it is justified to characterize the nineteenth century
as the age of confirmation by experience, then it is understandable that it could never
feel itself wholly satisfied by its own striving. For full confirmation by experience
of the greatest and most significant thoughts can
never be had. Even the success a hypothesis has is --- as Leibniz already
saw --- no proof of its truth. The very concepts one
forms of truth and of humanity must again and again stand their
test. The idea of the struggle for existence, one of the most remarkable thoughts of the nineteenth
% --- p. 153 ---
\opage{153}century, teaches that work and struggle are constantly required
to maintain what has been won. The most glorious types can
perish when they do not satisfy what circumstances demand.

Already some of the foremost men of the eighteenth century had an eye
for how long the way was to what could rightly stand as human
ideals. Rousseau condemned the culture of his age but looked forward
to a ``natural culture'' proceeding from life itself. Lessing was repelled
by both rationalism and orthodoxy and hoped for ``a third
age,'' ``the time of the new, eternal Gospel.'' And Kant saw clearly that
the finished works of men --- the complete forms of belief and
systems of thought, the existing states --- easily become dead treasures and
hindrances to development, and his striving was to set free the
forces that had in their time produced these works, so that new work
might become possible.
In the nineteenth century both Romantics and positivists were at times
inclined to think that ``the third kingdom'' was immediately
at hand, if it was not already in our midst. One thought
that one had acknowledged what was valuable in the culture of earlier ages and
made it fruitful in new forms. But it was nevertheless an essential
moment for these tendencies that there was still a resistance
to be overcome. Hegel expressly laid weight on the significance of negations and
oppositions; without passing through a purgatory
one could not enter the paradise of ``higher unity.''
This did not shake his optimism, which reveals itself in a characteristic
manner in his conception of the tragic (in
art as in life); this consisted for him in a conflict between
two powers each in itself justified, which then precisely through such
conflict received their proper limitation. The tragic means in
Hegel not catastrophe. For Comte there was indeed still resistance to be
overcome from theological and metaphysical tendencies, but the positive
stage, which was to become the definitive one, had on most points
already been reached, and the stage where both science received its full due
and the religion of humanity its full unfolding was not far off.
And although Herbert Spencer distinguished between evolution and progress
(after having from the first made the two concepts one),
he retained the belief that through division (differentiation)
as an intermediate stage new, ordered wholes were to form.
The difference between the Romantics and the positivists consisted on this
point especially in this, that the Romantics thought the new was already present
in the old, if only one opened one's eyes, whereas the positivists
placed the new in greater opposition to the old, although it
% --- p. 154 ---
\opage{154}brought full equivalence for this. On both sides there prevailed a
confident mood toward the problem that the spiritual fathers of the nineteenth century
in the preceding century had left behind, --- --- namely
the preservation of the closedness and instinctive
energy of the primitive culture under advancing and restless inquiry and the carried-through
division of labor. Only a single voice sounded in the first half
of the century in the opposite direction, but it was for the time being little heard.
Arthur Schopenhauer sought in his work ``Welt als Wille und Vorstellung''
(1819) to show what deep irrationality manifests itself when
we open our eyes to all the obstacles and inhibitions that every tendency
to development meets, and above all when we turn our eyes
to the deep, insatiable craving of all living things to exist at any
price, and when we at the same time in compassion make ourselves one with the craving
that other beings feel just as we ourselves do. It was a grating sound that
for a time only was drowned out by the harmony orchestra of Romanticism and positivism.
It later gained a hearing, and it
even became the occasion for the word ``pessimism'' now being used to designate
a whole view of life, whereas before it had been used only
(in English literature) in a more limited sense. It may be said to
be characteristic of the course of development in the nineteenth century that
this expression has gradually gained currency. In the year 1878
it was recognized by the French Academy, whereas the opposing
word ``optimism,'' which was formed to designate Leibniz's bright view
of existence, was recognized by the Academy as early as 1762. When Schopenhauer,
and later (1869) in his footsteps Eduard v. Hartmann,
could win so much attention for their systematization of
pessimism, it must be because the general life of mood
was prepared in that direction by the way of experience itself. Political and
social conditions worked here in a decisive manner. The time after the end of the
Napoleonic wars was in many respects an empty and oppressive
time; a greatness had vanished; small men stepped into
his place; broken promises and disappointed expectations aroused resentment
and weariness. It was the time of Leopardi, Byron and Heine. A corresponding
period came after 1848, after the popular risings had been subdued, and
after revolutionary idealism had proved powerless against
an ever watchful reaction. And for Germany it was so far
from being the case that the founding of the new Empire after the victorious war with France
brought a feeling of happiness with it that precisely the seventies in that country became a
time of pessimistic moods. Bismarck once asked in the
German Reichstag whether any of the gentlemen had ever seen a contented
German. Setting aside such moods of the time, there can
% --- p. 155 ---
\opage{155}be pointed to various grounds which explain why the nineteenth century
has given the word pessimism the right of citizenship, whereas it was the eighteenth century
that established the word optimism.

It was a manly faith that in the first half of the century was nourished
by Romantics and positivists, that a harmony could be reached
in spite of all doubt, all contradictions and all obstacles. But it became clear on
closer investigation that there was a difficult point in their
grounding of this faith. If we look more closely at the threefold structure
in all development that Hegel, Comte and Spencer all assumed, then
the transition from the second to the third member is not so certain or necessary
as the transition from the first to the second. One can come from
faith to doubt without through doubt reaching a higher form of
faith. A concentrated and uniform state can be succeeded by a differentiated
state, without the dividedness afterwards coming to be an intermediate stage
to a higher kind of concentration. The advancing specialization of science
is not favorable to a large and unified view of existence.
In social life the division of labor threatens to lead to dissolution
or at least to one-sidedness and isolation. It is, after all, also out in
nature far from being the case that there are always favorable conditions for the formation
of totalities in which the scattered elements are united into unified action.
There can, moreover, be progress in particular domains and in particular
respects without life as a whole therefore making progress.
And it is not always that social and technical progress in reality
means true and lasting goods for all individuals. It
could finally be thought that for human culture the law held,
as for physical processes, that the energy gradually distributes itself
and an equilibrium arises which makes the release of energy impossible; the result
would then be dullness, in the end spiritual death. Such possibilities
one must face, and it was no wonder that pessimistic
currents came when they began to dawn on consciousness.
One understands why Hamlet figures are so frequent in the literature of the nineteenth
century, although they do not have the greatness that Shakespeare's
genius gave the figure after which the type is named.

It is the honor of the nineteenth century that it has not pushed back such
thoughts, although they threatened to burst the harmony
with which the century began its course. In the work of thought and
imagination they may for a time recede, as Prospero
in ``The Tempest'' is so absorbed in his visions that he forgets that Caliban
is still about. One does not despair because Caliban is there,
and because he cannot be converted at such a speed as happens in
Shakespeare. And the great thoughts which Romanticism and positivism each
% --- p. 156 ---
\opage{156}in its own way shaped do not lose their value because ``the higher
unity'' has not yet revealed itself. Who says that it must
be so near? And who says that we can construct it in advance?
In no domain can one derive the special character of a whole
from the elements one knows only in their separate existence.
But for that reason one cannot in advance deny the possibility
that a new building can be erected from the elements.

It would be wrong to call the nineteenth century the age
of pessimism. It is too many-sided for that. If the nineteenth century
has in the foregoing presentation rightly been characterized as the age of confirmation
by experience, then it is thereby given how a son of
this century will stand toward the misgivings that it itself
has raised. There is no other way out than this: in life to go on
struggling to overcome the scattered and the disharmonious, and in
thought to go on inquiring in order to expand experience and to see
whether the expanded experience --- even if it should bring new,
unforeseen problems --- does not lead to a solution of the problems at which we now
stop, or perhaps to insight into their groundlessness. We can retain
faith in a third kingdom, even if it is not so near or
so easy to describe as has been thought. The best and the most faithful
in the nineteenth century have lived and worked in such a faith.
